item_001.title_short: Anon./Lollianus, Greek novel papyri (Ninus fr. A–D; + Sesonchosis)
item_001.ru_found: REFUTES the "unknown" status. T. I. Kuznetsova, «Роман о Нине и другие папирусные отрывки греческого романа», in «Античный роман» (Moscow: Nauka, 1969), pp. 107–131. It was online at philology.ru/literature3/kuznetsova-69.htm, which is now offline; I read the 2021 Wayback snapshot. It contains Russian translations of three pieces: (1) Ninus A II 1 – A IV 13, Ninus's whole speech to Derkeia, about 60 lines and roughly a quarter of the Ninus text; (2) Metiochus and Parthenope fr. A, lines 6–29, Metiochus's speech on Eros; (3) Calligone fr. II, lines 33–42. It also has one sentence from Ninus B III 32. The rest of Ninus (A IV 26 – A V 38, B II–III) and Chione, Herpyllis and the Sesonchosis papyrus are only paraphrased. Kuznetsova says explicitly that no Russian translations existed. Other Russian sources discuss or summarise the fragments without translating them: История греческой литературы vol. 3 (1960) ch. XII.7, «Античные писатели: Словарь» (1999), and the Russian translation of Licht's «Сексуальная жизнь в Древней Греции» (I did not check it for quotations). Searches that found no other translation: ru.wikipedia («Роман о Нине», «Греческий роман», Метиох, Лоллиан); CyberLeninka API (Роман о Нине, папирусные фрагменты греческого романа, Лоллиан Финикийские, Сесонхосис, Иолай, among others); Google («Метиох и Парфенопа», «Роман о Нине» перевод, «романом о Нине»). Ladynin 2015 (CyberLeninka) translates passages of the Alexander Romance and scholia about Sesonchosis, not the papyri. Levinskaya 2010/2016 deal only with P.Oxy. 4762. I found no Russian translation of Sesonchosis, Iolaus, Lollianus' Phoinikika, Antheia, Daulis or Tinouphis. Gaps: Google, Yandex and DuckDuckGo started blocking automated searches, so post-1969 anthologies (e.g. «Античная литература. Греция. Антология», 1989) and dissertations were not checked. A Vestnik drevnei istorii 2020 no. 3 conference report that mentions the Ninus novel could not be opened.
item_001.en_found: Confirmed full. Stephens & Winkler, Ancient Greek Novels: The Fragments (Princeton UP, 1995) gives text plus facing English translation of every fragment: Ninos, Metiochos and Parthenope, Sesonchosis, Kalligone, Antheia, Chione, Lollianus' Phoinikika, Iolaos, Daulis, Tinouphis and others. Sources: Project MUSE table of contents (muse.jhu.edu/book/34147) and BMCR 1995.12.26 ("translations of all the fragments"). Also Reardon (ed.), Collected Ancient Greek Novels (Univ. of California Press, 1989; 2nd ed. 2008); per the archive.org contents note, its "Fragments" section is translated by Gerald N. Sandy and B. P. Reardon and includes Ninus. Also Hägg & Utas, The Virgin and Her Lover (Brill, 2003): the Greek and Persian Metiochus–Parthenope material in English.
item_001.other_found: Spanish, full: M. P. López Martínez, Fragmentos papiráceos de novela griega (Universidad de Alicante, 1998; 505 pp., Greek and Spanish), per the Open Library record. Italian: Q. Cataudella (ed.), Il romanzo antico greco e latino (Sansoni, 1958; repr. 1973) includes "Il romanzo di Nino" in Italian (Open Library contents note). German, not verified: R. Kussl, Papyrusfragmente griechischer Romane (Classica Monacensia 2, 1991) is a study of selected fragments, and I did not confirm whether it translates them; A. Henrichs, Die Phoinikika des Lollianos (Bonn, 1972) is the standard edition, translation not confirmed; B. Kytzler, Im Reich des Eros (1983/2001) is a "sämtliche Romane" anthology, but whether it includes the fragments is unconfirmed. French: none found (not searched exhaustively).
item_001.source_text: The candidate's source claim is wrong. papyri.info is not an open text source for these fragments. DDbDP covers documentary papyri only. The DCLP records, CC BY 3.0 in the GitHub papyri/idp.data repository, are metadata only: their edition sections are empty. This applies to Ninus TM 63069 (P.Berol. 6926 + P.Gen. inv. 100, LDAB 2616), PSI XIII 1305, O.Edfou 306, Metiochus P.Oxy. 435, and Sesonchosis P.Oxy. 1826, 2466 and 3319. Public-domain texts: U. Wilcken, Hermes 28 (1893) 161–193, the first edition of Ninus A–B; B. Lavagnini, Eroticorum Graecorum fragmenta papyracea (Teubner, 1922; public domain in the US); and Grenfell–Hunt's P.Oxy. III 435 (1903), XI 1368 (1915, Lollianus) and XV 1826 (1922, Sesonchosis). I did not find a verified scan URL for Wilcken or Lavagnini on archive.org. Still in copyright: Stephens–Winkler 1995 (the standard modern edition), López Martínez 1998, Kussl 1991, Henrichs 1972, P.Gen. II 85 (1986), ZPE 6 (1970), and P.Oxy. 2466 (1962), 3010 (Iolaus, 1974) and 3319 (1980). Ninus fragments C–D and most of Sesonchosis therefore depend on modern, copyrighted editions.
item_001.research_yield: Ninus and Sesonchosis set beside the Alexander Romance: the young conqueror-king, Ninus's elephant campaign in Armenia, Alexander as the "new Sesonchosis". Also: Hellenistic historical romance, the Metiochus–Vāmiq Persian afterlife, and a study of AI translation of gappy papyri. Kuznetsova 1969 gives a Russian baseline to cite.
item_001.recommendation: Keep, but correct the record: Russian has excerpts only (Kuznetsova 1969, about a quarter of Ninus), there is a full Spanish translation, and the source is not on papyri.info. Best first unit: the first complete Russian Ninus (fragments A–D, plus O.Edfou 306 if it is confirmed as Ninus), with a precise apparatus marking text versus supplement, then the Sesonchosis papyri as an Alexander-Romance companion piece.

item_002.ru_found: REFUTED. There is a complete Russian translation of all 20 Homilies, translated directly from the Greek. The book: «Климентины. Гомилии. Краткое изложение проповедей апостола Петра в его странствиях» / пер. с древнегреч. Е. Б. Смагиной; сопровод. статьи Е. Б. Смагиной, Д. В. Щедровицкого. Москва: Теревинф; Sapienti Sat, 2026 (copyright page says ©2025). 384 pp. ISBN 978-5-4212-0788-7 (Теревинф) and 978-5-4499-5366-7 (Sapienti Sat). Approved by the academic council of the Institute of Oriental Studies, Russian Academy of Sciences (ИВ РАН). Reviewed by М. Г. Селезнев and Г. Г. Ястребов. The subtitle is a rendering of the manuscripts' own title (ἐπιτομή), not a sign of an abridgement. I checked the publisher's own front-matter PDF. Its contents list Гомилия 1 to Гомилия 20 on pp. 26–308 with translator's notes. The proposed pilot unit, Hom. 12–14, is on pp. 185–222. Appendix: Послание Петра к Иакову, p. 361. Name index: p. 365. The introduction says the translation follows Rehm's GCS edition, checked against Dressel 1853 and Migne PG 2. The annotation says «Перевод с древнегреческого на русский язык выполнен впервые». Sources: https://terevinf.com/books/religiozno-istoricheskaya-literatura/klimentiny-gomilii-kratkoe-izlozhenie-propovedey-apostola-petra-v-ego-stranstviyakh/ ; front matter and fragment PDFs https://terevinf.com/upload/fragmenty/Klimentiny_frag.pdf and https://terevinf.com/upload/fragmenty/Klimentiny_sod.pdf ; an e-book listing at https://e-univers.ru/catalog/t0017045/ . Smagina also gave a talk on the Homilies at ИВ РАН on 28.02.2024, listed in her 2025 IMLI doctoral autoreferat. Before this book I found only encyclopedia summaries in Russian: Лопухин, Православная богословская энциклопедия т. XI, «Климентины»; ПЭ; Мень's Библиологический словарь. Russian Wikipedia lists no translation. Searches: 3 Russian web searches completed, then the session's web-search budget ran out. After that I fetched the publisher catalogue, the PDFs, e-univers and Bing directly. The finding comes from the book's own front matter, so it is decisive.
item_002.en_found: Complete and in the public domain: Thomas Smith, Peter Peterson and James Donaldson, 'Pseudo-Clementine Literature', Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8 (1886; repr. 1903, 1978). Peterson did Hom. VI–XII and Donaldson did Hom. XIII–XX. Online at newadvent.org, ccel.org/ccel/schaff/anf08, en.wikisource and EWTN. Selections: Irmscher in Hennecke–Schneemelcher, NT Apocrypha II (1965; 1992); J. K. Elliott, The Apocryphal NT (1993), pp. 431–38. Syriac-version translations: F. S. Jones (Brepols 2014) and J. G. Gebhardt (2014); these cover the Syriac Recognitions and parts of the Homilies. Accordance sells a tagged Greek-English edition. Amazon lists a 'Quadrilingual Edition' (Greek-Latin-Syriac-English, Aug. 2025, ISBN 9798298132084); I have not checked it. Sources: nasscal.com e-Clavis 'Pseudo-Clementines'; ewtn.com library; accordancebible.com. 2 English web searches completed; the e-Clavis bibliography was fetched directly.
item_002.other_found: French: A. Siouville, Les Homélies clémentines (Rieder, 1933), full. P. Geoltrain et al., 'Roman pseudo-clémentin', Écrits apocryphes chrétiens II (Pléiade, Gallimard 2005), pp. 1173–2003, from Rehm's text. German: J. Wehnert, Pseudoklementinische Homilien: Einführung und Übersetzung (Kommentare zur apokryphen Literatur 1/1, V&R 2010), full. Also Wehnert, Der Klemensroman (V&R 2015). Selections in Irmscher–Strecker, NTApo II (5th ed. 1989). Italian: selections in M. Erbetta, Gli apocrifi del NT II (Marietti), pp. 211–36. I did not verify whether a full Italian translation of the Homilies exists. Norwegian: Hvalvik and Sandnes, 'Pseudo-Klemens homilier', in Tidligkristne apokryfer (Oslo 2011), pp. 257–94. Spanish: none found. Source for the list: the nasscal e-Clavis bibliography.
item_002.source_text: Public-domain Greek texts. A. R. M. Dressel, Clementis Romani quae feruntur Homiliae viginti nunc primum integrae (Göttingen 1853); archive.org identifiers clementisromani00igoog, clementisromani01igoog, clementisromaniq0000clem. P. de Lagarde, Clementina (Leipzig 1865); archive.org clementina00lagagoog. Migne, PG 2 (Dressel's text). The standard critical edition is B. Rehm and J. Irmscher, Die Pseudoklementinen I: Homilien, GCS 42 (Akademie-Verlag 1953; 2nd ed. 1969; 3rd ed. by G. Strecker 1992; now De Gruyter). It is in copyright.
item_002.research_yield: Low for Neoscholia now. A full scholarly Russian translation (Smagina 2026) and full English and German ones exist. Remaining options: a review article on Smagina's translation, or Homilies–Recognitiones comparisons. The Latin Recognitiones' Russian status is unverified and could be a better target.
item_002.recommendation: Drop it. The Homilies, including the pilot unit Hom. XII–XIV, came out in full in Russian in 2026 (Smagina, Terevinf/ИВ РАН), and English (ANF 8) has been complete since 1886. If the Clementine novel stays of interest, check the Russian status of Rufinus's Latin Recognitiones instead, especially the recognition books VII–IX.

item_003.title_short: Prodromos, Rhodanthe and Dosikles + Manasses, Aristandros and Kallithea (fragments)
item_003.ru_found: No Russian translation of either work, full or partial, was found. Book I of Rhodanthe and the Manasses fragments have none either. What was checked: (1) WebSearch for «Роданфа и Досикл» перевод, «Феодор Продром роман Роданфа русский перевод» and «Аристандр и Каллифея» Манассия перевод. These returned only encyclopedia and wiki entries. The session's WebSearch budget (200) then ran out, after 3 Russian and 1 English searches. (2) ru.wikipedia articles: Роданфа и Досикл, Аристандр и Каллифея, Феодор Продром, Константин Манассия, Византийский роман, Повесть о Дросилле и Харикле. None lists a Russian translation. A ru.wiki full-text search for «Роданфа» gives only 4 articles, none of them a translation. (3) Православная энциклопедия, «Константин Манасси» (т. 37, В.Ю. Жаркая), pravenc.ru/text/2057092.html: the bibliography lists Mazal 1967 and no Russian translation of the novel. (4) «Памятники византийской литературы IX–XIV вв.» (М.: Наука, 1969, ред. Л.А. Фрейберг). Its Prodromos section (facetia.ru/node/4800) has the speech on Alexios Aristenos, letters and the schedos «О мыши». It contains no part of the novel, and the introduction only describes Rhodanthe and Aristandros. I could not verify the full table of contents for a possible Manasses item. (5) The vostlit.info author indexes have no Prodromos, Manasses or Eugenianos entries. (6) Only scholarly interest turned up, for example П.А. Королева (МГУ), «Фольклорные мотивы в романе Константина Манасси „Аристандр и Каллифея“», Ломоносов-2021 student paper. Soviet surveys (Фрейберг–Попова 1978; Полякова 1979) discuss both novels and may quote short passages; this was not verified. The search catalogues of the RSL and НЭБ could not be used: НЭБ blocks foreign IPs. Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google Scholar and Yandex blocked automated queries or returned unrelated results. Only Eugenianos (Петровский, ЛП 1969) and Makrembolites (Полякова–Феленковская 1965) exist in Russian.
item_003.en_found: E. Jeffreys, Four Byzantine Novels: Theodore Prodromos, Rhodanthe and Dosikles; Eumathios Makrembolites, Hysmine and Hysminias; Constantine Manasses, Aristandros and Kallithea; Niketas Eugenianos, Drosilla and Charikles (Liverpool University Press 2012, Translated Texts for Byzantinists 1). Confirmed by Open Library (OL21249802W) and bookseller listings. It translates Rhodanthe in full and all of the Manasses fragments.
item_003.other_found: German: K. Plepelits, Theodoros Prodromos, Rhodanthe und Dosikles, eingeleitet, übersetzt und erläutert (Stuttgart: Hiersemann 1996), confirmed in the DNB and BnF catalogues. Italian: F. Conca, Il romanzo bizantino del XII secolo: Teodoro Prodromo, Niceta Eugeniano, Eustazio Macrembolita, Costantino Manasse (Torino: UTET 1994, reprinted 1997; Greek and Italian), which includes both works; confirmed in Open Library and BnF. French: P.-F. Godard de Beauchamps, Les amours de Rhodante et de Dosiclès (1746, a free rendering, reprinted 1786 and 1797), and an anonymous 'traduction nouvelle' (Paris: Merlin 1823, ed. A. Trognon, with Dio's Euboicus; facsimile Adamant 2001); confirmed in BnF. Modern Greek: Kostas Poulos, Rodanthi kai Dosiklis (Athens: Nea Synora 1996); confirmed in BnF. Manasses: the edition with reconstruction is O. Mazal, Der Roman des Konstantinos Manasses (Graz/Wien 1967; DNB). I did not confirm whether it includes a German translation. Apart from Jeffreys and Conca, I found no other complete modern translation of the Manasses fragments.
item_003.source_text: Public domain: R. Hercher, Erotici Scriptores Graeci, vol. II (Leipzig: Teubner 1858/59). Its title page lists Chariton, Eustathius Macrembolites, Theodorus Prodromus, Nicetas Eugenianus and Constantinus Manasses (Manasses' Amatoria in 9 books, after Boissonade). Scans with OCR: https://archive.org/details/erotiknlognsyng00hercgoog and https://archive.org/details/erotiknlognsyng02hercgoog. Hercher probably prints only the Rhodonia (Macarius Chrysocephalus) excerpts. The extra 346 lines from Vindob. phil. gr. 306 and Monac. gr. 281 probably need Mazal 1967; I did not check this. Standard modern editions, in copyright: M. Marcovich, Theodori Prodromi De Rhodanthes et Dosiclis amoribus libri IX (Stuttgart/Leipzig: Teubner 1992); O. Mazal 1967 (Wiener Byzantinistische Studien 4) for Manasses; Conca 1994 (Greek text).
item_003.research_yield: Would complete the Russian set of Komnenian novels. Possible articles: Prodromos' rewriting of Heliodorus; how the novel was performed at court; Manasses' fragments as a gnomic anthology (Rhodonia) and how the plot is reconstructed; how Russian scholarship received the Byzantine novel (Полякова). Little direct Alexander material.
item_003.recommendation: Keep as a secondary candidate. The only gap is Russian: English, German, Italian, French and Modern Greek translations exist, and the work is medieval, not ancient. Best first unit: Rhodanthe Book I (c. 500 trimeters, Hercher's PD text checked against Marcovich), followed by the Manasses fragments.

item_004.title_short: Anonymous ummânū, Mesopotamian cuneiform commentaries (literary section: Ludlul, Theodicy, Enūma eliš, Lugale)
item_004.ru_found: For the proposed literary unit I found no Russian translation. That covers the commentaries on Ludlul (K.3291), the Theodicy (BM 66882+), Enūma eliš Comm. I and II, and Lugale. For the genre as a whole, Russian has scattered excerpts. (1) V. V. Emelyanov, "Problemy izucheniya vavilonskoi germenevtiki", Voprosy filosofii 2017 no. 8, pp. 155–165 (academia.edu/34034265). It gives Russian versions of about 11 example glosses, all omen, medical, hemerological or Marduk's-Address commentaries cited from Gabbay 2016 and Frahm 2011. None comes from the literary unit. (2) Emelyanov, Nippurskii kalendar' i rannyaya istoriya Zodiaka (St Petersburg 1999), which has a section on cuneiform commentaries on the zodiacal constellations. He has further calendar-commentary articles, e.g. Antropologicheskii forum 2017 and Etnografiya 2021. (3) E. N. Duvakin and R. M. Nurullin, "Lev na lune", Indoevropeiskoe yazykoznanie i klassicheskaya filologiya 2022: short excerpts from KAR 307 and the Marduk's Address commentary. Searches that returned nothing for the unit: Google in Russian ("клинописные комментарии"; Энума элиш + комментарий + имена Мардука; "Вавилонская теодицея" + комментарий; Лудлул + древний комментарий; Лугаль-е/Лугале + комментарий; Емельянов + "пояснительные тексты"; вавилонская герменевтика). Also CyberLeninka API queries ("мукаллимту", "Лудлул бел немеки" and "Лудлул" each returned 0; "пятьдесят имен Мардука", "аккадские комментарии", "месопотамская экзегетика", "Энума элиш перевод"). Russian translations of the base texts exist (Afanas'eva, Dyakonov and others) but not of the commentaries. Not checked: elibrary.ru full text and RSL/NLR catalogues.
item_004.en_found: Across all 882 catalogue entries English coverage is partial, as the colleague says. But the proposed pilot unit is almost entirely in English already. Ludlul commentary (CCP 1.3, K.3291): full English translation by A. Lenzi (CCP, 2015, revised by Jiménez; ccp.yale.edu/P394923). Earlier editions: Lambert, BWL 1960, pp. 31–56; Annus & Lenzi 2010 (SAACT 7, as MS G); Oshima 2014, pp. 376–438. Theodicy commentary (CCP 1.4, BM 66882+): full English by E. Jiménez (CCP, 2017; ccp.yale.edu/P404917). Earlier: Lambert 1960, pp. 63–89, and Oshima 2014, pp. 439–464. Lugale (CCP 1.2, BM 51213+): English by M. Frazer (CCP, 2017; P461247). The commentary column there is almost entirely lost. Enūma eliš Comm. I (on Tablets I–VII; CCP 1.1.A.a–h): full edition with English translation in E. Frahm & E. Jiménez, "Myth, Ritual, and Interpretation", HeBAI 4/3 (2015), pp. 293–343 (DOI 10.1628/219222715X14507102280856). Lambert, Babylonian Creation Myths (2013), gives it only in transliteration. The one gap is Enūma eliš Comm. II, the sign-by-sign commentary on the Tablet VII names (CCP 1.1.B.a–b; Rm.366+, Sm.11+). Lambert 2013, pp. 139–142 gives transliteration only, with discussion on pp. 147–168. Frahm 2011 and Seri 2006 discuss it in part. I found no full English translation of it.
item_004.other_found: French: J. Bottéro, "Les noms de Marduk, l'écriture et la 'logique' en Mésopotamie ancienne", in the Finkelstein memorial volume (1977). CCP lists it as an edition of Enūma eliš Comm. II. Also T. Genty, Les commentaires dans les textes cunéiformes assyro-babyloniens (MA thesis, 2010), pp. 659–713. CCP lists it as an edition of Comm. II. Older French: R. Labat, Commentaires assyro-babyloniens sur les présages (1933), pp. 102–109, which covers the Theodicy commentary. German: discussion and excerpts in Frahm 2011 (GMTR 5, English) and scattered articles. I found no German, Italian or Spanish translation of the corpus.
item_004.source_text: The best open source is the CCP online editions (transliteration and English translation), licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 per ccp.yale.edu/citation-guidelines (verified). These cover Ludlul (P394923), the Theodicy (P404917) and Lugale (P461247). The standard print editions are all in copyright: Lambert, BWL 1960; Lambert, Babylonian Creation Myths 2013 (Eisenbrauns); Oshima 2014 (Mohr Siebeck); Frahm & Jiménez 2015 (HeBAI, Mohr Siebeck). The Enūma eliš Comm. II survives in public-domain cuneiform copies (II R 31 no. 2; V R 21 nos. 3–4; King, STC II 1902, pp. li–lx). Its only modern full transliteration is Lambert 2013, which is in copyright. Any Russian translation adapted from the CCP English must itself be released CC BY-SA.
item_004.research_yield: First Russian translation of Babylonian exegesis. Articles could compare it with Greek scholia and etymology (Cratylus, Stoic etymology, Alexandrian glossography). Other topics: Berossus's scholarly setting, notarikon-type sign-splitting against later midrash, and how commentators read the Theodicy and Ludlul. One more: Marduk's names as theology through writing.
item_004.recommendation: Keep only as a Russian-first item and drop the "no English translation" angle. Four of the five pilot pieces have full English translations, three of them free under CC BY-SA. Akkadian is also outside the editor's Greek and Latin strengths. Best first unit: the Theodicy and Ludlul commentaries (CCP 1.4 and 1.3, about 100 lines together) in Russian, from the CC BY-SA CCP editions, with the Enūma eliš Comm. II (no English) as a possible later expert-checked addition.

item_005.title_short: Babylonian Astronomical Diaries (historical sections) + BCHP chronicles (Alexander years 333–322 BCE)
item_005.ru_found:
No Russian translation of the corpus, of any whole chronicle, or of the pilot unit was found. These were checked:
(1) Turaev, История Древнего Востока, vol. II, ch. "Последние века Вавилона" (1913; Wikisource text). It has a Russian rendering of the historical section of the diary for SE 37/38 (274/3 BCE): the king going to Sardis, 20 elephants from the satrap of Bactria, famine and disease. It also gives the full Antiochus I Borsippa Cylinder and the Laodice land-grant ("Lehmann") text. These are real 19th/20th-c. excerpts, but none falls in the Alexander unit.
(2) Russian scholarship cites Sachs–Hunger and BCHP directly, giving only one-line paraphrases or translations: Стоянов 2016 (Via in tempore, diary −322 on Peithon's expedition); Берзон 2015 (ПИФК, king-list and diary lines); Сивкина & Кривощекова 2023 (BCHP 3, 5–9 cited, no translations in the bibliography); Балахванцев, doctoral dissertation (ИВ РАН 2018), cites Sachs–Hunger only, with no Russian translation listed; Смирнов, Государство Селевка I (2013), whose appendix holds Greek inscriptions only.
(3) ru.wikipedia has no article on the diaries. The "Битва при Гавгамелах" and "Вавилонская война" articles mention the diaries and chronicles with no translation. CyberLeninka API, ru.wikipedia full-text and vostlit searches found nothing more.
Not checked: Хрестоматия по истории Древнего Востока (1980), История Древнего Востока. Тексты и документы (2002), Дандамаев 1985 (possible Gaugamela quote). The web-search quota ran out.
item_005.en_found:
Confirmed full, several times over.
- Sachs & Hunger, Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia I–III (Vienna 1988–96): transliteration and English translation. It is put online at attalus.org/docs/diaries.html, taken from the Berlin Ancient Astronomy Project / Edition Topoi digitisation. That covers −333, −332, −330, −329, −328, −324, −322 ("the king died"), −321 and later years.
- Grayson, Assyrian and Babylonian Chronicles (1975), ABC 8, 10, 11, etc.
- Glassner, Mesopotamian Chronicles (SBL WAW 19, 2004), CM 29, 30, 32, 35.
- BCHP 1–20 in English on livius.org (all rights reserved).
- Since the sweep: van der Spek, Finkel, Pirngruber & Stevens, Babylonian Chronographic Texts from the Hellenistic Period (SBL WAW 44, 2025, 1,173 pp.). It gives new transliterations and translations of all the chronicles and the historical sections of the diaries, plus king lists and the Antiochus Cylinder. It is commercial, not open access.
So the pilot unit specifically is fully translated into English.
item_005.other_found:
- French: Glassner, Chroniques mésopotamiennes (1993) has the Alexander, Diadochi, Antiochus I/Sin-temple and Seleucus III chronicles (CM 29, 30, 32, 35), per the en.wikipedia concordance. P. Bernard (BCH 114, 1990) discusses the Alexander-era diary passages, citing Sachs–Hunger. Whether he gives French renderings was not checked.
- Italian: Del Monte, Testi dalla Babilonia ellenistica I (Pisa 1997), a chronographic selection. Not re-verified online; not on archive.org.
- German: Kugler, Sternkunde und Sterndienst in Babel (1907–24, public domain on archive.org) treats Seleucid-era astronomical texts. Historical-section coverage not checked.
No Spanish translation was found.
item_005.source_text:
The standard editions are under copyright:
- Sachs & Hunger, ADART I–III (Austrian Academy of Sciences, 1988–96). An archive.org item "hunger-adart" carries a Public Domain mark, but that label is almost certainly wrong and should not be relied on.
- BCHP: van der Spek et al., SBL WAW 44 (2025), print and eBook at about $100.
- Grayson, ABC (1975).
The livius.org BCHP texts say "All rights reserved". The attalus/Edition Topoi English diaries state no licence, and the Edition Topoi repository currently returns a database error.
The best open source is Oracc ADsD (oracc.museum.upenn.edu/adsd/adart1/corpus), listed on en.wikipedia, with lemmatised transliterations of ADART. Oracc projects are normally CC BY-SA, but neither the licence nor the presence of translations could be checked today: the server was unreachable.
Public-domain pieces:
- Turaev's Russian excerpts (1913/1935).
- Sidney Smith, Babylonian Historical Texts (1924), probably the first edition of the Diadochi Chronicle. Unverified; not found on archive.org.
Practical route: translate from the Oracc transliterations and cite the BCHP 2025 readings.
item_005.research_yield: Babylonian view of Gaugamela and Alexander's entry into Babylon against Arrian, Curtius and Diodorus; Alexander's exact death date against Romance and Liber de morte accounts; Diadochi Chronicle and Diodorus XVIII–XIX chronology; Babylonian terms for Macedonian kingship.
item_005.recommendation: Keep, at lower priority (3), as a Russian-only candidate. English is fully covered (Sachs–Hunger, Grayson, Glassner, livius, and the new BCHP 2025 volume), so there is no first-ever English. Akkadian is also outside the editor's Greek/Latin strength. Best first unit: the historical sections of diaries −330 (Gaugamela, entry into Babylon) and −322 (Alexander's death) plus BCHP 1 and BCHP 3, translated into Russian from the Oracc/ADART transliterations with commentary against the Greek and Latin historians.

item_006.title_short: Anon., Akkadian literary 'prophecies' (Dynastic Prophecy BM 40623 + Uruk Prophecy)
item_006.ru_found: I found no scholarly Russian translation of any of the five texts (Dynastic, Uruk, Marduk, Šulgi, Text A), whole or partial. The only Russian text found is about 12 lines of the Marduk Prophecy (the Esagil passage, starting «Царь в Вавилоне возвысится; в моём городе Вавилоне...»). They are quoted in Zecharia Sitchin's «Боги Армагеддона», ch. 7, a Russian translation of his fringe book The End of Days (2007). The lines were translated from English, not from Akkadian (https://history.wikireading.ru/13299). Russian Wikipedia only mentions the texts: «Династическое пророчество» in the article «Набонид», and «Пророчество Мардука» in «Vaticinium ex eventu». Afanasyeva's chapter on Akkadian literature in История всемирной литературы, vol. 1 (1983, feb-web.ru) does not discuss these texts. Searches: 4 Russian web searches (Династическое пророчество; Пророчество Мардука; Урукское пророчество / Пророчество Шульги; аккадские литературные пророчества ex eventu). CyberLeninka API (7 queries): no hits on the texts. Full-text checks of Акимов 2016, Мурашко 2014, Карева 2015, Юревич 2007, Ладынин 2015 and Новиков & Анохин 2015 found nothing. Not checked, because the search budget ran out: Клочков, «Духовная культура Вавилонии» (1983), the most likely place for Russian excerpts; «Когда Ану сотворил небо» (2000); Хрестоматия по истории Древнего Востока (1980); История Древнего Востока. Тексты и документы (2002). Check these by hand before publishing.
item_006.en_found: Full English translations exist, several of them. Dynastic Prophecy: Grayson, BHLT (1975), first edition with translation; R.J. van der Spek's translation is free online at Livius (livius.org/sources/content/mesopotamian-chronicles-content/dynastic-prophecy/), along with his article 'Darius III, Alexander the Great and Babylonian scholarship' (2003). Uruk Prophecy: Hunger and Kaufman, 'A New Akkadian Prophecy Text', JAOS 95 (1975) 371-375; also 'The Uruk Prophecy: a New Assessment', JANER 25.1 (2025). Marduk and Šulgi Prophecies: Longman, Fictional Akkadian Autobiography (1991); Foster, Before the Muses (2005); a master's thesis edition of the Marduk Prophecy on academia.edu; an academia.edu study of the Šulgi Prophecy. Text A: Biggs in ANET, 3rd ed. (1969). All five together: Neujahr, Predicting the Past (2012). Context of Scripture vol. 1 (Longman) probably has them too; not re-verified.
item_006.other_found: French: a Brepols journal article, « Après lui un roi se lèvera » : les prédictions historiques dans la Prophétie d'Uruk et la Prophétie dynastique (doi 10.1484/J.SEC.5.116793). I could not see whether it translates the texts in full. German: Borger, BiOr 28 (1971), for the Marduk and Šulgi Prophecies; Hunger's German edition of the Uruk tablet; TUAT. These German items are not re-verified. I found no Italian or Spanish translation; I did not search for one exhaustively.
item_006.source_text: No public-domain or openly licensed edition exists. All standard editions are in copyright: Grayson, BHLT (University of Toronto Press, 1975); Hunger and Kaufman, JAOS 1975; Borger 1971; Neujahr 2012 (Brown Judaic Studies / SBL); the 2025 JANER Uruk edition. The tablets are publicly viewable: BM 40623 is in the British Museum collection online (image licence believed to be CC BY-NC-SA, not re-verified), and Livius hosts photos. In practice a translation would have to work from the published transliterations. The words are ancient, but the restorations, which are the disputed part, are editorial. Treat Neujahr 2012 and Grayson 1975 as the base and cite them.
item_006.research_yield: Babylonian ex eventu view of Darius III and Alexander (van der Spek's reading of Dynastic Prophecy col. iii). Comparisons with the Oracle of the Potter, the Demotic Chronicle, Nectanebo in the Alexander Romance, and Daniel 8/11. Russian article on Babylonian anti-Macedonian prophecy (ВДИ/Аристей).
item_006.recommendation: Keep, but lower to priority 3. The Russian gap is real, since the only Russian text is about 12 lines in Sitchin's fringe book, but English is full and freely available online. The source is Akkadian, which the editor cannot check as well as Greek or Latin, and no edition is public domain. Best first unit: the complete Dynastic Prophecy (BM 40623), translated from Grayson/Neujahr with van der Spek's alternatives, with an Assyriologist reviewer. Add the Uruk Prophecy next.

item_007.ru_found: No Russian translation of any EAE tablet was found, whether complete or as excerpts. Checks made: (1) ru.wikipedia 'Энума Ану Энлиль' cites only secondary and pop works (Брoль; Саггс, «Вавилон и Ассирия», tr. Л. А. Карпова 2004; Бэйджент et al. 1999; Brown 2000; Натараян 2019) and no translation; (2) a web search for «"Энума Ану Энлиль" перевод» found only Wikipedia, blogs and stihi.ru/proza.ru items. A copy of the anthology «Когда Ану сотворил небо» (2000) also came up but could not be opened (coollib timed out), so its contents were not checked; (3) a search on вавилонская астрология / лунные предзнаменования found no Russian publication. The earlier wave-1 sweep also found nothing on CyberLeninka or archive.org. Not done: the session's WebSearch budget ran out (200/200) after 2 Russian queries, so the ВДИ index, elibrary, RSL/NLR catalogues and the Емельянов/Козырева monographs were not searched. A few omens may appear inside Russian popular books, e.g. the Saggs translation, but that is unverified.
item_007.en_found: No complete English translation of EAE 1–6 exists. en.wikipedia lists only Verderame 2002 (Italian) for Tablets 1–6 and says less than half the series is in English. Excerpts do exist in English: (a) the mythological bilingual prologue of Tablet 1 is translated in W. G. Lambert, Babylonian Creation Myths (Eisenbrauns 2013), pp. 175–177, and by Van De Mieroop 2016. Both are cited on CCP 3.1.1.C (ed. E. Jiménez 2014). (b) The Cuneiform Commentaries Project (Yale) publishes around 30 ancient commentaries on EAE 1–5 in English (3.1.1.A–G, 3.1.2.A–C, 3.1.3.C–H, 3.1.4.A–B, 3.1.5.A–F; eds. Frahm, Frazer, Jiménez, 2013–16). These quote lemmata from the base text, not complete omens. (c) Neo-Assyrian astrological reports quoting first-crescent and lunar-visibility omens: R. C. Thompson, Reports of the Magicians and Astrologers (1900, public domain), and H. Hunger, SAA 8 (1992, online on Oracc). This comes from memory; Oracc was unreachable during this check. (d) An English overview article by Verderame, 'Enūma Anu Enlil Tablets 1–13' (academia.edu 2075880, apparently in Under One Sky, AOAT 297, 2002), which presumably quotes sample omens; I could not open it. Rumen Kolev's 'EAE: A Panoramic View' (2007) is a survey, not a translation; his site was unreachable.
item_007.other_found: Italian, complete: L. Verderame, Le tavole I–VI della serie astrologica Enūma Anu Enlil (Nisaba 2, Di.Sc.A.M., Messina 2002). This is the editio princeps, with transliteration, Italian translation and commentary, built from 65 manuscripts listed in CDLI publication 1740934 (mostly Nineveh, some Hellenistic Babylon). German, excerpts or partial: E. Weidner, 'Die astrologische Serie Enûma Anu ilu Bêl', AfO 14 (1941–44), with the prologue at p. 193. Jastrow, Religion Babyloniens und Assyriens II (1912), probably translates scattered lunar omens; I have not verified this. French: Virolleaud's L'Astrologie chaldéenne (1905–12) gives cuneiform and transliteration only, with no full translation. The eBL corpus has only an empty placeholder, 'Enūma Anu Enlil Sîn (EAE 1–22)', with no chapters edited.
item_007.source_text: Standard modern edition: Verderame 2002 (Nisaba 2). Its Italian translation and commentary are under copyright. The reconstructed composite text may fall under Italy's 20-year neighbouring right for critical editions (art. 85-quater L. 633/1941), which would have expired in 2022; this needs legal checking. Public-domain sources: J. A. Craig, Astrological-Astronomical Texts (AB 14, Leipzig 1899; Craig died 1932, so public domain worldwide), cuneiform copies. Ch. Virolleaud, L'Astrologie chaldéenne, Sîn fascicles and supplements (1905–12) are public domain in the US. In the EU they remain protected until about 2038 (Virolleaud died 1968), although bare cuneiform copies and transliterations have thin originality. Virolleaud's text is composite and outdated, and his chapter numbering does not match the canonical tablets. I could not find an online scan on archive.org. CDLI holds catalogue records, with some images and transliterations, for the 65 manuscripts. A usable composite text therefore in practice requires Verderame's transliteration.
item_007.research_yield: Babylonian first-crescent, lunar-horn and halo omens compared with Greek lunar signs (Aratus' Diosemeia, Theophrastus' De signis, Hephaestion, John Lydus' De ostentis). Also the Chaldaeans' omens to Alexander at Babylon (Arrian 7.16–24; Diodorus 17.112) and the substitute-king ritual.
item_007.recommendation: Keep, but at a lower priority. RU none is confirmed so far, but EN has excerpts (Lambert's prologue, the CCP lemmata, SAA 8 reports), a full Italian translation exists, and the text has to be built from Verderame's copyrighted edition. Best first unit: Tablet 1 (prologue plus first-crescent omens), checked against CCP 3.1.1 and SAA 8, with Akkadian review by a specialist.

item_008.title_short: Seleucid-era temple rituals of Babylon and Uruk (Babylon Akītu ritual)
item_008.ru_found: The sweep's 'none' is wrong for the proposed pilot unit. V.V. Emelyanov, 'Ритуал в древней Месопотамии' (СПб.: Азбука-классика / Петербургское востоковедение, 2003), Appendix, Akkadian texts: 'Новогодний ритуал из Вавилона (фрагменты)'. He translated it from Akkadian and Sumerian using Thureau-Dangin, Rituels accadiens (1921), pp. 127–154. The translation is prose without line division and has 5 fragments: day 2 (urigallu's prayers to Bel), day 3 (making the two statues), day 4 (prayers; the Enuma elish recitation), day 5 (kuppuru purification, the mashmashu and the slaughterer leave for the steppe), and the royal rite (the king's humiliation, his negative confession, the slap and the tears omen). Emelyanov himself calls it 'на русском языке появляется впервые, но не в полном виде: переводятся только хорошо сохранившиеся фрагменты'. It is freely readable online (culture.wikireading.ru/4443, royallib.com, coollib.com). It does not use Debourse's 2022 joins. No Russian translation was found for the Uruk rituals (TU 38–44: daily sacrifices to Anu, the Anu procession, days 16–17, the nocturnal fire ceremony, the kalû drum ritual). Searches: WebSearch (RU); about 13 CyberLeninka API queries (акиту; ритуал Урук селевкидский; новогодний праздник Вавилон; Тюро-Данжен; Эсагила жрец; унижение царя; калу барабан; храм Реш Урук; and others); ru.wikipedia 'Акиту'; Emelyanov's anefest.spbu.ru articles (paraphrase only). Articles by Vipulis (2017), Kutsubina (2007), Emelyanov (2014) and Amir Abed (2015) only paraphrase. One lead is unchecked: Shileiko, 'Ассиро-вавилонский эпос' (ЛП, 2007), contains unspecified 'фрагменты ритуалов', but Emelyanov's 'впервые' (2003) suggests the Babylon ritual is not among them. Yandex and DDG returned CAPTCHAs, so elibrary and RSL catalogues were not searched.
item_008.en_found: Several English translations exist. (1) A. Sachs, 'Akkadian Rituals', in Pritchard, ANET (1950, 1955, 1969), pp. 331–345. I verified its contents list from the archive.org text: Temple Program for the New Year's Festival at Babylon (p. 331); Ritual of the Kalû-priest when covering the temple kettle-drum (p. 334); Temple ritual for the 16th–17th days of an unknown month at Uruk (p. 338); Ritual for the repair of a temple (p. 339); Program of the pageant of the statue of Anu at Uruk (p. 342); Daily sacrifices to the gods of Uruk (p. 343). (2) M.J.H. Linssen, The Cults of Uruk and Babylon: The Temple Ritual Texts as Evidence for Hellenistic Cult Practice (Brill, Cuneiform Monographs 25, 2004; DOI 10.1163/9789047412335). It has an Appendix of text editions with translations; the contents were not inspected online. (3) C. Debourse, Of Priests and Kings: The Babylonian New Year Festival in the Last Age of Cuneiform Culture (Brill, CHANE 127, 2022; DOI 10.1163/9789004513037). This is a new edition and translation of the Babylon New Year texts. Crossref shows no open licence, and a review in OLZ gives the price as EUR 237.99. (4) J. Krul, The Revival of the Anu Cult and the Nocturnal Fire Ceremony at Late Babylonian Uruk (Brill, 2018; DOI 10.1163/9789004364943). (5) Also Pallis, The Babylonian Akitu Festival (1926), and Bidmead, The Akitu Festival (2002/2004).
item_008.other_found: French: F. Thureau-Dangin, Rituels accadiens (Paris: Leroux, 1921), a full transliteration and translation of the Babylon New Year texts and the Uruk rituals then known; it is public domain. German: H. Zimmern, 'Zum babylonischen Neujahrsfest' (BVSGW 58, 1906; 70/3, 1918), covering the Babylon texts; cited from the English Wikipedia bibliography, contents not inspected. Dutch: K. van der Toorn, 'Het Babylonische Nieuwjaarsfeest' (Phoenix 36/1, 1990), which may contain a translation (not inspected).
item_008.source_text: The best public-domain source is Thureau-Dangin, Rituels accadiens (1921), archive.org/details/rituelsaccadiens00thuruoft. The record is marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT for the US, and the author died in 1944, so it is also public domain in the EU. It gives transliteration plus French translation, but the readings are outdated and it lacks later joins. Hand copies of the Uruk tablets are in Thureau-Dangin, Tablettes d'Uruk (TCL 6, 1922); I did not check online availability. The standard modern editions are all Brill and in copyright, and none appears to be open access: Linssen 2004 (Uruk and Babylon), Debourse 2022 (Babylon New Year festival, with new fragments), Krul 2018 (the Uruk nocturnal fire ceremony). A faithful modern translation would have to be built from the public-domain 1921 transliteration, checked against the copyrighted editions.
item_008.research_yield: Articles possible on: the king's humiliation and Seleucid kingship (Antiochus I, chronicles, Berossus); the Alexander-in-Babylon reception; the Anu-cult revival at Hellenistic Uruk (Anu-uballiṭ); how late cuneiform priests put ritual into writing; and Russian reception, set against Debourse's new joins.
item_008.recommendation: Keep, but replace the pilot unit. Emelyanov (2003) already put the core of the Babylon Akītu ritual into Russian, including the king's humiliation, so the first unit should be the untranslated-in-Russian Uruk rituals: the daily sacrifices to Anu (AO 6451), the Anu procession, the days 16–17 ritual and the nocturnal fire ceremony. A full Babylon version could follow, presented as the first complete Russian text based on Debourse's joins. Akkadian is outside the editor's Greek/Latin strength, and English translations exist (ANET, Linssen), which lowers its priority.

item_009.title_short: Anon., Demotic Chronicle (P. BN 215 recto, entire text)
item_009.ru_found: REFUTED: a Russian translation exists. (1) M.V. Panov, Документы по истории храмов и культов в поздний и греко-римский периоды, ч. 2 (Египетские тексты XXII), Новосибирск 2024, 460 pp. Its abstract says ch. VI 'contains translations of about sixty inscriptions… The most notable documents are… The Demotic Chronicle (BnF 215, rt)'. A Google snippet shows the entry header 'ДЕМОТИЧЕСКАЯ ХРОНИКА. Место хранения: BnF 215, rt.' The book is open access (academia.edu/126206345; hieroglyphica.com/documents/94/Panov_ET_XXIIs.pdf; full text in the KHM repository). The PDF was behind a CAPTCHA, so I could not check whether the whole recto is translated. It is probably complete. (2) An AI-made Russian translation of chapters 6-10 (about 2,500 words, uncredited, following Felber/Spiegelberg) is on the WLA 'Антология всемирной литературы' site (nevmenandr.github.io/WLA). The site says all its translations were made with AI. (3) Excerpts: Б.А. Тураев, История Древнего Востока т. II ('временем гибели, дележа в 18-й день…'); В.В. Струве, 'У истоков романа об Александре', Восточные записки I (Л. 1927) 131-146, which quotes oracles (cited by Кинжалов 1962, ancientrome.ru); В.Г. Борухович 1990 (cyberleninka) quotes passages; И.А. Ладынин, «Снова правит Египет!» (СПб.: РХГА 2017), §1.2.1, pp. 75-81 on the Chronicle. (4) Active work in progress: Ладынин's HSE student М. Сергеева gave a paper on ch. XII at the Сергеевские чтения 2025 and is writing her coursework on the Chronicle. ru.wikipedia has no article on it. Searched: WebSearch; Google.ru with 7 queries; site:cyberleninka; Bing; ru.wiki API; Panov's catalogue ET XVI (2021). Yandex was blocked by a CAPTCHA.
item_009.en_found: J.F. Quack, 'The Demotic Chronicle', in K.L. Younger (ed.), The Context of Scripture vol. 4: Supplements (Leiden/Boston: Brill 2017), 27-32. This is a complete English translation. It is confirmed by Quack's Heidelberg publication list and by his WiBiLex article (2021), which lists it among the 'Gesamtübersetzungen'. There is also a free online English translation of chapters 6-13 (the whole surviving recto) by P. Swarney, 'after H. Felber' and Spiegelberg (yorku.ca/pswarney/2110/dem-chron). Partial translations and studies: J.H. Johnson, Enchoria 4 (1974); JSSEA 13 (1983) 61-72; Grammata Demotika (1984) 107-124; Johnson & Ritner 1990 (Studies Lichtheim). The colleague's 'partial / no standard published English' is wrong.
item_009.other_found: German, complete: W. Spiegelberg 1914 (edition with translation); H.-J. Felber, 'Die demotische Chronik', in Blasius/Schipper (eds.), Apokalyptik und Ägypten (OLA 107, 2002) 65-111; F. Hoffmann & J.F. Quack, Anthologie der demotischen Literatur, 2nd ed. (2018) 244-251. Quack also gives an overview in Einführung in die altägyptische Literaturgeschichte III, 3rd ed. (2016) 196-200, and studies (2009, 2015). French: E. Revillout 1877, 1880a/b, 1882 (Revue archéologique; Revue égyptologique 1-2), early extracts and partial translations. Italian: E. Bresciani, Letteratura e poesia dell'antico Egitto (Einaudi 1969) 551-560, later reissued. The Thesaurus Linguae Aegyptiae has an object record 'Demotische Chronik (BiblNat 215)'; its contents could not be checked because of bot protection.
item_009.source_text: Best public-domain source: W. Spiegelberg, Die sogenannte demotische Chronik des Pap. 215 der Bibliothèque Nationale zu Paris (Demotische Studien 7, Leipzig: Hinrichs 1914), 196 pp. It has transliteration, German translation, glossary and full-size plates. Spiegelberg died in 1930, so it is public domain in the EU and US: https://archive.org/details/diesogenanntedem00spieuoft. Papyrus images are on Gallica (BnF): https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/btv1b8304631p. Quack (2021) says Spiegelberg is outdated in many details. The current standard translations (Felber 2002, Quack 2017, Hoffmann/Quack 2018) are in copyright. Panov 2024 (Russian) is free to read online; its licence was not checked. The text is in Demotic, outside the editor's Greek/Latin competence, and LLMs are weak in Demotic.
item_009.research_yield: Remains a key source for the Nectanebo legend, Egyptian views of Persian, Greek and Ptolemaic rule, and oracle-plus-exegesis ('Egyptian scholia'). But a Russian text (Panov 2024), English (Quack 2017) and three German versions exist, so a new translation would add little that is new.
item_009.recommendation: Drop it as a 'first-ever translation' candidate. A full English version (Quack 2017), three complete German versions and a Russian translation (Panov 2024) already exist, plus an AI Russian version of chapters 6-10 online, and Ladynin's school at HSE is working on the text. The Chronicle can still be cited in an Alexander Romance article without being translated anew.

item_010.title_short: Assyrian court scholars, Letters SAA 10 (substitute-king dossier)
item_010.ru_found: I found no scholarly Russian translation of SAA 10 or of the substitute-king (šar pūḫi) letters. The only Russian versions are a few letters in an amateur machine translation. Internet Archive item "AlexLibMesopotamia" ("Александрийская Библиотека") holds a DeepL/Yandex-labelled Russian rendering of C. H. W. Johns, Babylonian and Assyrian Laws, Contracts and Letters (1904). It covers about 5–6 scholars' letters to Esarhaddon, translated from Johns' English, not the Akkadian: Adad-šumu-uṣur's "old men dance" letter, Balasi and Nabû-aḫḫē-erība on lucky days for travel, Nabû'a's lunar observation, and Nabû-šumu-iddin's eclipse report addressed to "the gardener", a form of address possibly used during a substitute-king period. Full-text checks found no SAA 10 letters in: (1) Хрестоматия по истории Древнего Востока, ч. 1 (Коростовцев/Кацнельсон/Кузищин 1980; IA 11980-583202508); (2) История Древнего Востока. Тексты и документы (Кузищин 2002; IA 2002-3166120250814); (3) Струве, Хрестоматия по истории древнего мира т. I (1950). Its Assyrian letters are Sargon II intelligence reports and Esarhaddon's queries to Šamaš (SAA 1/4/5, tr. Дьяконов), not SAA 10. (4) Меликишвили, Древневосточные материалы... Наири–Урарту (1954). (5) БВЛ т. 1, Поэзия и проза Древнего Востока (1973). About 25 CyberLeninka API searches (заместительный/подменный царь, царь-заместитель, ассирийские/новоассирийские письма, Асархаддон, Мар-Иссар, Адад-шуму-уцур, ассирийские астрологи, Энума Ану Энлиль, ritual terms) found nothing relevant. Випулис 2017 and Ясеновская 2018 do not translate any SAA 10 letters. ru.wikipedia and ru.wikisource API searches: no article on the ritual and no translations. Not verified (no access): Дьяконов, АВИУ (ВДИ 1951), possibly 1–2 Esarhaddon-era letters on Cimmerians or Urartu; Емельянов, Ритуал в древней Месопотамии (2003); the Russian edition of Oppenheim's Ancient Mesopotamia, likely short quotations. eLibrary and vdi.igh.ru were not reachable.
item_010.en_found: Full English translation: S. Parpola, Letters from Assyrian and Babylonian Scholars, SAA 10 (Helsinki UP 1993); also on ORACC/SAAo with English translation. Earlier: Parpola, Letters from Assyrian Scholars to the Kings Esarhaddon and Assurbanipal, AOAT 5/1 (1970) and 5/2 (1983; Eisenbrauns reprint 2007). LAS II includes a commentary and an appendix on the substitute-king ritual. Older English: L. Waterman, Royal Correspondence of the Assyrian Empire (Univ. of Michigan 1930–36), covers all ABL letters; R. H. Pfeiffer, State Letters of Assyria (AOS 1935), a selection; A. L. Oppenheim, Letters from Mesopotamia (Chicago 1967), a selection; C. H. W. Johns (1904), excerpts. Companion corpus: H. Hunger, Astrological Reports to Assyrian Kings, SAA 8 (1992; Penn State reissue 2017). R. C. Thompson, Reports of the Magicians and Astrologers of Nineveh and Babylon (1900) is public domain and on IA. Book data verified via Open Library and IA. WebSearch quota was used up, so general web search was not possible.

Its existence is verified on Open Library; it translates many cultic letters by exorcists and scholars that are now in SAA 10. Italian: F. M. Fales and G. B. Bottéro, "Le substitut royal et son sort en Mésopotamie ancienne", Akkadica 9 (1978), reprinted in his Mésopotamie (1987; English 1992). Both translate the core substitute-king letters. item_010.source_text: Public domain: R. F. Harper, Assyrian and Babylonian Letters (ABL), 14 vols., 1892–1914, cuneiform copies, on archive.org (e.g. assyrianbabyloni01harp). Thompson 1900 is public domain for SAA 8. Behrens 1906 is public domain (German). Waterman 1930–36 has a transliteration plus translation; its US public-domain status is uncertain and I found no free scan. Standard modern edition: Parpola, SAA 10 (1993), © Neo-Assyrian Text Corpus Project / Helsinki UP, in copyright. Its online version is on ORACC SAAo (oracc.museum.upenn.edu/saao/saa10). item_010.research_yield: Possible articles: the substitute-king dossier and the Babylon omens of Alexander's death (Arr. 7.16, 7.24; Diod. 17.116; Plut. Alex. 73–74; the Alexander Romance); the source of Greek images of the "Chaldaeans"; eclipse politics and scholarly patronage at Esarhaddon's court. This would be the first Russian scholarly version.
item_010.recommendation: Keep, but only as a Russian-first project. English is complete (SAA 10, LAS, SAAo), and the editor's Akkadian validation is weaker than his Greek, so it should stay at moderate priority. Best first unit: the šar pūḫi letters, about 30 (Parpola's list in LAS II), from the SAAo transliteration, published with an Alexander/Arrian 7.24 commentary article.

item_011.title_short: Anon., Myth of the Sun's Eye (P. Leiden I 384 + Greek P.Lond.Lit. 192)
item_011.ru_found:
Only the embedded fables exist in Russian, in popular literary versions by И.С. Кацнельсон and Ф.Л. Мендельсон, made from Spiegelberg's transcription:
(a) «Сказки и повести Древнего Египта» (М.: Худлит, 1956), with «Коршун и кошка» and «Лев и мышь» (archive.org 1956-202473350816).
(b) «Фараон Хуфу и чародеи» (1958), pp. 212–222, which adds «Коршун Зоркий Глаз и коршун Чуткое Ухо». I checked this against the full OCR on archive.org (1958-203699250816).
(c) Reprints: «Древний Егип. Сказания. Притчи» (2015) and a 2021 edition (fantlab edition325894).
The frame dialogue, the hymns and the Greek version have never been translated into Russian. Кацнельсон, «Культура Древнего Египта» (1976), only describes the fables. Popular retellings, not translations, also exist, e.g. И.В. Рак, «Мифы Древнего Египта», «Бегство Хатхор в Нубию… Сказки Тота» (supermif.com).
Warning: an AI-generated "translation" is online in Б. Орехов's «Антология всемирной литературы» (nevmenandr.github.io/WLA, «Миф о Солнечном Оке»). The project says all its texts are made by AI. This one is a short, partly invented "reconstruction": the fable plots are wrong, and it does not follow P. Leiden 384 or P. BM 274, although its note cites both.
Searched with no further hits: CyberLeninka API (5 queries), ru.wikipedia API, the egyptology.ru bibliographies of 23 Russian Egyptologists (Кацнельсон, Коростовцев, Эдаков, Рубинштейн, Ладынин etc.), archive.org full-text search for «Солнечном Оке/Ока/Глазе» and «Коршун и кошка», and the contents of М.В. Панов's «Египетские тексты» series. Panov's catalogue of Russian translations (ЕТ XVI, 2021) is behind a CAPTCHA, so I could not check it. Not checked: the contents of the Алетейя anthology «Сказки Древнего Египта» (1998).
item_011.en_found:
The colleague's "unknown" is refuted.
(1) Full: attalus.org, "Egyptian Texts 1.16: The Myth of the Solar Eye" (A. Smith, dated 30.08.2024), https://www.attalus.org/egypt/solar_eye.html. It is an annotated English version of about 12,000 words covering P. Leiden 384 and P. Lille 31, with all four fables and the hymns. It was compiled from modern translations (de Cenival, Bresciani, Loprieno, Chauveau & Agut-Labordère, Hoffmann & Quack, TLA), not translated directly from the Demotic. The Greek version is not included.
(2) Print excerpts: M. Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature III (1980), pp. 156–159, "The Lion in Search of Man" (reprinted in Asante, African Intellectual Heritage, 1996). W.J. Tait, Acta Orientalia 37 (1976), pp. 38–40, the fable of Sight and Hearing.
(3) Greek version: S. West, "The Greek Version of the Legend of Tefnut", JEA 55 (1969) 161–183. It is an edition with commentary; I could not confirm that it contains a full English translation.
I found no complete scholarly English translation in print.
