Frank, Oracular Tablets from Dodona (Brill, Mnemosyne Suppl. 504, Sept. 2026): thematic study, probably with many translated questions; count not verified. (5) Bowden & Eidinow (eds.), Visiting the Oracle at Dodona (CUP 2026, Open Access CC BY-NC-ND): translations scattered through the chapters. (6) Older selected translations: Parke, The Oracles of Zeus (1967); Parker, G&R 63 (2016).
item_042.other_found: FRENCH, the biggest omission in the sweep: (a) É. Lhôte, Les lamelles oraculaires de Dodone (Droz 2006) gives 167 lamellae, each with text, critical notes, French translation and commentary (Kernos review, doi 10.4000/kernos.378). (b) CIOD, Choix d'inscriptions oraculaires de Dodone (É. Lhôte & J.-M. Carbon, 2018–, dodonaonline.com/ciod): about 1,200 free PDF fiches (I counted 1,206 links across the DVC and LOD pages). Each gives a revised Greek text, apparatus, French translation and commentary for "the most interesting" of the 4,216 DVC inscriptions. SPANISH: I.Dodone Online (see EN). GERMAN: O. Hoffmann in SGDI II (1899), nos. 1557–1598, gives text and commentary but no translation; a Münster/Berlin project (Funke, Knäpper) is editing the Berlin tablets, but whether it translates them was not verified. ITALIAN: Piccinini 2017 (in English), on public consultations. MODERN GREEK: DVC 2013 itself has no translation (DOL notes «l'absence de toute traduction»).
item_042.source_text: Public domain: Carapanos, Dodone et ses ruines (1878), archive.org dodoneetsesruine01carauoft (pl. vol. dodonecarapanos), has a few dozen tablets with outdated readings. O. Hoffmann, "Die Orakelinschriften aus Dodona", SGDI II.1 (Collitz/Bechtel, 1899), nos. 1557–1598, about 42 texts with concordance to Pomtow; archive.org sammlungdergriec0201colluoft. The standard edition is in copyright: Dakaris–Vokotopoulou–Christidis, Τα χρηστήρια ελάσματα της Δωδώνης (Archaeological Society at Athens Library 285–286, 2013). Lhôte 2006 (Droz) is also in copyright. CIOD and I.Dodone Online are free to read, but no open licence was found on the pages I fetched. Their revised readings can be cited with attribution, but not bulk-copied.
item_042.research_yield: Russian articles possible: private religiosity and risk; questions on slaves and manumission; women as consultants; migration and settlement questions; dialect and onomastic notes. A methods paper is also possible: LLM translations tested against CIOD, Eidinow and I.Dodone Online, a rare human benchmark.
item_042.recommendation: Keep, but only as a Russian-first project at lower priority. The proposed pilot unit, Lhôte's set, already exists in full in French (Lhôte 2006) and English (Eidinow 2007), and CIOD gives French translations of about 1,200 more texts, so drop that unit. Best first unit: a Russian translation of the public-domain SGDI II nos. 1557–1598 (about 42 texts, copyright-safe). After that, a thematic Russian (and, where new, English) dossier of about 100 DVC questions not in Eidinow or I.Dodone Online, checked against CIOD readings with attribution.

item_043.title_short: Anonymous, Carmina Latina Epigraphica (pilot: 150 Roman verse epitaphs)
item_043.ru_found: REFUTES the sweep's claim that there is no Russian collection. F. A. Petrovsky (Ф. А. Петровский), «Латинские эпиграфические стихотворения» (М.: Изд-во АН СССР, 1962, 153 pp.; edited by M. L. Gasparov) is a dedicated anthology. It has about 161 numbered poems, each with the Latin text, a Russian verse translation and notes. Sections: dedications (pp. 17–41); epitaphs (pp. 41–133, in 7 thematic groups); varia (pp. 133–147). Concordances to CIL and Bücheler are on pp. 147–150. I checked the scan myself (free PDF at biblio.imli.ru/images/abook/zarublitra/Latinskie_epigraficheskie_stikhotvorenia_1962.pdf). About 45 items come from CIL VI (Rome) and about 20 from CIL IV (Pompeii), and they include numbers from the Lommatzsch supplement (CLE 1923–2151). Even the sweep's own example, CIL IX 2689 = ILS 7478, is in Petrovsky (p. 16). The book was reviewed by L. A. Freiberg in ВДИ 1965. Petrovsky died in 1978, so his translations stay in copyright until 2048. Other Russian translations are single poems scattered across many places: A. E. Kuznetsov on the Calidius Eroticus epitaph (ИЯКФ 2014, Latin with commentary, no full translation); the Allia Potestas epitaph (CLE 1988) translated by I. A. Shurygin, 2019, on ancientrome.ru; an ancientrome.ru article on the Scipio epitaph (Moir); and an article on the epigraphy of Praetextatus (Scholae 2021, probably covering CLE 111). Searches used: CyberLeninka API (латинская эпитафия, эпиграфическая поэзия, помпейские надписи, стихотворные надписи, Бюхелер, CIL VI, надписи Помпей, Претекстат), ru.wikipedia and the IMLI library. No second Russian anthology turned up. M. E. Sergeenko's «Помпеи» (1949) is likely to translate Pompeian graffiti, but I did not verify this. Overall: roughly 7–8% of CLE exists in Russian.
item_043.en_found: E. Courtney, Musa Lapidaria (Scholars Press/APA, 1995): 204 poems with facing English translation and commentary (BMCR 1998.03.12). E. H. Warmington, Remains of Old Latin IV (Loeb, 1940): republican verse inscriptions with translation, including the Scipio epitaphs. R. Lattimore, Themes in Greek and Latin Epitaphs (1942): many excerpts in translation. Peter Kruschwitz's blog The Petrified Muse (thepetrifiedmuse.blog, 2012–2021, CC BY 4.0): English translations and discussion of many CLE poems. Pompeian verse also appears in English in the sourcebooks and in graffiti studies (Cooley & Cooley; Milnor 2014; Ancient Graffiti Project); I did not count these. As far as I could find, there is no complete English translation. Cumulative English coverage is probably about 15–20%, uneven and weighted toward famous pieces.
item_043.other_found: Spanish: Concepción Fernández Martínez, Poesía epigráfica latina I–II (Biblioteca Clásica Gredos, Madrid, 1998 [526 pp., ISBN 84-249-1983-1] and 1999 [430 pp., ISBN 84-249-1984-X]; Dialnet, Open Library). This is a two-volume translation, and its size suggests it may cover all or nearly all of Bücheler–Lommatzsch. I did not verify the full scope. Catalan: M. Miró Vinaixa, Perennia (Godall, 2015), a bilingual anthology. German: H. Geist & G. Pfohl, Römische Grabinschriften (Heimeran/Tusculum 1969; 2nd ed. 1976), a large anthology of epitaphs in translation that includes many CLE poems (number not counted). Italian: P. Cugusi and M. T. Sblendorio Cugusi, regional CLE corpora for Sardinia (2003), Moesia/Thrace (2008), Hispania (2012) and Africa (2014), with Italian translations, mostly of finds made after Bücheler. Spanish regional corpora: Baetica 2007/2010, Carthago Nova 2006. French: D. Porte, Tombeaux romains (1993), an anthology (scope not checked). New critical edition: CIL XVIII/2 (Hispania, 2022) and CLEO online (Seville).
item_043.source_text: The best public-domain texts are F. Bücheler, Carmina Latina Epigraphica = Anthologia Latina II.1–2 (Teubner 1895–97; archive.org/details/buecheler-franciscus-al-2.-carmina-latina-epigraphica-f-1 and ...-f-2). Add E. Engström, Carmina Latina Epigraphica post editam collectionem Buechelerianam (1912; archive.org/details/carminalatinaepi00engsuoft). E. Lommatzsch's Supplementum (1926) should also be public domain now (Lommatzsch died in 1949), but I did not locate a scan. Check each text against CIL VI/EDCS/EDR; EDH is CC BY-SA. The new standard edition, CIL XVIII (De Gruyter/BBAW; fasc. XVIII/2 Hispania, 2022), is in copyright. Its companion database CLEO (institucional.us.es/cleo) is CC BY-NC-ND 3.0. Neither covers Rome yet, so for the city of Rome Bücheler is still the standard text, and it is public domain.
item_043.research_yield: Articles: a source-critical study of Petrovsky's 1962 selection against the full CLE; Virgil and Ovid in Roman epitaphs; female epithets and family ideals; Vulgar Latin prosody; mors immatura topoi; Latin versus Greek funerary epigram. There is strong potential for a reader for Russian Latin teaching.
item_043.recommendation: Keep, but downgrade. The 'no Russian collection' claim is false because Petrovsky (1962) covers about 161 poems, and Spanish (Gredos 1998–99) may be complete. Present the project as the first Russian translation beyond Petrovsky. For the pilot, take 150 Roman (CIL VI) sepulchral carmina that are absent from Petrovsky's concordance (pp. 147–150) and preferably also from Courtney.

item_044.title_short: Anonymous, Attic curse tablets (DTA / IG II/III³ 8.1; judicial and commercial subset)
item_044.ru_found: No Russian corpus translation found, only single tablets quoted in articles. (1) V.P. Emelyanova, «Связывающие проклятия… классических Афин», Журнал интегративных исследований культуры 5.2 (2023): one 4th-c. BC DTA tablet (the Galene curse) in Russian. (2) T.V. Kudryavtseva, «Судебная магия в классической Греции», Вестник РГГУ (2010): cites many DTA numbers but quotes them in Greek only, with no Russian translations. Her survey of Russian work on the subject lists Pomyalovsky (Эпиграфические этюды, 1873), Pridik (1899), Shkorpil (1908, Olbia), Tolstoy (1953, Black Sea graffiti), and E.G. Kagarov, «Греческие таблички с проклятиями» (Kharkov 1918, 81 pp., a study; expanded German version Griechische Fluchtafeln, 1929). None of these is a translated corpus of the Attic tablets. The Philologia Classica 2019 article was not checked. I also did not confirm whether A.V. Belousov's Black Sea defixiones work includes any Attic texts. Searches: 2 Russian web searches (Аттические таблички/дефиксионы перевод; Белоусов дефиксионы), which returned only popular items. The session's web-search budget then ran out, so I followed up by fetching the cyberleninka articles and the ru.wikipedia article on Kagarov directly.
item_044.en_found: This refutes the colleague's claim. J. Curbera (ed.), IG II/III³ 8.1, Defixiones Atticae (De Gruyter 2024; 483 tablets, superseding Wünsch/DTA). Its BBAW digital edition (telota.bbaw.de/ig, volume 'IG II/III³ 8, 1', 486 entries) gives every tablet with a full English translation by Jaime Curbera and a German one by Klaus Hallof, under CC BY 4.0. I checked this in the TEI XML of entries 30, 250, 310, 380 and 450 (for example, 380 begins 'I bind these down… his workshop and the works and the hands'). The proposed pilot unit (judicial and commercial DTA tablets) is therefore already fully translated into English and German online. Also: Gager, Curse Tablets and Binding Spells (1992), with 134 curse texts in English; Eidinow 2007, catalogue; Lamont, In Blood and Ashes (OUP 2023), many Attic tablets translated. A Papakonstantinou/Gellar-Goad/Riess project, 'Magic in Ancient Athens: A Complete Translation of Attic Curse Tablets', was announced in Colloquia Attica (Steiner 2018, 261-276); I could not verify whether it has appeared as a book. For Audollent's Latin tablets: Urbanová, Latin Curse Tablets of the Roman Empire (2018).
item_044.other_found: German: full Attic corpus by K. Hallof in the IG II/III³ 8.1 digital edition (2024, CC BY 4.0); Latin tablets in Kropp, Defixiones (2008), stated from memory and not re-verified. Spanish: Amor López Jimeno, Textos griegos de maleficio (Akal, Clásica 62, 2001; ISBN 978-84-460-1484-3). The publisher says it collects 'all the defixiones' preserved in Greek, 6th c. BC to 4th-5th c. AD, and it is widely described as the first complete modern-language translation. French and Italian collections were not checked because the search budget ran out; it makes no difference to the verdict.
item_044.source_text: Best source: the IG II/III³ 8.1 digital edition, https://telota.bbaw.de/ig/ (volume 'IG II/III³ 8, 1, Attika, Fluchtafeln'). It has the Greek text plus EN and DE translations under CC BY 4.0, with TEI XML at https://telota.bbaw.de/ig/api/xml/IG II_III³ 8, 1, N. Derivative translations are allowed with attribution. The print edition (Curbera, De Gruyter 2024, €390) is in copyright, but the online text is openly licensed. Wünsch 1897 (IG III.3 appendix) and Audollent 1904 are public domain on archive.org but superseded by autopsy rereadings.
item_044.research_yield: There is little new to find. A Russian version would add access, not a first translation. Possible articles: the Russian history of defixio study (Pomyalovsky, Kagarov); readings of the judicial tablets alongside the orators. Riess, Papakonstantinou, Lamont and Curbera have already covered the field heavily.
item_044.recommendation: Drop it as a 'first-ever translation' candidate. Since 2024 the whole Attic corpus, including the proposed judicial and commercial unit, has had full English and German translations online under CC BY, and there has been a complete Spanish translation since 2001. Keep it at most as a Russian-only access project, for example about 100 judicial tablets translated from the CC BY Greek text of IG II/III³ 8.1 with credit to Curbera.

item_045.title_short: Priene, Hellenistic honorific decrees for benefactors (pilot of 30)
item_045.ru_found: I found no Russian translation of any Priene decree, full or as a corpus. Russian studies paraphrase the decrees or quote short phrases only. (1) A.A. Antonov, «Политическая элита раннеэллинистической Приены по данным почётных декретов», Изв. Саратовского ун-та. Сер. История. Межд. отношения 26.1 (2026) 40–46 (cyberleninka). It cites I.Priene² 1–34, 46, 64, 68, 132 etc., summarises their content, gives no full text and cites no earlier Russian translation. (2) A.G. Grushevoy, «Римская власть в восприятии греков (надписи из Лампсака, Метрополиса, Клароса и Приены II в. до н.э.)», Verbum 2018 (cyberleninka). It analyses I.Priene 40 and the Moschion decree (I.Priene 108 = IK 64) without a translation. (3) Grushevoy, Verbum 2016, on the Seleucids and the cities: it only mentions I.Priene 34. (4) A.I. Voronkov's bibliography of Russian translations of inscriptions (ancientrome.ru, section VI), which goes up to the 1970s: no Priene inscription is listed. It does list the Soviet anthologies that translated OGIS/Syll texts: Античный способ производства в источниках 1933; Струве, Хрестоматия 1936 and 1951. (5) ancientrome.ru, the CyberLeninka catalogue (37 hits for "Priene") and general Russian web searches for Мосхион, Сотас, «почётный декрет Приены» found nothing else. Not checked: the contents of Каллистов, Хрестоматия по истории Древней Греции (1964), and dissertations on elibrary/RSL. The web-search budget ran out after 9 Russian queries.
item_045.en_found: This refutes the claim that the core of the unit is untranslated. The longest and most important decrees already have full free English translations by Andrew Smith on attalus.org ("Translations of Hellenistic Inscriptions", THI). THI 175, "Priene honours its benefactors" (c. 129–80 BC), is about 8,800 words. It translates I.Priene 108 (Moschion), 121 (an envoy), 111 (Krates; partly after C. Wallace, Historia 2014) and 112–114 (A. Aemilius Zosimos): http://www.attalus.org/docs/other/inscr_175.html. Also on attalus.org: THI 41 (I.Priene 11, liberation from the tyrant Hieron, 297 BC); THI 132 (I.Priene 21–22, Nymphon); THI 16 (I.Priene 19, Helikon at Teloneia, partly after Thonemann, The Hellenistic Age); THI 133 (I.Priene 53); OGIS 11 (I.Priene 14, Lysimachos); OGIS 215 (I.Priene 18, Larichos); Syll. 282 (I.Priene 3 + 231, Megabyxos). Print translations: the Sotas decree against the Galatians (I.Priene 17 = OGIS 765) is in Burstein, Translated Documents 3 (1985), no. 17. Ma, Antiochos III and the Cities, nos. 32–33, covers I.Priene 59 and 82 (Diokles). The attalus concordance lists all of these at http://www.attalus.org/docs/inscriptions4.html. That concordance does not include I.Priene 109, 110 or 117–119, but their English status was not verified elsewhere. I could run only about 2 English web searches before the budget ran out. Attalus.org and its concordance were checked directly.
item_045.other_found: German: the whole corpus is translated. IK 69 is W. Blümel and R. Merkelbach (with F. Rumscheid), Die Inschriften von Priene, 2 vols (Bonn: Habelt, 2014), described as "zusammengestellt, übersetzt und kommentiert". French: Isabelle Carbonneau's Université Laval thesis «L'évergétisme à Priène à la fin de l'époque hellénistique» (year not verified) translates I.Priene 108 (pp. 45–52) and 112–114 (pp. 90–100), according to attalus.org; the PDF at corpus.ulaval.ca returned 403. Ph. Gauthier's study of the Larichos decrees (I.Priene 18) is on Persée; I did not check whether it gives a French translation. A 2016 REA review article, «Un nouveau corpus des inscriptions de Priène», discusses IK 69. Attic Inscriptions Online has English translations of IK Priene 98–99, but these are Athenian decrees, not Priene's own. Italian and Spanish: nothing found (not searched in depth).
item_045.source_text: Public domain: F. Hiller von Gaertringen, Inschriften von Priene (Berlin 1906), on archive.org as FredrichInschriftenVonPriene1906 (Public Domain Mark 1.0; PDF and OCR text) and as inschriftenvonpr00hill. Greek texts based on the new edition are freely readable on PHI Greek Inscriptions (epigraphy.packhum.org, "Priene_NN") but are not openly licensed. The standard modern edition, IK 69 (Blümel–Merkelbach 2014, Habelt), is in copyright and renumbers the texts (e.g. Moschion = I.Priene 108 = IK 64). The plan should be: translate from the 1906 text, check readings against IK 69 and PHI, and keep a concordance of the old and new numbers.
item_045.research_yield: A first Russian annotated dossier would support articles on late-Hellenistic euergetism (Moschion, Krates, Zosimos), on Priene against the Roman publicani (I.Priene 111), and on the Galatians, Hieron's tyranny and royal relations. Comparison with Chersonesos and Bosporan decrees would interest Russian scholarship.
item_045.recommendation: Keep the item only as a Russian-first project, with lower priority. The core decrees (I.Priene 108, 111, 112–114, 121, 11, 14, 17, 18, 19, 21–22, 3) are already freely available in English, and IK 69 translates the whole corpus into German, so this is not a first-ever English translation. If it goes ahead, start with the THI 175 cluster (108, 111, 112–114) in Russian with commentary, then check whether I.Priene 109, 110 and 117–119 lack an English version.

item_046.title_short: Welles, Royal Correspondence (Hellenistic royal letters, RC 1–75)
item_046.ru_found: The "partial" label holds, but more letters are in Russian than the sweep reported, and they are exactly the Seleucid letters proposed as the pilot. Verified: (1) Антология источников по истории, культуре и религии Древней Греции, ed. В. И. Кузищин (СПб.: Алетейя, 2000; PDF at sno.pro1.ru/lib/antologiya_istochnikov_greziya/). Section XVI (С. В. Новиков; translations by В. А. Гаибов and С. В. Новиков, made from Welles) gives full Russian versions of RC 10–13 (the Aristodikides dossier), RC 18–20 (sale of land to Laodike), RC 45 (Seleucus IV to Seleucia in Pieria) and RC 70 (Baitokaike), plus the post-Welles Hefzibah and Ikaros letters. Section XV (Новиков) translates RC 75 (Artabanus III to Susa) in full. (2) Античный способ производства в источниках (Л., 1933), no. 305, has RC 10–13, reprinted from the older chrestomathy «Древний мир», ч. II. It is online at annales.info/ant_lit/nadpisi/ilion.htm. (3) А. Б. Ранович, Эллинизм и его историческая роль (М.–Л., 1950) quotes RC 18 in full and cites RC 1, 5, 11, 14, 15, 19, 20, 38, 41, 44, 75. (4) О. Ю. Климов, Пергамское царство (СПб., 2010) translates RC 54 (Amlada) in full; the Attis/Pessinus letters RC 55–61 and RC 47, 68, 69 are only paraphrased or quoted. (5) Э. Бикерман, Государство Селевкидов (Russian translation, М., 1985) quotes several letters. (6) А. Б. Шарнина (ПИФК 2021) and Е. М. Берзон (ПИФК 2015) give only short fragments of RC 31–32. Three chrestomathies listed in Климов's SPbU manual were not checked; they probably add more: Каллистов ed. (1964, pp. 430–592), Струве ed., vol. II (1951), and Борухович–Монахов–Парфенов (1998). About 12 of the 75 letters are verified in full Russian translation, with scattered excerpts of others. There is no Russian collection of the corpus.
item_046.en_found: Welles 1934 gives the Greek text, an English translation and a commentary for all 75 letters. HathiTrust record mdp.39015010575713 has rights code "pd" and full view; it is also on archive.org as welles-1934-royal-correspondence. Attalus.org (www.attalus.org/docs/rc/index.html) hosts Welles' English translations of RC 1–75 and links about 54 letters found after Welles, translated there or in Austin, The Hellenistic World, and Ma, Antiochos III and the Cities. Other English selections exist in sourcebooks such as Bagnall–Derow and Burstein; these were not re-verified in this pass. Only 2 English WebSearch calls could be run before the session's search quota ran out; the rest of the English evidence comes from direct fetches of the attalus.org, HathiTrust and archive.org records.
item_046.other_found: German: Brodersen, Günther and Schmitt, Historische griechische Inschriften in Übersetzung (WBG; three volumes, Studienausgabe 2011 per de.wikipedia). It translates a selection that includes royal letters; which letters it covers was not checked. French: Virgilio, Le roi écrit (2011) contains no translated corpus. Per BMCR 2012.10.31 it is an essay on royal letter-writing plus studies of the Sinuri and Soloi letters, and it announces a new complete edition to replace Welles, not yet out. Italian and Spanish: no complete translation found. French selections in Bertrand, Inscriptions historiques grecques (1992) are likely but not verified.
item_046.source_text: Best open source: Welles 1934 (Yale University Press). HathiTrust treats it as public domain (rights code "pd", full view; US copyright apparently not renewed). Welles died in 1969, so countries using life+70 could treat it as protected until 2039. The Greek texts of the inscriptions are not copyrightable. Further public-domain texts: Dittenberger, OGIS (1903–05) and Syll.³ (1915–24). No modern edition replaces the whole corpus: Virgilio's new corpus was still announced, not published, in 2012. Many letters have been re-edited in copyrighted volumes (IK series, SEG, Ma 1999/2002), so restorations should be checked against them. Post-Welles letters (about 54) have to be taken from copyrighted editions.
item_046.research_yield: Strongest article: Alexander Romance letters compared with real chancery forms (greeting formulae, φιλάνθρωπα, εὔνοια). Others: a Russian glossary of chancery terms; the Attalid "council of relatives" (RC 61); Russian translation history since 1933.
item_046.recommendation: Downgrade from 3 to 2. Keep only as a Russian-only teaching corpus, without the "first-ever translation" framing: English is complete and public domain, and about 12 letters already exist in Russian. Drop the Seleucid pilot, because RC 10–13 and 18–20 are already in Russian. Use instead the Attalid Pessinus dossier, RC 55–61 (Eumenes II and Attalus II to the priest Attis, about 1.5k words), where only paraphrases were found.

item_047.title_short: Diogenes of Oenoanda, Epicurean inscription (Ethics + Letter to Antipater)
item_047.ru_found: There is no scholarly Russian translation from the Greek, but there is a near-complete amateur one made from English. Echafaud (ru.echafaud.org/inscription-of-diogenes-from-enoanda/) posted it on 4 June 2023 and revised it in October 2023. The translator is anonymous. The page calls it a translation of Smith's English: Smith 1993 plus the 2003 Supplement. It covers Physics, Ethics, Maxims, Letters, Letter to Antipater, Old Age and fr. 180-181, plus NF up to 132. That is about 11k Russian words, closely matching the English on enoanda.cat. A Ukrainian version also exists. The proposed pilot unit (Ethics + Letter to Antipater) is therefore already in Russian, at an amateur level. NF 133-219 (the 1997 leftovers and the 2007-2017 finds) have no Russian version. Other Russian items are only short studies. Verlinsky's 'Утопический фрагмент Диогена из Эноанды' (1987) is a 2-page abstract, and Melnikov (2009) is a 2-page congress paper. The 2008 encyclopedic dictionary Античная философия, the Античные писатели entry (ancientrome.ru) and simposium.ru list no Russian translation. Smith's Hyperboreus 25.2 (2019) article on fr. 157 is in English. I ran 8 Russian searches (Эноанды/Эноандский/Ойноанды/Эноандская надпись/Верлинский/Мельников/cyberleninka/dissertations). No journal or Soviet anthology translation was found.
item_047.en_found: English is fully covered. Chilton, The Fragments (OUP for Hull, 1971) translates the fragments known at the time. Smith, The Epicurean Inscription (Bibliopolis 1993), the Supplement (2003; NF 126-135) and Hammerstaedt & Smith, Ten Years of New Discoveries (Habelt 2014; NF 136-212; BMCR 2016.07.38) all carry English translations. So do the articles for NF 213 (Epigraphica Anatolica 49, 2016) and NF 214-219 (EA 51, 2018). Most importantly, there is now M. F. Smith, Urbi et Orbi: The Epicurean Inscription and Prescription of Diogenes of Oinoanda (Tab edizioni, Rome, Doxai V, March 2026). It is open access (OA ISBN 979-12-5669-345-0) and is billed as the first English translation to include all 305 pieces. Smith's English is also online at english.enoanda.cat (with permission) and on epicurus.info (abridged). Only 1 general English web search ran before the search budget ran out. The rest was checked by fetching specific pages directly: en.wikipedia, two BMCR reviews, martinfergusonsmith.com and tabedizioni.it.
item_047.other_found: French: P.-M. Morel in D. Delattre & J. Pigeaud (eds), Les Épicuriens (Pléiade 2010), covering all fragments published by 2009; and A. Étienne & D. O'Meara, La philosophie épicurienne sur pierre (Fribourg 1996). German: Jürss, Müller & Schmidt, Griechische Atomisten (Reclam, Leipzig 1977), partial; and Hammerstaedt & Smith, a German account in Istanbuler Forschungen 57 (2025). Italian: Casanova, I frammenti di Diogene d'Enoanda (Florence 1984), an edition; whether it includes an Italian translation was not verified this session. Grilli's 1960 edition is in Milan. Catalan: a translation of the inscription on enoanda.cat. Ukrainian: amateur, on Echafaud. Spanish: not verified.
item_047.source_text: Public domain but obsolete (64-88 fragments, superseded readings): Cousin, BCH 16 (1892); Heberdey & Kalinka, BCH 21 (1897); J. William, Diogenis Oenoandensis Fragmenta (Teubner 1907; archive.org/details/diogenisoenoand00dioggoog, marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT). The standard modern text is in copyright: Smith 1993 and Supplement 2003 (Bibliopolis), Hammerstaedt & Smith 2014 (Habelt), and the EA 42/49/51 articles. Those articles are free-to-read PDFs on the Köln IfA site, e.g. EA 42 'Discoveries of 2009 (NF 167-181)'. Smith 2026 (Tab, open access) is an English translation only; its licence was not confirmed. No openly licensed Greek text of the current 305-piece corpus exists. The surviving text is only about 8,000 Greek words (Smith), not the 15-25k the candidate states; 25k was the original length.
item_047.research_yield: Possible articles: Diogenes' cosmopolitan 'single country' fragment and his utopia (fr. 56) set against Stoic and Russian Verlinsky scholarship; the 2007-2017 fragments (Plato's cosmogony polemic, the letter to women NF 186, the Ethics preface NF 207); and the epigraphy of a 'book on a wall' in Hadrianic Lycia.
item_047.recommendation: Downgrade and drop the proposed pilot: Ethics + Letter to Antipater already exists in Russian (amateur, from English), and English is complete and open access (Smith 2026). If kept as a Russian-only project, start with the first-ever Russian translation from the Greek of NF 133-219 (2007-2017 finds, Hammerstaedt & Smith 2014 + EA 49/51, ~2k words), later expanding to a scholarly Russian translation of all 305 pieces.

item_048.title_short: Papyri Graecae Magicae (pilot PGM XIII, Eighth Book of Moses)
item_048.ru_found: The claim that this is untranslated is REFUTED, both for the corpus and for the pilot unit. Scholarly translations from the Greek: (1) A. V. Petrov, "Памятники античной синкретической магии", AKADEMEIA: Материалы и исследования по истории платонизма, vol. 3, St Petersburg: SPbU, 2000, pp. 349-376, translated from Preisendanz. It covers PGM IV 153-285, 286-295, 296-466, 467-849 (including the Mithras Liturgy), 850-929, 930-1114, 1265-1274, 1596-1715, 1716-1870, 1871-1929, 3086-3124 and 3209-3254, plus PGM XIII 1-233 (the Monas / Eighth Book of Moses, version A up to "спрячь эту книгу"). Online at plato.today/AKADEMIA/akademia3/12.htm; the old centant.spbu.ru URL is dead. (2) E. S. Lazarev, "Литургия Митры (PGM IV 475-834)", with an appendix translation from the Greek and commentary by Lazarev and A. L. Rychkov, in Россия и гнозис, vol. I, St Petersburg: RKhGA, 2015, pp. 306 and 314ff. The same volume has A. V. Garadzha's translation of Suppl. Mag. I 42 (p. 375). Online and amateur: (3) Anna Blaze (Анна Блейз), greek.thesaurusdeorum.com, about 20 passages: PGM I 1-42, 42-195, 262-347; II 1-64; III 1-164, 494-611; IV 1115-1165, 1331-1389, 1390-1495, 1716-1870, 2145-2240, 2714-2784; V 96-172, 459-489; VII 593-619, 628-642, 862-918; VIII 1-63; XIa; LXX 4-25. None of these are from XIII. (4) Castalia club, castaliasilvasacra.ru, 13 Jan 2021: "Восьмая книга Моисея", the WHOLE of PGM XIII in four parts (1-343, 343-646, 646-734, 734-1077), translated by "Lucas Moorings" (a pseudonym) from Betz's English and edited by "Fr. Nyarlathotep Otis". It is an esoteric, indirect translation and acknowledges Petrov's 2000 version. (5) Andrey Vasilyev, "Ритуал гептаграммы (PGM XIII 734-934)", skifos.wordpress.com, 2018; the page is a placeholder and its content could not be read. (6) S. Belokon, a-guru.com: a few spells (PGM VII 973-980, XXXVI 69-101), source not stated. Overall: there is no complete scholarly Russian PGM. For XIII, the only scholarly Russian covers lines 1-233 (about 22%), and an amateur version from English covers all of it. Searches: 4 Russian WebSearch queries plus direct fetches. The pages of Petrov, Castalia and Lazarev were inspected directly.
item_048.en_found: H. D. Betz (ed.), The Greek Magical Papyri in Translation, Including the Demotic Spells, Chicago, 1986; 2nd ed. 1992. It is complete and includes PGM XIII; I recall Morton Smith as the XIII translator but did not re-verify this. The archive.org item "the-greek-magical-papyri-in-translation-betz" (dated 1986) was confirmed through its metadata. English Wikipedia also notes Goodwin's 1853 English translation of PGM V. Caveat: the session-wide WebSearch budget ran out after the Russian searches, so I could not run the required 4 English web searches. English status rests on Wikipedia and archive.org fetches, and it is not in doubt.
item_048.other_found: German: Preisendanz's facing translation (1928-31; 2nd ed. by Henrichs, 1973-74). Also Merkelbach and Totti, Abrasax III (Papyrologica Coloniensia 17.3, 1992), with text, German translation and commentary of PGM XIII; this is from memory and was not verified online this session. Latin: Leemans 1885 (P. Leid. J 395 = W = PGM XIII); English Wikipedia confirms a 1885 Latin translation of PGM XII-XIII. Spanish: J. L. Calvo Martínez and M. D. Sánchez Romero, Textos de magia en papiros griegos, Madrid: Gredos (BCG), 1987, reprinted 2004 (ISBN 978-84-249-1235-2), confirmed via Spanish Wikipedia. French and Italian: no complete translation identified, but these were not searched exhaustively.
item_048.source_text: The standard edition is Preisendanz, PGM vol. II (Leipzig/Berlin: Teubner, 1931), which contains XIII; the 2nd ed. by Henrichs (Stuttgart, 1973-74) was reprinted 2001. Copyright: Preisendanz's German translation is protected in Germany until the end of 2038 (he died in 1968). The Greek text as constituted likely falls under §70 UrhG's 25-year term for scholarly editions, which has expired for both the 1931 and 1974 editions. In the US, vol. II (1931) enters the public domain on 1 Jan 2027. The archive.org scan "PapyriGraecaeMagicae" (vol. 1 only) is now dark/removed. Public-domain alternatives for XIII: C. Leemans, Papyri graeci Musei antiquarii publici Lugduni-Batavi II (Leiden: Brill, 1885), with Greek text and Latin translation of Leiden W; and A. Dieterich, Abraxas (Leipzig, 1891), with the text of the cosmogony sections (from memory). The modern critical text, Merkelbach and Totti 1992, is in copyright.
item_048.research_yield: A synoptic RU/EN of PGM XIII's versions A, B and C and the Tenth Book would support articles on how magical handbooks were redacted, on Moses pseudepigrapha and Jewish elements, on the "seven laughs" cosmogony versus the Hermetica and Genesis, and on Nectanebo's magic in the Alexander Romance.
item_048.recommendation: Keep the candidate only after demoting it, since its Russian is partial and its English complete. Re-target the pilot to PGM XIII 234-1077 (or a complete synoptic XIII), presented as the first scholarly Russian translation from the Greek that completes Petrov's 2000 version of lines 1-233. Cite Petrov and the Castalia version openly.

item_049.title_short: Abinnaeus archive, P.Abinn. 1–82 (petitions dossier 44–57 as first unit)
item_049.ru_found: I found no Russian translation of the archive, whether full or partial. I ran 6 Russian web searches: «архив Абиннея папирусы перевод», «Флавий Абинней», «Авиннея архив Дионисиада», «Абинней префект алы Дионисиада папирус», the Kaor letter in Russian, and the 2025 Chepel/Shavrin/Lekhnovich papyrus-letter chrestomathy (ЦЕИ РАН). That chrestomathy has only 15 letters from Tbilisi, Moscow and Hermitage collections, none from P.Abinn. I also searched the CyberLeninka API for Абинней, Абиннея, Авинней, Абиней, «архив Абиннея», Каор and Abinnaeus, with 0 relevant hits. The ru.wikipedia article «Флавий Абинней» only paraphrases the documents. It cites Павловская А.И., «Египетская хора в IV в.» (М.: Наука, 1979) and her ВДИ 2001 no. 1 article on Athanasius. These are the most likely places for translated excerpts, but I could not check them. Серафимов (Para bellum! 29, 2009, late-roman.ru/xlegio) quotes P.Abinn. 1 in Latin only, with no translation. I could not check Soviet anthologies such as Хрестоматия по истории Древнего Рима for the Kaor letter. My web-search budget ran out, and Google Books, DDG and Mojeek blocked automated queries.
item_049.en_found: The claim is refuted. The editio princeps is H.I. Bell, V. Martin, E.G. Turner, D. van Berchem, The Abinnaeus Archive: Papers of a Roman Officer in the Reign of Constantius II (Oxford: Clarendon, 1962; xiv+191 pp.). It gives the Greek and Latin texts with an English translation. en.wikipedia says it was "edited and published with an English translation in 1962", and the Google Books record (id Wv7SAAAAMAAJ) and WorldCat agree. A lending copy is at archive.org/details/abinnaeusarchive0000hibe. The very small account and list scraps may lack translations, but I could not verify this. Individual texts also appear in other English collections. Kaor's letter P.Abinn. 32 is in Hunt–Edgar, Select Papyri I (Loeb 1932) no. 161, and in Winter, Life and Letters in the Papyri (1933) p. 152. P.Abinn. 34 is in Bagnall–Cribiore, Women's Letters from Ancient Egypt (2006) p. 358, and in the online edition (2008) no. 251. Review: J.D. Thomas, JHS 84 (1964) 185–186.
item_049.other_found:
I checked the HGV metadata in papyri/idp.data for 51 P.Abinn. records. Translations are listed for these texts:
- P.Abinn. 32, in German (Schubart, Ein Jahrtausend am Nil 1912/1923; Metzger, Nachrichten aus dem Wüstensand 1974 no. 75; Guyot–Klein, Das frühe Christentum 1994 II 65), French (Burnet, L'Égypte ancienne 2003 no. 37) and Italian (Tibiletti, Lettere private 1979 no. 24; also Naldini, Il Cristianesimo in Egitto no. 40).
- P.Abinn. 7 and 8, in Italian (Tibiletti 1979 nos. 25–26).
- P.Abinn. 33, in German (Schubart).
- P.Abinn. 34, in French (Schubert, Vivre en Égypte 2000 no. 70).
I found no complete French, German, Italian or Spanish translation of the archive.
item_049.source_text: The best open text is the Greek and Latin of P.Abinn. in the DDbDP on papyri.info (github.com/papyri/idp.data, CC BY 3.0), with HGV metadata and Berichtigungsliste (BL) corrections. Older public-domain first editions exist for part of the archive: Kenyon, P.Lond. II (1898), and Nicole, P.Gen. I (1896–1906), both on archive.org. The standard edition is Bell, Martin, Turner and van Berchem (Oxford 1962). It is still in copyright (Turner died 1983, van Berchem 2000).
item_049.research_yield: This would be the first Russian translation with commentary. Possible articles: army–village relations and abuses (petitions 44–57); Abinnaeus's career and the protectores, from P.Abinn. 1 and the Barnes 1985 debate; Kaor's letter and 4th-c. Christianity; an updated text drawing on BL corrections since 1962.
item_049.recommendation: Keep, but at lower priority. It is a Russian-first project only, since a full English translation exists (1962), so it cannot be called a first-ever translation. The best first unit is the petitions dossier P.Abinn. 44–57, with P.Abinn. 1 and 32 added.

item_050.title_short: Tabulae ceratae Daciae (Alburnus Maior wax tablets), whole corpus of c. 25
item_050.ru_found: No Russian translation of the corpus or of any single tablet found. About 12 Russian queries were run: «трансильванские триптихи», «Альбурнус/Альбурн Майор», «восковые таблички Дакия», the hire contract with Флавий Секундин / Аврелий Адиутор / «Меммий, сын Асклепия», the collegium of Jupiter Cernenus, Колосовская, Штаерман, хрестоматии Утченко/Кузищина, and site:ancientrome.ru. What turned up: Борухович, «В мире античных свитков» (1976, ancientrome.ru) only mentions the tablets and translates none. Штаерман's appendix of Latin inscriptions in ВДИ 1955 no. 3 (elib.gsu.by) gives Latin texts only, and none of the Dacian tablets. Сайко's Russian article on bankers' books (Белгород 2014, cyberleninka) has no Dacian tablets. A Ukrainian rendering exists: М. М. Сайко, Вісник ХНУ. Історія 50 (2015) 216–225 (periodicals.karazin.ua/history/article/view/1559) translates nearly all of the societas danistaria (CIL III p. 950 no. XIII) and the opening of the deposit tablet (p. 949 no. XII). Not checked because the search limit ran out: Федорова, «Введение в латинскую эпиграфику» (1982); Soviet sourcebooks (Хрестоматия, vol. 3, 1953; Утченко 1962; Кузищин 1987/2004); К. М. Смирнов, «Банки и банкирский депозит в Риме» (1909). These may quote the 164 AD hire contract or the deposit tablet in Russian. A full Russian corpus is very unlikely.
item_050.en_found: No complete English translation found in about 8 English searches. Only single tablets are translated inside secondary works: the 164 AD hire contract of Memmius son of Asclepius (CIL III p. 948 no. X) on historyofinformation.com; the sale of the girl Passia, 139 AD, in Humanities (MDPI) 8.1.1 (2019), 'Dalmatians and Dacians'. Meyer, Legitimacy and Law in the Roman World (CUP 2004), discusses the tablets, but it is not known whether it translates them. Johnson, Coleman-Norton and Bourne, Ancient Roman Statutes (1961), covers statutes, and no triptychs were found in it. Lewis and Reinhold, Roman Civilization II, probably has the hire contract and/or the collegium dissolution, but this was not checked. Pólay's 1980 English booklet on the contracts' Hellenistic features (Akadémiai Kiadó, 18 pp.) is a study, not a translation.
item_050.other_found: Romanian, full: I. I. Russu, Inscripțiile Daciei romane I (Bucharest: Ed. Academiei, 1975), covering the diplomas and 'tăblițele cerate' with Latin text and Romanian translation. Library records and adevarul.ro confirm the translations are there. Hungarian, probably partial or full: E. Pólay, A dáciai viaszostáblák szerződései (Budapest 1972; listed in the BnF record and Nótári 2020); whether it contains translations is not verified. Ukrainian, partial: Saiko 2015, two tablets. German: G. Ciulei, 'Die Arbeitsverträge in den siebenbürgischen Wachstafeln', RIDA 38 (1991) 121–152, covers the hire contracts; whether it translates them is unknown. French: Ciulei, Les triptyques de Transylvanie (1983), from memory and not verified. No Italian or Spanish translation found. FIRA III (Arangio-Ruiz 1943) gives Latin only.
item_050.source_text: The base text is CIL III pars II (Berlin 1873), pp. 921–960, 'Instrumenta Dacica in tabulis ceratis' (Zangemeister/Mommsen), nos. I–XXV. It is public domain and available as scans on archive.org; Latin texts are also in EDCS/EDH. FIRA III (Arangio-Ruiz 1943) has improved Latin texts of the legal acts; the Latin text itself carries no copyright problem, but the editorial apparatus is under Italian copyright until 2035. The standard modern edition, IDR I (Russu 1975, with Romanian translation), is in copyright. Newer readings have appeared since, e.g. the 2022 digitisation and reinterpretation of TabCerD XVI (Aiud museum) and work by Ciulei and Pólay. Use CIL III as the base text and check difficult cursive readings against IDR I and FIRA III.
item_050.research_yield: First Russian corpus of Roman documentary law in practice. It enables articles on provincial locatio operarum (miners' hire), slave sales and Aedilician guarantees, societas danistaria and banking, collegium dissolution, Illyrian/Pirustae migrants' onomastics, and scribal vulgar Latin. It also invites comparison with the Pompeian (Sulpicii, Iucundus), Vindolanda and Bloomberg tablets.
item_050.recommendation: Keep it: the 'untranslated' claim holds, since there is no Russian or English corpus, only English excerpts and a full Romanian translation. Best first unit: the dated legal acts from CIL III. These are the three hire contracts (nos. IX–XI), the slave sales (nos. VI, VII, XXV), the deposit and loans (nos. V, XII), the societas danistaria (no. XIII) and the collegium dissolution (no. I), about 1.5k words. Before publishing, check the Soviet sourcebooks and Федорова 1982 for Russian excerpts.

item_051.ru_found: There is one Russian translation and it does not reach the proposed unit: Пасхальная хроника, tr., intro. and commentary by Л.А. Самуткина (СПб.: Алетейя, 2004, «Византийская библиотека. Источники», 214 pp., ISBN 5-89329-686-9). The full text is on azbyka.ru (azbyka.ru/otechnik/konfessii/pashalnaja-hronika/). I checked its Dindorf markers directly. It covers the Prologue of Philo, the Apollinaris excerpt, and the Epitome from Adam through the patriarchs. That is roughly Dindorf I pp. 3–88, ending at Serukh/Nahor/Terah with Cecrops, Hellen, Picus, Faunus and Hephaestus. It stops before Abraham, and the notes end at Serukh/Terah. Juhász (2013 thesis) also describes the Russian as "erster Teil (Adam bis Abraham)". I found no continuation volume. Ru-Wikipedia lists only Самуткина 2004. Searches of ancientrome, vostlit, the Вестник ПСТГУ / Богословские труды / ВизВрем range, dissertations, Latyshev's Scythica and Alexander/Olympiad excerpts found no Russian for any part between Abraham and 628. The only other Russian, the Свод древнейших известий о славянах т. II, likely has 7th-century excerpts, which fall outside the unit. Verdict for the proposed unit (Abraham–284): none in Russian.
item_051.en_found: This refutes part of the sweep's claim. (1) Whitby & Whitby, Chronicon Paschale 284–628 AD (TTH 7, Liverpool UP 1989; repr. 2007) covers AD 284–628. (2) An anonymous online English translation on attalus.org (www.attalus.org/translate/paschal.html, page dated 27.02.18) covers "Olympiads 112 to 187", i.e. c. 332–32 BC. It is translated from Dindorf as reprinted in PG 92. It is selective, giving entries only for years with events (about 44 of 76 Olympiads). It includes Alexander's capture of Babylon, his 12 cities and his death, the Ptolemies, the high priests and the Maccabees, plus one later passage (the John the Baptist / high-priest list). It leaves out the consular list. (3) A companion attalus page (www.attalus.org/translate/consuls.html) tabulates the Chronicon's Olympiad-year / consul / Egyptian-king equivalences for 336–30 BC, with notes on omitted and inserted consul years. English Wikipedia links both pages. As a result, the proposed pilot unit (Ol. 100–130, Alexander and the Diadochi) is largely available in English already from Ol. 112 on. There is no English for Abraham–Ol. 111 or for c. 30 BC–AD 284, apart from scattered passages that scholars quote (possibly some as Africanus parallels in Wallraff/Adler, GCS 2007; not verified). sourcelibrary.org holds an OCR of Dindorf vol. I (762 pp., Public Domain Mark) and translates texts CC BY-SA, but has no translation of this one so far.
item_051.other_found: Juhász's 2013 PhD thesis (PPKE, Vorarbeiten zur neuen Editio critica der Osterchronik) states that other translations are only "Auszüge" in French, Hungarian and Serbian, plus a French translation of the preface. The French preface translation is probably Beaucamp et al., "Le prologue de la Chronique pascale", Travaux et Mémoires 7 (1979). I recall this from memory and could not confirm it by search. The Serbian and Hungarian excerpts most likely concern 7th-century Avars and Slavs (VIINJ-type collections), but that is not verified. I found no German, Italian, Spanish or Modern Greek translation of any part. The only full-text version of Abraham–284 remains the Latin of Rader (1615) and Du Cange, reprinted in Dindorf and PG 92. My web-search budget ran out before two final checks: Hungarian/Serbian scope, and Russian excerpts of the AD 1–284 Nativity/Passion sections.
item_051.source_text: The best public-domain text is L. Dindorf, Chronicon Paschale, CSHB, Bonn: Weber 1832, vol. I (Google Books id N3AGAAAAQAAJ; an OCR copy is on sourcelibrary.org under the Public Domain Mark). It has the Greek and Du Cange's Latin and is reprinted in PG 92 (also public domain). Dindorf is still the standard edition, but it is defective: according to Juhász it follows Rader and Du Cange rather than the readings of the codex unicus Vat. gr. 1941, has few parallel-source markings, and contains misprints. A new CFHB (Series Vindobonensis) edition was prepared in FWF project P25485 (PI C. Gastgeber, with E. Juhász, 2014–2018). It is not listed as published or forthcoming in the 2024 CFHB report. Once it appears it will be in copyright, and nothing currently blocks using Dindorf. Plan to flag textual problems in the commentary (and if possible check Vat. gr. 1941 images). Also verify numerals and consul names against the attalus consul table and standard fasti.
item_051.research_yield: Articles could cover how the Chronicon Paschale builds its Olympiad, consul and regnal synchronisms and why its fasti drift. They could also cover its sources (Africanus, Eusebius, Malalas), the Passion/Nativity computus and the 5509 BC era, and the Republic and Augustus in 7th-century chronography. A comparison of Alexander/Diadochi entries with Malalas, Syncellus and the Excerpta Barbari is another option.
item_051.recommendation: Keep the candidate, but drop the proposed Ol. 100–130 pilot: from Ol. 112 it is already in English online (attalus.org), although still first-ever in Russian. The best first unit is the gap between attalus and Whitby, c. 30 BC (Augustus/Nativity) to the Diocletian entry where TTH 7 begins. That would give the first RU+EN translation of the chronicle's core Christological and paschal chronology and close the English coverage. Ol. 1–111 (archaic and classical Greece, the Roman kings and early Republic) is the second choice.

item_052.title_short: Hippolytus of Rome, Chronicon (Synagoge chronon): Diamerismos
item_052.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation of the Greek Chronicon itself (H1, Matritensis gr. 121/4701). The Pravoslavnaya Entsiklopediya article "Ипполит Римский" (vol. 26, online 2016, pravenc.ru/text/673797.html) lists Russian translations of his works, and none is of the Chronicle. azbyka.ru, ru.wikipedia and searches for «Хроника», «Συναγωγὴ χρόνων», «диамерисмос/диамеризмос», «Liber generationis» and «Стадиасм» also turned up nothing. However, the Diamerismos is already readable in Russian in two derived versions:
(1) Пасхальная хроника, translated from Greek with an introduction and commentary by Л. А. Самуткина (СПб.: Алетейя, 2004, «Византийская библиотека. Источники», 214 pp., ISBN 5-89329-686-9; full text at azbyka.ru/otechnik/konfessii/pashalnaja-hronika/). Its section «Расселение народов» is the Chronicon Paschale's reworking of the Hippolytan Diamerismos: 72 nations, peoples who know writing, lands, islands. The commentary checks it against Hippolytus section by section, citing § numbers from Bauer–Helm, and translates a few Hippolytan readings. One example is §§ 146–149.
(2) Хроники Фредегара, translated from Latin with commentary by Г. А. Шмидт (СПб.: Евразия; М.: Клио, 2015, 464 pp.). Book I, chapters 1–24, is the Liber generationis, the Latin version of Hippolytus' Chronicon, and the translator says so. Chapters 3–11 are the whole Diamerismos in Fredegar's form: the division of the earth, the 72 languages, the sons of Japheth/Ham/Shem, peoples who know writing, regions, islands, recent colonists, mountains and rivers. That is about 1,900 Russian words, which I confirmed in the online text. The earlier Kazan translation, «Творения св. Ипполита» (1898), came before Bauer's 1905 editio princeps of the Madrid text and does not contain it.
item_052.en_found: The colleague's claim (en "partial", only an online draft, no published English) is refuted. The full English translation is T. C. Schmidt with Nick Nicholas as co-translator, Hippolytus of Rome: Commentary on Daniel and 'Chronicon' (Piscataway: Gorgias Press, 2017; Gorgias Studies in Early Christianity and Patristics 67; 311 pp.; ISBN 978-1-4632-0658-1, ebook 978-1-4632-3735-6). Source: gorgiaspress.com/hippolytus-commentary-on-daniel-and-chronicon. Its contents include "Text of the 'Chronicon'" and the Periplus, lines 240–613. There is also a free precursor: Schmidt & Nicholas, "The Chronicon of Hippolytus", 2nd edition (rough draft), 2010, chronicon.net. A copy is at ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/AUTHORS/Schmidt2010-ChroniconHippolytus.pdf. I checked that PDF: it is a complete annotated translation of §§ 1–778, made from Helm's GCS 46 using both H1 and H2. It covers the whole Diamerismos (sons of Japheth, the 72 nations, lettered peoples, islands, rivers and mountains) and the Stadiasmus, and it uses the Latin and Armenian versions where the Greek fails.
item_052.other_found: German: J. Markwart's German translation of the Armenian version is printed in Bauer–Helm, GCS 46. The Gorgias volume is described as the first English translation. My searches for a French (Budé/SC), Italian or Spanish translation of the Chronicon found nothing, and the item's "none found" stands. Caveat: those checks were limited because the web-search budget ran out mid-task. The Diamerismos also survives in derivative chronicles that do have translations: Synkellos in English (Adler & Tuffin, 2002), plus the Russian Chronicon Paschale and Fredegar described above.
item_052.source_text: Best public-domain text: A. Bauer, Die Chronik des Hippolytos im Matritensis graecus 121 (Leipzig: Hinrichs, 1905; TU 29.1), with O. Cuntz on the Stadiasmus. It is on archive.org as diechronikdeshi00hippgoog, flagged NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT; Bauer died in 1919. Public-domain Latin versions: Mommsen, MGH AA 9 (Chronica minora I, 1892), and Frick, Chronica minora I (Teubner, 1892). The Greek Chronicon Paschale parallel is in Dindorf's 1832 edition, also public domain. The standard critical edition is R. Helm (after A. Bauer), Hippolytus Werke IV: Die Chronik, GCS 46 (Berlin: Akademie-Verlag, 2nd ed. 1955; 1st ed. GCS 36, 1929). It is in copyright: Helm died in 1966. Use Bauer 1905 as the base text and cite Helm's section numbers.
item_052.research_yield: A synoptic Russian Diamerismos: Greek H1 alongside the Liber generationis, the Chronicon Paschale and Synkellos, with gazetteer identifications. Possible articles: Pontic, Caucasian and Sarmatian ethnonyms; the list of "lettered peoples"; how the text reached the ethnographic introduction of the Russian Primary Chronicle (Повесть временных лет) via Hamartolos; Hippolytus' chronology.
item_052.recommendation: Drop as a "first translation" candidate. A full English translation was published in 2017 (Gorgias), and the Diamerismos already exists in Russian in two derived versions: Samutkina 2004 and G. A. Schmidt 2015 (Fredegar Book I). Keep it only as a secondary project, a commented Russian translation of the Greek Madrid text of the Diamerismos (about §§ 1–239, before the Periplus) set synoptically against those Russian versions.

item_053.title_short: Georgios Monachos (Hamartolos), Chronicon, Book I (Alexander and Brahmans)
item_053.ru_found: REFUTED. There is a complete modern Russian translation: В. А. Матвеенко, Л. И. Щеголева, «Временник Георгия Монаха (Хроника Георгия Амартола). Русский текст, комментарий, указатели» (М.: Богородский печатник, 2000, 543 pp.). It is free online at azbyka.ru/otechnik/Istorija_Tserkvi/vremennik-georgija-monaha/. It is translated from the Old Slavonic (Trinity/Tver MS) and checked line by line against de Boor's Greek. Losses against the Greek are marked in angle brackets and Slavonic additions in italics. Every passage carries Istrin (И) and de Boor (Б) page sigla. Its Book 1 ("Краткий Временник") covers the whole proposed unit: ch. 4 Nimrod; ch. 16 Cyrus; ch. 23 and 25 Alexander (Darius, and Candace capturing him); ch. 26–27 the Brahmans, the Macrobians and the Amazons. I checked this on the site and found, for example, the line on Candace: "Царь Александр, ты пленил весь мир, а тебя пленила женщина". Bibliographies also cite a later two-volume Matveenko–Shchegoleva edition, «Книги временные и образные Георгия Монаха» (М., 2006–2011). I did not inspect it. Older items: Istrin's edition of the Slavonic text (1920–1930), and Senina 2012 (the reign of Leo V only). I found no Russian translation made directly from the Greek. Searches run: Матвеенко/Щеголева, Богородский печатник, брахманы/Кандакия, Афиногенов, and Palladius in Russian.
item_053.en_found: The pilot unit is already in English. (1) R. Stoneman, Legends of Alexander the Great (London: J.M. Dent / Everyman, 1994) includes "a translation of I.19" of George's Chronicle, the Alexander chapter with the visit to Jerusalem and the India material (confirmed by BMCR 1995.08.06, bmcr.brynmawr.edu/?p=20506). (2) Philip A. Harland's blog (2023) gives free English versions of Chronicle 1.19 on the Brahmans (from Palladius) and of the customs catalogue (Seres, Bactrians, Brahmans, Chaldaeans, Gauls, Britons, Amazons), made in consultation with Stoneman (philipharland.com/Blog/2023/02/...). (3) J. Crow, J. Bardill and R. Bayliss, The Water Supply of Byzantine Constantinople (SPRS 2008), App. 1: only aqueduct excerpts from the later books. I found no complete English translation of Book I or of the whole chronicle. Di Serio's article (Studia Ceranea 11, 2021, CC BY-NC-ND) studies the I.19 ethnographic catalogue and lists no translations.
item_053.other_found: French: Thomas Picciola, «La Chronique de Georges le Moine. Avant-propos, livre I et extraits des livres II à VI : traduction et commentaire», a doctoral thesis at Aix-Marseille Université, defended 18 June 2024. It gives the Greek text from Dmitry Afinogenov's unpublished new edition, with an apparatus comparing MS P and de Boor, and a French translation of the whole of Book I. It is not yet a commercial publication, and I could not confirm whether it is online on HAL or theses.fr. Medieval translations: Slavonic (10th–11th c.) and Georgian. My Italian and German searches found nothing.
item_053.source_text: C. de Boor, Georgii Monachi Chronicon, vol. 1 (Leipzig: Teubner, 1904), public domain, archive.org/details/georgiimonachic01boorgoog. The standard modern citation is the corrected reprint by P. Wirth (Stuttgart: Teubner, 1978); Wirth's corrections and additions are probably still in copyright, but de Boor's text is free. Muralt 1859 and PG 110 are also public domain but follow a different recension. D. Afinogenov's new critical edition is still unpublished.
item_053.research_yield: Little room for a first-ever translation. What remains open: Greek and Slavonic divergences in Book I, George's handling of his sources (Palladius, Pseudo-Caesarius, Josephus on Alexander at Jerusalem), and how the customs catalogue passed into the Primary Chronicle (ПВЛ). All of these are already well studied.
item_053.recommendation: Drop as a first-ever candidate. Russian has a full annotated translation keyed to de Boor (Matveenko–Shchegoleva 2000, free online). The Alexander and Brahmans unit is in English (Stoneman 1994; Harland 2023) and in French (Picciola 2024 thesis). A direct translation from the Greek of I.19 could only be a secondary revision project, collated against the existing Russian text.

item_054.ru_found: REFUTED: the claim "ru none" is wrong. There is a full Russian translation of Book 1, but it is amateur and made from the English. Translator "Агностик" (agnostik), simposium.ru, posted 06/08/2013, at https://simposium.ru/ru/node/10525 with chapters at nodes 10526–10540. It was made from Bedrosian's English (rbedrosian.com/euseb.html). It has all 15 sections: Introduction, Chaldean (Abydenus and Polyhistor fragments present, "Бероз"), Assyrian, Median, Lydian, Persian, Hebrew ×2, Egyptian (Manetho), Greek, Olympiads, Corinth/Sparta/thalassocracies/Macedon/Thessaly, Kings of Asia and Syria (Porphyry on the Ptolemies and Seleucids), Romans ×2. It ends with the note "[Армянская рукопись ... обрывается]". By my page count it runs to about 35k words. A mirror on royallib.com is titled "Хронология". The translator corrects some of Bedrosian's errors but did not use the Armenian and published no apparatus. Partial items: ancientrome.ru has only the Ptolemy list (A. S. Martynov 2007, from the attalus English). B. Filin's «Древние фрагменты Кори» (Ridero 2021, from Cory/Hodges 1876) has Berossus and other fragments. simposium.ru node/10143 has Manetho's «Египтика» (Д. В. Мещанский; ru.wikisource cites the 1940 Loeb, i.e. Waddell). Jerome's Canons appeared in Russian in Kiev in 1910 (not Book 1). I found no scholarly Russian translation from the Armenian (searched ВДИ, cyberleninka, azbyka, ru.wikisource, Yerevan/Матенадаран).
item_054.en_found: Full English, two versions. (1) Robert Bedrosian 2008, Book 1 translated directly from the Classical Armenian (Aucher 1818). He dedicated it to the public domain ("This work is in the public domain"). It is on tertullian.org/fathers/eusebius_chronicon_02_intro.htm, archive.org (EusebiusChroniclechronicon) and attalus.org/armenian/euseb.html. (2) Andrew Smith, attalus.org/translate/eusebius.html, from Petermann's Latin (Schoene ed.); ToposText work 531 uses it. Both are online and not peer-reviewed. The pilot unit (the Chaldaean section) is also well covered in scholarly English: Burstein, The Babyloniaca of Berossus (1978); Verbrugghe & Wickersham, Berossos and Manetho (U Michigan 1996); BNJ 680 Berossos (De Breucker). Adler & Tuffin's Synkellos (OUP 2002) gives the Greek parallels. I could not confirm a BNJ entry for Abydenus 685.
item_054.other_found: FRENCH, full and scholarly: Eusèbe de Césarée, Chronique, Tome I. Intro by A. Cohen-Skalli, translated from the Armenian by Agnès Ouzounian, commentary by S. Brillante, S. H. Aufrère, S. Morlet and A. Ouzounian. Les Belles Lettres, La Roue à Livres 90, Paris 2020, 576 pp., ISBN 9782251450797. The blurb calls it "la première traduction française de la première partie". It was reviewed in REA 123 (2021). GERMAN, full: J. Karst, GCS 20 (Leipzig 1911), from the Armenian. LATIN: Aucher 1818; Petermann in Schoene 1875. Italian and Spanish: none found. A new Armenian edition with German translation by A. Drost-Abgarjan was announced (1998–2006); I could not confirm that it has been published.
item_054.source_text: Armenian text: Aucher (Awgerean), Eusebii Pamphili Caesariensis episcopi Chronicon bipartitum, Venice, San Lazzaro, 1818, 2 vols, Armenian plus Latin. It is public domain, with Google Books PDFs (tertullian.org links them). Schoene–Petermann, Eusebi Chronicorum libri duo I (Berlin 1875), Latin, is public domain. Bedrosian 2008 is a public-domain English crib. Karst's GCS 20 (1911) is public domain in the US. In the EU it is probably protected until 2032, assuming Karst died in 1962; I took that date from memory and did not verify it. There is no modern critical edition of the Armenian, and the announced Drost-Abgarjan GCS edition is unconfirmed. For the Greek fragments, Synkellos is in Dindorf, CSHB 1829 (public domain). Mosshammer's Teubner (1984), FGrH and BNJ are in copyright, as is the 2020 French translation.
item_054.research_yield: Little is new. Possible articles: a critique of the existing Russian relay translation (English to Russian) against the Armenian; a first annotated Russian translation of the Abydenus/Polyhistor Chaldaean fragments with comparison to Synkellos. Both depend on Armenological expertise that the editor lacks.
item_054.recommendation: Drop. A full Russian version exists online (simposium.ru 2013, an amateur relay from English), and there are full English (Bedrosian 2008, public domain), French (Les Belles Lettres 2020) and German (Karst 1911) translations, so it fails the "first-ever" criterion. If kept at all, the only option is a scholarly Russian translation of the Chaldaean section directly from Aucher's Armenian, as a low-priority side project needing an Armenologist reviewer.

item_055.title_short: Cassius Dio, Roman History 1–35 (fragments + Zonaras 7–9); pilot: regal period
item_055.ru_found:
No Russian translation of the books 1–35 fragments or of Zonaras 7–9 found. I ran about 10 Russian searches, checked ru.wikipedia (Дион Кассий, Иоанн Зонара), the ancientrome.ru author index and its Dio page, simposium.ru, vostlit, azbyka, cyberleninka and VDI.

What does exist in Russian:
- Books 51–63 and 64–80, Makhlayuk et al., Нестор-История 2011/2014.
- Book 52 in ВДИ 2008; book 53 by Trukhina on the PSTGU site.
- Books 36, 37 (Tariverdieva and Lyubimova) and 48 (Ryazanov), translated from English, on ancientrome.ru. Its Dio index lists only these three books, and it has no Zonaras page.
- Books 57–63 by Talakh (Kyiv 2013).
- Excerpts: Kazhdan in «Поздняя греческая проза» (1961; e.g. 37.11–14); Грабарь-Пассек (51.5–15); themed excerpts on Germans (1937), Scythia/Caucasus (ВДИ 1948) and India (2007); Photius cod. 71 and Xiphilinus as amateur versions on simposium.ru.

Zonaras exists in Russian only for the canon commentaries and a marriage treatise (Bondach, Вестник ПСТГУ 2007). The «Паралипомен Зонарин» (Moscow 1847, ed. Bodyansky) is a medieval Church Slavonic abridgement, not a modern Russian translation. Isolated early-book fragments may sit in Soviet chrestomathies (1962 Хрестоматия по истории Древнего Рима); I could not verify this.
item_055.en_found:
E. Cary, Loeb vols. I–III (1914–), translate the fragments together with Zonaras' epitome. Vol. I covers books 1–11, with the labelled Zonaras passages interleaved. It is free online at LacusCurtius (penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Cassius_Dio/), marked public domain in the US.

H. B. Foster, Dio's Rome vol. 1 (1905), translates the Zonaras epitome of books 1–21 and the fragments of books 22–35. It is on Project Gutenberg (ebook 18047).

Banchich and Lane (Routledge 2009) translate only Zonaras 12.15–13.19, not books 7–9. No new 21st-century English translation of the early books was found. Burden-Strevens and Lindholmer (eds.), Cassius Dio's Forgotten History of Early Rome (Brill 2019), is a volume of essays, not a translation.
item_055.other_found:
Spanish, full: Dión Casio, Historia romana. Libros I–XXXV, translated by Domingo Plácido Suárez (Gredos, Madrid 2004; reprint ISBN 9788424998226).

Italian, partial:
- BUR Storia romana vol. X, libri I–XII, introduction and notes by G. Urso, translation by A. Stroppa (Rizzoli 2022, ISBN 9788817174510; Greek text from Boissevain).
- G. Urso, Cassio Dione e i sovversivi (LED 2013): fragments of books 21–30 with Italian translation and commentary.
- No Italian found for books 13–20 or 31–35.

French, full but old: E. Gros and V. Boissée, Histoire romaine de Dion Cassius (Didot, Paris 1845–70), with facing Greek and the fragments. The modern Budé volumes cover only books 36 onward.

German: older full translations by J. A. Wagner (1783–96) and L. Tafel (1831–44). The O. Veh translation (Artemis 1985–87; De Gruyter reprint 2012, 5 vols.) covers all 80 books according to a retail listing, but I did not verify its exact contents for the fragments.
item_055.source_text:
Greek text, all public domain:
- Fragments: U. P. Boissevain, Cassii Dionis Cocceiani Historiarum Romanarum quae supersunt, vol. I (Berlin: Weidmann 1895). It contains the book 1–35 fragments with the relevant Zonaras text printed alongside. Archive.org scan: https://archive.org/download/cassiidioniscoc01cass/cassiidioniscoc01cass.pdf. Perseus catalogue: urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0385.tlg001.opp-grc4.
- Zonaras 7–9: L. Dindorf, Teubner vol. II (Leipzig 1869), scan on HathiTrust via the Online Books Page; or M. Pinder, CSHB (Bonn 1841–44).
- For provenance checks: the Excerpta Constantiniana editions (de Boor; Büttner-Wobst/Roos; Boissevain, De sententiis 1906), all public domain.

Boissevain is still the standard critical edition of the fragments; no newer critical edition replaces it. The BUR 2022 volume reprints Boissevain with minor variants. Its translation and notes are in copyright, but the base text is not. The Cary Loeb English is public domain in the US and freely available as a check text.
item_055.research_yield: Dio's regal and early-Republican narrative compared with Livy and Dionysius; Zonaras as an abbreviator (how far he can be trusted as Dio); Dio's kings as proto-emperors; the Constantinian excerpt themes as a filter on the text; Dio on Pyrrhus, the Punic Wars and the Gracchi. All of these are new to Russian scholarship.
item_055.recommendation: Keep at priority 4. The Russian gap is confirmed, the text is fully public domain and the Russian audience is broad, but English, Spanish, French and partial Italian versions exist. Start with books 1–3 fragments plus Zonaras 7.1–12 (Aeneas to the Tarquins), tag every excerpt by its source (EV/EL/ES/Tzetzes/Zonaras), and use Cary's Loeb and the Urso/Stroppa BUR as check texts.

item_056.title_short: John Malalas, Chronographia (Books I–XIII; pilot Book VIII)
item_056.ru_found:
The claim is refuted. A complete Russian translation of all 18 books exists. Ed. N. N. Bolgov, tr. N. N. Bolgov and A. M. Bolgova (vol. 2 also prepared by A. V. Kobzeva and K. O. Popkov), series «Мир поздней античности. Документы и материалы», Belgorod: НИУ «БелГУ»:
- Вып. 2 (2014): Books XIII–XVIII.
- Вып. 6 (2016): Books I–VI.
- Вып. 7 (2016): Books VII–XII. Book VIII («Время македонян», all chapters on Seleucus and the founding of Antioch) is translated in full on pp. 17–29. I downloaded the PDF and checked it: ancient-life.ru/wp-content/uploads/2016/12/МАЛАЛА-том-2-кн.-7-12.pdf.

Vol. 6 is also at ancient-life.ru/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/ and facetia.ru/node/4599. Vostlit hosts Books I–VI at vostlit.info/Texts/rus15/Malalas_2/. Kobzeva's dissertation (БелГУ 2017, dissercat) calls these volumes a «полный перевод». The volumes are labelled educational editions, free to distribute. Their notes and introduction are largely translated from the Jeffreys 1986 Australian apparatus.

Other Russian translations:
- Bolgov, Book XIII separately (rrhumanities.ru) and Book XI (Белгород 2014).
- Talakh 2013 (Kiev), Book VIII chapters 11, 13 and 15.
- Freiberg 1968, Book V.
- Averintsev 1987, excerpts from Books II and V.
- Samutkina 2000/2003, Books XIV–XVII.
- Chekalova 2001, Book XVIII.
- Istrin 1897–1914, edition of the Old Slavonic version.

Russian Wikipedia, the colleague's only source, leaves out the Bolgov volumes.
item_056.en_found: E. Jeffreys, M. Jeffreys, R. Scott et al., The Chronicle of John Malalas (Byzantina Australiensia 4, Melbourne: AABS 1986), translates all books including Book VIII. Confirmed in the BnF catalogue and on Russian Wikipedia.
item_056.other_found:
- German: Johannes Malalas, Weltchronik, tr. J. Thurn and M. Meier, introduction by C. Drosihn et al. (Bibliothek der griechischen Literatur 69, Stuttgart: Hiersemann 2009, 565 pp.). Complete; reviewers call it the first complete German translation.
- Italian: M. Maiuro, «La storia dell'impero in Giovanni Malala», translation and commentary of Books 9–14 (Tübingen dissertation, 2025, publikationen.uni-tuebingen.de). Does not include Book VIII.
- German commentary: Heidelberg Academy / Tübingen historical-philological commentary project under M. Meier (2013–2024), with the Malalas-Studien series (Steiner).
- Medieval: Old Slavonic translation, edited by Istrin.
- No complete French or Spanish translation found. The French «Recherches sur la Chronique de Jean Malalas» volumes are studies.
item_056.source_text:
- Best public-domain text: L. Dindorf, Ioannis Malalae Chronographia (CSHB, Bonn: Weber 1831), scan at https://archive.org/details/ioannismalalaec00malagoog (marked public domain). Reprinted in PG 97 (1865).
- Standard critical edition: I. Thurn, Ioannis Malalae Chronographia (CFHB 35, Berlin/New York: De Gruyter 2000), in copyright.
- Dindorf's text is outdated: it rests on Chilmead 1691 without re-collating the Baroccianus manuscript. Thurn's chapter numbering differs from Dindorf's.
item_056.research_yield: Low as a first translation. Possible articles: a critique of the Belgorod translation, which depends on the English one; Book VIII set against the Alexander Romance and the Slavonic version; the Antioch foundation legends. None would need a new Neoscholia translation.
item_056.recommendation: Drop: complete Russian (Bolgov 2014–16), English (1986) and German (2009) translations exist, and Book VIII is fully translated in Russian (2016, vol. 7, pp. 17–29). Revisit only as a possible revised philological translation from Thurn's Greek, which falls outside the first-ever mandate.

item_057.title_short: George Synkellos, Ecloga chronographica (whole work; pilot: Alexander–Diadochi section)
item_057.ru_found: No full or continuous Russian translation of the Ecloga was found. The ru.wikipedia bibliography lists only the Adler-Tuffin English translation and the Church Slavonic abridgement (ed. Totomanova, Sofia 2008). Russian versions do exist of the source fragments that Synkellos preserves, and most were translated from English, not from his Greek. (1) Manetho, "Египтика", tr. Д.В. Мещанский, simposium.ru, 2012, from Waddell's Loeb (1940): http://simposium.ru/ru/node/10143. It covers the full Epitome, including the Africanus and Eusebius dynasty lists "из Синкелла" (node/10150), the Old Chronicle (node/10144) and the Book of Sothis (node/10145). (2) Eratosthenes' "Канон царей Фив", which survives only through Synkellos, tr. "Агностик", 2013, from Cory 1828 (node/10515). (3) Berossus, "Вавилонская история" on ancientrome.ru (https://ancientrome.ru/antlitr/berossos/fragments.htm), from Verbrugghe-Wickersham 1997. It contains the Synkellos passages (Mosshammer pp. 30-32, 50-56, 71-72, 390, 416-418). For F1 the site borrows the Russian text of «Георгий Синкелл, Хронологические эксцерпты» printed in «История Древнего Востока. Тексты и документы», ed. В.И. Кузищин (М.: Высшая школа, 2002). (4) The fragments of Julius Africanus's Chronographia, many of them from Synkellos: «Историография», tr. Виктор Заславский from the English ANF, azbyka.ru/otechnik/Julij_Afrikan/istoriografija/. (5) A Russian edition of Cory's Ancient Fragments on Yandex Books; I did not check its contents. Unknown: whether Latyshev's Scythica et Caucasica (vol. I, 1893-1900; repr. ВДИ 1947-49) includes Synkellos passages, since the archive.org OCR is unreadable, and whether Smirnov's Книга Еноха (Казань 1888) translates the Greek Enoch fragments that Synkellos preserves. Nothing turned up for the Alexander–Diadochi section. Searches run: ru.wikipedia (Георгий Синкелл, Беросс), ru.wikisource (Манефон), simposium.ru, ancientrome.ru, azbyka.ru, and queries on Синкелл/Манефон/Беросс/Енох/Африкан/Латышев.
item_057.en_found: Full: William Adler and Paul Tuffin, The Chronography of George Synkellos: A Byzantine Chronicle of Universal History from the Creation (Oxford: OUP, 2002), lxxxviii + 638 pp., translated from Mosshammer's text. The BMCR review (2004.10.27, https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/?p=23595) says the work "had never been translated into any modern language" before it. The embedded fragments are also in English many times over: Manetho (Waddell, Loeb 1940), Berossus and Manetho (Verbrugghe-Wickersham 1996/97), Africanus (ANF; Wallraff et al., GCS 2007), the Enoch fragments (in the standard 1 Enoch translations), and Cory's Ancient Fragments (1828/1876).
item_057.other_found: I found no full French, German, Italian or Spanish translation; English is the only modern one. Older versions: Goar's Latin translation (Paris 1652), reprinted in Dindorf's CSHB (1829). Medieval: a Church Slavonic abridgement that survives in five Russian manuscripts of the 15th–16th c., edited by A.-M. Totomanova (Славянската версия на Хрониката на Георги Синкел, Sofia 2008). The Perseus catalogue tags the Mosshammer record "Greek, Modern", which looks like a cataloguing error: it is the Teubner edition, not a translation. The fragments have many partial modern-language versions (FGrHist/BNJ, Schnabel's Berossos, and others), but I did not go through them one by one. Caveat: only 2 dedicated English-language web searches were run, plus direct fetches of BMCR and the Perseus catalogue. The shared web-search limit ran out before more searches (including the Latyshev check) could be done.
item_057.source_text: Public domain: (a) Dindorf, Georgius Syncellus et Nicephorus CP, CSHB vol. 1 (Bonn 1829), Greek with Goar's Latin, scans on archive.org / Google Books and at https://sourcelibrary.org/book/ecloga-chronographica-bonn-cshb-syncellus. (b) Goar's editio princeps (Paris 1652). Standard edition: A.A. Mosshammer, Georgii Syncelli Ecloga chronographica (Teubner, Leipzig 1984), in copyright (now De Gruyter). It is the TLG text (tlg3045.001), available under licence only. Recommended workflow: translate from Dindorf and check readings against Mosshammer, citing Mosshammer's pagination only.
item_057.research_yield: Synkellos as a source critic (his attacks on Panodorus and Annianus); his Alexander and Diadochi chronology set against the Alexander Romance and Josephus; the Enoch/Watchers reception in Byzantium; how his Greek relates to the Slavonic abridgement and to Old Russian chronography.
item_057.recommendation: Keep at reduced priority: a full English translation exists, and the proposed Manetho-dynasties pilot is already online in Russian (Мещанский 2012, via English), so drop that unit. Start instead with the Alexander–Diadochi section (no Russian found; it matches the editor's expertise) or the antediluvian Enoch/Watchers section together with Synkellos's critique of Panodorus and Annianus.

item_058.title_short: Dexippus(?), Scythica Vindobonensia (Vind. hist. gr. 73, fols. 192–195)
item_058.ru_found:
I found no full or partial Russian translation of the Vienna fragments, only excerpts.
- Makhlayuk A.V., 'Историк на службе отечества: к вопросу о роли Публия Геренния Дексиппа в событиях 267/268 г. н.э.', Вестник РУДН. Всеобщая история 17.3 (2025) 317–336 (https://journals.rudn.ru/world-history/article/view/46287). I checked the PDF. It summarises all the fragments and gives short Russian renderings: one sentence of fol. 194r lines 5–10 (Ptolemy the Athenian guarding the Macedonian–Thessalian passes) and phrases from 192v–193r (Philostratus, 'мощный в речах и мыслях'). It has no continuous translation.
- Destunis 1860 and the reprint in 'Византийские историки' (2003) cover only the old Constantinian and Vatican fragments.
- The historica.ru forum has a thread 'Венский Дексипп' (topic 12782). It is login-gated, so I could not check whether users posted an amateur translation.
Russian searches run:
- 'Дексипп венские фрагменты Scythica Vindobonensia перевод'
- 'Дексипп палимпсест Вена новые фрагменты готы Книва'
- 'новые фрагменты Дексиппа Скифика перевод'
- Scythica Vindobonensia with cyberleninka/elibrary
- 'Дексипп Декий речь Берое Острогота перевод'
- 'Венский Дексипп' / 'венских фрагментов Дексиппа'
- one extended Russian query
- one Ukrainian query ('Дексіпп Скіфіка віденський палімпсест переклад')
None found anything else. The 2020 project bibliography (Empire in Crisis, Anhang III) lists no Russian work.
item_058.en_found:
English covers essentially everything published so far, so the sweep's 'partial' is too low.
- Martin & Grusková, GRBS 54 (2014) 728–754: fols. 194r.29–194v and 195r, Greek plus English translation, CC BY 3.0. This is exactly the proposed pilot unit, translated by the editors themselves. I checked the PDF ('Translation' section).
- Mallan & Davenport, JRS 105 (2015) 203–226: fols. 192v–193r (Thessalonica/Thermopylae). The abstract says it 'presents an English translation'. The accepted manuscript is open on ORA (Oxford).
- Martin & Grusková, 'Facing the Plague and the Goths', GRBS 62 (2022) 437–493: new fol. 192r lines 13–30, edition plus English translation, CC BY 4.0.
- C.P. Jones, 'Further Fragments of Dexippus (2)' (academia.edu 26199041, 2016): an informal English translation of all the new fragments then published. Boteva confirms this in Empire in Crisis (2020) p. 207 n. 59. This covers 194r and 195v, whose formal publications are in German.
- Possibly K.B. Robinson, 'A Historical and Historiographical Commentary on the Scythica Vindobonensia' (MPhil, UWA 2023), cited by Makhlayuk. I could not check whether it contains a translation.
item_058.other_found:
German: the editors published working translations of every page they released.
- 'Dexippus Vindobonensis (?)', Wiener Studien 127 (2014) 101–120: fols. 192v–193r.
- Tyche 29 (2014) 29–43: fol. 194r.
- Tyche 30 (2015) 35–53: fol. 195v.
- ZPE 204 (2017) 40–46: new readings for 195v lines 6–10.
- Many passages are also quoted in translation in Empire in Crisis (2020).
Italian: L. Mecella, Dexippo di Atene. Testimonianze e frammenti (Tivoli 2013) includes fol. 195r as D 14, from Grusková's 2010 transcript. It probably carries an Italian translation, but I did not confirm this.
Unverified leads, where it is not confirmed whether these works contain a translation:
- French: P. De Cicco, Nantes doctoral thesis 2017 on fragmentary imperial Greek historians, with translations; it is listed in the Scythica bibliography.
- Macedonian: Panovski & Leitner-Stojanov, Živa Antika 68 (2018) 81–98, on the 'Saga of Ostrogotha'.
- Dutch: Hekster 2015, a popular chapter.
- Bulgarian: Grozdanova, Sofia PhD 2019.
The editio princeps by Martin & Grusková (critical edition, translation, commentary) is still 'in preparation' according to the ÖAW project site (2026).
item_058.source_text:
The best open sources are the editors' preliminary diplomatic transcriptions (Greek, with gaps):
- GRBS 54 (2014): fols. 194v and 195r, CC BY 3.0 (https://grbs.library.duke.edu/index.php/grbs/article/view/15071).
- GRBS 62 (2022): fol. 192r lines 13–30, CC BY 4.0 (https://grbs.library.duke.edu/index.php/grbs/article/download/16854/7534/22609).
