- Empire in Crisis, ed. Mitthof, Martin & Grusková (Tyche Suppl. 12, Holzhausen 2020), Anhang I, pp. 543–548: a reprint of all six pages published 2014–15 (fragments Ia–Ib, IIa–IIb, IIIb–IIIc), CC BY-NC 4.0, free PDF at https://e-book.fwf.ac.at/o:1440 (OAPEN mirror 20.500.12657/37435).
Restricted or unchecked:
- WS 127 (2014) and JRS 105 (2015) are under publisher copyright.
- I did not check the licences of the Tyche 2014 and 2015 articles.
There is no standard critical edition yet. The editio princeps is forthcoming and will be in copyright.
The size is overstated in the sweep. The fragments occupy 4 leaves (8 pages), of which about 6.5 pages are published: roughly 1,700 Greek words in all, not 3–5k. The GRBS 2014 pilot unit is about 550–600 words.
item_058.research_yield:
A Russian first translation with commentary for ВДИ or Аристей. Topics:
- dating the Thessalonica/Thermopylae invasion (254 vs 262)
- Ostrogotha versus Jordanes
- Decius' speech and imitation of Thucydides
- the Plague of Cyprian (192r)
- civic militias
- Gothic ethnography for Black Sea and Chernyakhov-culture studies
item_058.recommendation: Keep at priority 3, as a Russian-only candidate: Russian has excerpts only, and the editors themselves have English and German translations of all the published text. Best first unit: the whole published corpus (about 1,700 words; GRBS CC BY texts plus Empire in Crisis Anhang I), checked against the editors' English and German. Label it provisional until the editio princeps appears, and consider contacting Martin and Grusková.

item_059.title_short: John Lydus, De ostentis (brontoscopic calendar, chs. 27–38)
item_059.ru_found:
Partial, and the colleague's claim holds. Sinitsa & Bolgov, «Иоанн Лид…» (Belgorod: BelGU, 2022), PDF at if.bsuedu.ru, footnote on p. 34: they had published only «вводная часть (главы 1-8) и глава 71 "О знамениях"». The same page says there were no Russian translations of Lydus before them. ru.wikipedia «Иоанн Лид» gives the citation: «Иоанн Лид. О небесных знамениях (De ostensis). Введение / [Пер.] М. М. Синица», in «Классическая и византийская традиция '2018», Belgorod, 2018, pp. 424–431. I did not find where ch. 71 was published. The Pravoslavnaya Entsiklopediya article (pravenc.ru/text/471355.html) lists no Russian translation.

Risk for the pilot unit: Л.А. Ельницкий, «Социально-политические аспекты "Бронтоскопического календаря" П. Нигидия Фигула», ВДИ 1971, №2 (116), pp. 107–116. This article analyses the calendar itself and may quote it in Russian. I could not open it: the full-issue PDF is on publ.lib.ru (VDI 1971 №02) and sno.pro1.ru returned 403. So its contents are unknown.

Searches with no hits for any Russian translation of chs. 27–38, under «О знамениях», «бронтоскопический календарь», «громовой календарь», «Иоанн Лидиец De ostentis» and «О небесных знамениях». Russian books on the Etruscans may quote a few calendar entries (for example, translations of French works); not verified.
item_059.en_found:
Full. A.C. Bandy (tr. and ed.), Ioannes Lydus, On Celestial Signs (De Ostentis), The Works of Ioannes Lydus III, Lewiston: Edwin Mellen, 2013, xxxii+271 pp. It has a revised Greek text and an English translation, and is confirmed in the Princeton Byzantine translations database and in Sinitsa–Bolgov 2022.

The proposed pilot unit (the brontoscopic calendar, chs. 27–38) has two more English versions by J.M. Turfa:
- (a) "The Etruscan Brontoscopic Calendar", in N.T. de Grummond & E. Simon (eds.), The Religion of the Etruscans (Austin: Univ. of Texas Press, 2006), pp. 182–190.
- (b) Divining the Etruscan World: The Brontoscopic Calendar and Religious Practice (Cambridge UP, 2012). Text and translation are on pp. 71–101, with full commentary (BMCR review at bmcr.brynmawr.edu/?p=37678).

The pilot unit is therefore translated into English three times.
item_059.other_found:
Italian, two complete versions:
- (1) Giovanni Lido, Sui segni celesti, translated by Erika Maderna, introduction and notes by Ilaria Domenici (Milan: Medusa, 2007, Le porpore 29). The translation is on pp. 47–135, and only the Tages sections are printed in Greek. BMCR 2008.07.14 (bmcr.brynmawr.edu/?p=25973) calls it complete and notes that no complete English translation existed at that time.
- (2) M. Basile, L'interpretazione dei segni celesti: traduzione di De ostentis di Giovanni Lido (CreateSpace, 2016), cited in Sinitsa–Bolgov 2022.

Latin: Hase's version is in Bekker's CSHB volume (Bonn, 1837).

French, German and Spanish: no full translation found. Searching was cut short because the web-search budget ran out. Sinitsa–Bolgov mention excerpts in European languages in studies of Etruscan religion. Bezold & Boll 1911 and Briquel 1997 are cited for the work but are not described as translations.
item_059.source_text:
Public domain and still the standard critical text: C. Wachsmuth (ed.), Ioannis Laurentii Lydi Liber de ostentis et calendaria Graeca omnia, 2nd ed., Leipzig: Teubner, 1897 (288 pp.; De ostentis on pp. 3–160). The 1st edition (1863) and Bekker, CSHB vol. 29 (Bonn, 1837, Greek with Hase's Latin) are also public domain. Digitised copies very likely exist on archive.org and Google Books, but I did not verify a URL in this pass.

Bandy's 2013 Greek text (Edwin Mellen) is in copyright, and some reviewers find his emendations arbitrary. Turfa 2012 (CUP) and the Italian translations are in copyright. Basing the work on Wachsmuth 1897 is safe.
item_059.research_yield: Lydus as a translator of Latin (Nigidius, Fonteius, Labeo) into Greek; the Etruscan disciplina in 6th-century Constantinople; the calendar compared with Mesopotamian omen series (Turfa's thesis); re-evaluating Elnitsky 1971; Christian framing of pagan divination; a Russian commentary on the calendar's terminology.
item_059.recommendation: Keep as a Russian-first candidate only. The "no English" angle fails: there are full English (Bandy 2013) and Italian (Maderna 2007, Basile 2016) translations, and three English versions of the calendar. Check Elnitsky's article (ВДИ 1971 №2) before choosing chs. 27–38 as the first unit. If it already has the calendar in Russian, start instead with chs. 39–52 (Fonteius' brontoscopy, Labeo on the moon and on lightning).

item_060.title_short: John Zonaras, Epitome historiarum (Books I–VI; pilot IV.8–15 Alexander)
item_060.ru_found:
I found no modern Russian translation of any part of Books I–VI. Sources checked:
(1) ru.wikipedia, «Иоанн Зонара». It lists only the canon-law commentaries (1876–1881) and Bondach's treatise translation (Вестник ПСТГУ 2007, no. 17). It also lists «Паралипомен Зонарин» (Moscow 1847, preface by О. Бодянский). That is the medieval South Slavonic abridgement (Bulgarian c. 1170, Serbian redaction 1344/1383), printed as a source text, not a modern translation.
(2) vostlit.info, «Зонара, Иоанн. Всемирная история». It has only XII.34 and XIII.1, translated by А. Игнатьев in 2023 from Banchich and Lane's English. It also has Черноглазов's study of Zonaras' 9th–11th-c. sources (ВВ 63, 1999) and Удальцова on Malalas (ВВ 1971). Neither covers Books I–VI.
(3) ancientrome.ru. There is no Zonaras entry. The Dio pages hold only books 36, 37 and 48.
(4) ru.wikisource, author page. It has the canons plus one sentence on the 'Little Genesis' among the Jubilees testimonia (А.В. Смирнов 1895; reprinted «Ветхозаветные апокрифы», Амфора 2000). Wikisource itself marks that work as unclear, and it is not certainly from the Epitome. This is negligible.
(5) The Russian Dio volumes (Нестор-История 2011/2014, books 51–80) and the shorter fragments touch only Zonaras 7–12, not 1–6.
Three Russian WebSearch queries returned nothing relevant. The session web-search budget then ran out, so elibrary/cyberleninka and the РГБ/РНБ catalogues were not searched directly.
item_060.en_found:
No English translation of Books I–VI found.
- Banchich and Lane, *The History of Zonaras* (Routledge 2009), covers 12.15–13.19 and also translates the Prologue and Postscript. So the Prologue that opens Book I exists in English.
- Cary's Loeb Dio and H.B. Foster's *Dio's Rome* (1905–06, Internet Archive) give English for the Zonaras epitome of Dio (Books 7–9 onward), not 1–6.
- attalus.org (index and chronicles page) has no Zonaras.
- en.wikipedia lists only Banchich and Lane.
- An English WebSearch for 'Zonaras Epitome books 1-6 English translation' found only Banchich and Lane.

item_060.source_text:
There is no modern critical edition of Books I–XII; Büttner-Wobst 1897 covers only XIII–XVIII. The standard text, which TLG also uses, is therefore public domain:
- L. Dindorf, Teubner, vol. 1 (1868). Verified from the Internet Archive OCR (cuaioanniszonara01zona): this volume contains Books I–V only, about 400 pp. Book IV runs pp. ~261–333 (24 chapters). - Dindorf vol. 2 (1869) contains Book VI.
- M. Pinder, CSHB vol. 1 (Bonn 1841) = 'Annales I–VI', Greek with Wolf's Latin facing. Public domain; Internet Archive bub_gb_0dUFAAAAQAAJ / bub_gb_wNkFAAAAQAAJ_2.
Correction to the candidate file: 'Dindorf vol. I' does not cover I–VI. Books I–VI total about 100–120k words. The Alexander unit is about 4.5–5k words; IV.1–16 (Persian plus Alexander) is about 9–10k.
item_060.research_yield: Book IV's Alexander chapters allow articles on how Zonaras combines Plutarch, Arrian and Josephus (Jerusalem visit, Sanballat), how he treats or excludes Romance material, Byzantine Alexander reception and his Persian narrative, and Zonaras as an indirect witness to Josephus' Antiquities.
item_060.recommendation: Keep at priority 3. The 'untranslated' claim holds for Books I–VI, apart from the Prologue (Banchich and Lane 2009) and old Latin and Italian versions. Start with IV.8–15 (Alexander, Dindorf pp. ~284–307, about 5k words). It fits the editor's Alexander Romance expertise, and the extant Plutarch, Arrian and Josephus allow alignment checks.

item_061.title_short: John of Antioch, Historia chronica (fragments; pilot: 5th-c. West)
item_061.ru_found: REFUTED. Main finding (from the project's own verification cache, research/raw/wave2_verified_partial.json "verify:item_061"): a complete Russian translation of the Müller FHG corpus was posted on simposium.ru in Aug–Sep 2016 as «Археология Иоанна Антиохийского с объяснением мифических рассказов». The translator is the pseudonymous «Исихаст». It is split into 10 logoi: the Archaeology, the Trojan War, the beginnings of Rome, the consuls, and the Caesars (fr. 78–219, at /ru/node/13267; index at /ru/node/13260). It covers fr. 1–219 and includes fr. 201 (murder of Aetius and Valentinian III) and fr. 204, so the pilot unit is fully covered. It is an amateur version with no apparatus, and fr. 214a appears to be missing. The cached verifier read the archived text directly (Wayback captures 2016–2025). This session: the live simposium.ru node returns 404 and the other URLs timed out, so I could not re-read it live; I did not use the Wayback archive. Also confirmed this session: V. G. Изосин, «К убийству Одоакра: об источнике фрагмента 214a Иоанна Антиохийского», Studia historica XVII (2022), ancientrome.ru/publik/article.htm?a=1677951570, which gives Greek with Russian for fr. 214a/b. Negative checks this session: no John of Antioch in the vostlit author index «И» (only Иоанн Диакон and Иоанн Эфесский), the ancientrome.ru antlitr author list, or myriobiblion.byzantion.ru. Ru.wikipedia's Флавий Аэций article cites fr. 200–201 by number only. The cache reports the Свод I–II does not include John. Searches: 2 Russian WebSearch queries ran this session and found nothing; the turn's search budget then ran out. The cached run had made 8 more Russian searches.
item_061.en_found: S. Mariev, Ioannis Antiocheni fragmenta quae supersunt omnia (CFHB 47, De Gruyter 2008) gives an English translation of his own selective corpus. BMCR 2009.12.06 (Whittow, fetched this session) confirms he drops the bulk of the Salmasian excerpts, most low-style Constantinian fragments (fall of Maurice, Phokas), and the Troica/Hypothesis material. The pilot fragments on the 5th-century West are included. C. D. Gordon, The Age of Attila (Ann Arbor 1960) translates fr. 200–201; the en.wikipedia Petronius Maximus article cites it at pp. 51ff (seen this session). J. Given, The Fragmentary History of Priscus (Arx 2014) is cited on en.wikipedia (Flavius Aetius) for Aetius' assassination and very likely includes the John-derived Priscan passages; I did not verify this fragment by fragment. The cache also lists J. Colavito's online translation of fr. 1–8 Müller. The pilot unit is therefore in English at least 2–3 times. Most Salmasian fragments outside fr. 1–8 appear to have no English. 1 English WebSearch ran this session, plus BMCR and Wikipedia fetches.
item_061.other_found: Italian, full: U. Roberto, Ioannis Antiocheni Fragmenta ex Historia chronica (TU 154, De Gruyter 2005), with an Italian translation of both traditions. BMCR 2006.07.37 (Cameron, fetched this session) says there seems to have been no complete translation into any language before Roberto. French: excerpts only (cache: MOM Éditions, «Vienne dans les textes grecs et latins»). German: none found (cache). Spanish: not checked.
item_061.source_text: Public domain: C. Müller, FHG IV (1851) pp. 535–622 and V (1870) pp. 27–39, on archive.org. Also public domain: de Boor, Excerpta de insidiis (1905); Büttner-Wobst/Roos, Excerpta de virtutibus (1906–10); Cramer, Anecdota Graeca Paris. II (1839) for the Salmasian excerpts; Lambros (1904) for the Iviron 812 fragments. The standard modern editions, Roberto 2005 (TU 154) and Mariev 2008 (CFHB 47), are both De Gruyter and in copyright. Their numbering differs, and they disagree on which fragments are authentic.
item_061.research_yield: Low as a first translation. Possible pieces: a critique of the amateur simposium version against Roberto and Mariev; a Müller–Roberto–Mariev concordance; the Johannine attribution question for Russian readers; John versus Priscus on the coup of 455.
item_061.recommendation: Drop it as a first-translation candidate: a full amateur Russian version of the Müller corpus (simposium.ru, 2016) and English (Mariev, Gordon) and Italian (Roberto) versions already cover the pilot unit. Revive it only as a scholarly retranslation of material missing from the Russian Müller-based version (fr. 214a, Iviron 812, Roberto-only fragments), and check that gap first.

item_062.ru_found:
REFUTED: the claim that no Russian translation exists is wrong.

(1) Viktor Zaslavsky, «Юлий Африкан. Историография (фрагменты)». It was translated from the English "Extant Writings of Julius Africanus" in Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 6, not from the Greek. It is online, undated, at myriobiblion.byzantion.ru/africanus/africanus2.html and reposted on ru.wikisource («Историография (Африкан; Заславский)/фрагменты»). Earlier cached evidence says vostlit has had it since c. 2004 (vostlit.info/Texts/rus11/Afrikan/istoriografia.phtml?id=1987; today that page's encoding is garbled), and azbyka.ru/otechnik/Julij_Afrikan/istoriografija/ also has it. I checked ru.wikisource directly this session. It has all 19 ANF pieces, and they include the proposed pilot unit:
- fr. 12–13: the Ogyges / Exodus-under-Moses synchronism ("Огиг... жил примерно в то же время, когда евреи вышли из Египта с Моисеем"), the 189-year Attic interregnum before Cecrops, and the reckonings to Cyrus;
- fr. 13–15: the Olympiad synchronisms;
- fr. 16: the Seventy Weeks;
- fr. 17: Hyrcanus, Herod and Antony;
- fr. 18: the Passion darkness. Here Thallus is mistranslated as "Саллюс".
The same site also has Zaslavsky's versions of the Letters to Aristides and Origen, the Persian narrative and Symphorosa.

(2) Indirect pieces, from cached results of an earlier verification run:
- Meshchansky, «Манефон. Египтика» (simposium.ru, 2012, translated from Waddell's Loeb): the Manetho dynasty lists "according to Africanus" from Syncellus.
- A. G. Aleksanyan, a Syncellus excerpt on the Egyptian dynasties translated from the Greek (egyptology.ru/antiq/Syncellus.pdf).
- Jerome's Commentary on Daniel, Творения блаж. Иеронима ч. 12 (Kiev 1894; azbyka): quotes the Seventy Weeks passage, from Latin.

Not found: any Russian translation from the Greek of Wallraff's full corpus (about 100 fragments and 99 testimonia). Checked with no results: pravenc.ru, ancientrome.ru, and azbyka's Eusebius PE (only book XI exists in Russian).

Limitation: this session's WebSearch budget was used up before I could search, so I could not run the 4 Russian searches the task requires. These findings rest on the cached record verify:item_062 in research/raw/wave2_verified_partial.json and research/raw/ru_series_crosscheck.json, plus direct fetches of ru.wikipedia, ru.wikisource and newadvent. Journal coverage on CyberLeninka/eLibrary is unverified. Russian anthologies on the historical Jesus may contain the Thallus fragment, but I did not check them.
item_062.en_found:
FULL: W. Adler, English translation in M. Wallraff (ed.) with U. Roberto and K. Pinggéra, Iulius Africanus: Chronographiae. The Extant Fragments, GCS NF 15 (de Gruyter 2007). It has 100 fragments and 99 testimonia (BMCR 2008.04.43, per the cache).

PUBLIC-DOMAIN PARTIAL: "Extant Writings of Julius Africanus", ANF vol. 6 (1886). Its 19 Chronography fragments include the pilot unit (fr. 12–15). I checked it directly at newadvent.org/fathers/0614.htm; it is also on CCEL and en.wikisource.

More English pieces are in Adler & Tuffin's Synkellos (OUP 2002), Gifford's PE (1903) and Waddell's Manetho (Loeb 1940).

item_062.source_text:
PUBLIC DOMAIN:
- M. J. Routh, Reliquiae Sacrae vol. II, 2nd ed. (Oxford 1846), archive.org/details/reliquiaesacrae02rout; reprinted in PG 10.
- W. Dindorf, Georgius Syncellus, CSHB (Bonn 1829), for the fragments Syncellus preserves.
- Eusebius, PE X.10, Gifford's 1903 Greek text, for the Ogyges–Moses passage.
- The ANF vol. 6 English, usable for comparison.

IN COPYRIGHT: the standard modern edition, Wallraff et al., GCS NF 15 (de Gruyter 2007). I could not confirm open access: the de Gruyter page returned HTTP 405. Mosshammer's Synkellos (Teubner 1984) and Mras's PE (GCS 1954–56) are also in copyright.

Working approach: translate from Routh, Dindorf and Gifford, and check readings and fragment numbering against Wallraff.
item_062.recommendation: Drop it as a "first translation". The Moses–Ogyges/Olympiad pilot already exists in Russian (Zaslavsky, via the English), and the whole work exists in English (Adler 2007) and Italian (2016). If kept at all, reframe it as the first Russian translation from the Greek of the fragments outside the ANF selection, starting with the Synkellos-transmitted Hellenistic and Near Eastern king-list material, not the pilot unit.

item_063.title_short: Anon., Excerpta Latina Barbari (Hellenistic king-lists + Alexander section)
item_063.ru_found: I found no Russian translation, either of the whole work or of the pilot unit. What I checked: the ru.wikipedia article 'Excerpta Latina Barbari', which lists Scaliger 1606, Schoene 1875 and Frick 1892 and cites only Burgess 2013, Garstad 2011 and Wallraff 2007, with no Russian translation and no Russian scholarship; the ancientrome.ru author index (no entry for Barbarus, Alexandrian chronicle or Chronica minora); ancientrome.ru 'anon-lat', which has only De rebus bellicis; and the project's cached wave-1 notes, which list ELB under 'English yes, Russian no'. Important limitation: the shared web-search budget was used up before my first query, so I ran none of the required 4 Russian and 4 English searches, only direct page fetches. I did not check elibrary, cyberleninka, vostlit or simposium (Russian journal articles, dissertations, online translations), nor any RSL or NLR catalogue entry. A ВДИ or Византийский временник article could still translate the Alexander passage, so the Russian claim rests on thin evidence.
item_063.en_found: 1) Full: B. Garstad, Apocalypse of Pseudo-Methodius / An Alexandrian World Chronicle (Dumbarton Oaks Medieval Library 14, Harvard UP 2012). It has a new Latin text with facing English translation, at pp. 142ff per de.wikipedia's 'Ausgaben' section. fr.wikipedia also lists it as 'Latin texts with English translations'. The project cache (alexander.json) gives Ps.-Methodius at pp. 2–141, so the chronicle follows. 2) Partial, online and free: an English translation at attalus.org/translate/barbari.html, translator not named, 'translated from Schoene's text (Eusebius, Appendix VI)'. It covers MS pp. 32A–36B, 44A and 46A–55A: the testament of Alexander (33B), the twelve cities founded by Alexander (34B), the Ptolemies (35A), the Macedonian kingdom (44A), the Seleucids (46A), the kings of Egypt (46B), the Jewish high priests (47A), the Roman emperors (48A) and the consuls (49A). It omits the Assyrian list. So the proposed pilot unit is already in English twice, apart from the Assyrian list, which only Garstad covers. 3) Not verified, from memory: Burgess & Dijkstra, Millennium 10 (2013) may translate the consularia section, and Adler's English in Wallraff, Julius Africanus Chronographiae (GCS 2007) may include ELB passages.
item_063.other_found: German: the de.wikipedia article 'Excerpta Latina Barbari' (about 280k characters) contains a section 'Übersetzung'. It is an entry-by-entry German translation of the whole chronicle: Book 1, chs. 1–9 (Adam to Cleopatra, including the Alexander entries, the Babylonian/Persian/Greek kings, the division of Alexander's kingdom and the Ptolemies) and Book 2, chs. 1–11 (Assyrian, Egyptian, Argive, Sicyonian, Athenian, Latin, Spartan, Corinthian, Macedonian, Lydian, Median, Persian, Seleucid and Ptolemaic lists, the high priests, Roman emperors and consuls). The translators are anonymous Wikipedia contributors; the source edition is not stated; the licence is CC BY-SA. Some lists are condensed into tables. It cites Garstad 2012 and Mommsen, MGH AA 9 (1892), pp. 272–293. French: fr.wikipedia lists no French translation. Italian and Spanish: none found (es.wikipedia has no article). The sweep's 'None found' is refuted for German.
item_063.source_text: Public domain: (a) C. Frick, Chronica minora I (Teubner, Leipzig 1892), the full text; (b) A. Schoene, Eusebi Chronicorum libri duo I (Berlin 1875), Appendix VI, the full text and the base of the attalus translation; (c) Th. Mommsen, MGH Auct. Ant. 9 (1892), pp. 272–293, 'Excerpta ex Barbaro Scaligeri', only partial (consular/fasti portions), free at mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_Auct._Ant._9_S.272; (d) the unique manuscript, Paris BnF lat. 4884 (Corbie, 8th c.), digitized on Gallica at ark:/12148/btv1b84790083. In copyright: the standard modern edition is Garstad's Latin text and translation (DOML 14, Harvard UP 2012). For the pilot unit, use Frick (or Schoene) checked against the Gallica facsimile, with Garstad's English as a control (cite it, do not reproduce it).
item_063.research_yield: Russian commentary on the ELB Alexander section (testament, list of twelve Alexandrias, division of the kingdom) set against Ps.-Callisthenes III.33–35 and the Liber de morte. Also: Africanus-derived Hellenistic king-lists, and the Nebuchadnezzar–Alexander pairing (articles must engage Garstad's Iraq 2016 and WSt 2018 papers).
item_063.recommendation: Downgrade (scale: 5 = highest). Only the Russian gap is real: English exists in full (Garstad, DOML 2012) and in part online (attalus.org, which covers the pilot unit), and German exists in full (de.wikipedia). Keep only as a small Russian unit in an 'Alexander in late antique chronicles' cluster: MS pp. 32A–36B (Alexander's reign, testament, twelve cities, Ptolemies), from Frick/Schoene. Re-run the Russian searches (elibrary, cyberleninka, ВДИ, Византийский временник) before committing.

item_065.title_short: Julius Pollux, Onomasticon (Book 8: courts, laws, magistracies)
item_065.ru_found: I found no Russian translation of the Onomasticon as a whole, and none of Book 8 as a unit. Most of this rests on the cached verification (research/raw/wave2_verified_partial.json, "verify:item_065"), because the shared WebSearch budget ran out at the start of this run. That earlier run searched ru.wikipedia, ancientrome.ru, about 9 CyberLeninka queries (Поллукс/Полидевк Ономастикон; архонты фесмофеты; остракизм; эфеты; диэтеты; навкрары) and DuckDuckGo in Russian (перевод; Хрестоматия по истории Древней Греции; Мокульский; диссертация). In this run I re-checked ru.wikipedia «Юлий Поллукс» directly: it names only the Latin translation of 1502, no Russian one. The excerpts that do exist: (1) Янзина & Корнеев, IELCP 26 (2022), on Onom. 3.149–150, 155. (2) Герцман: Book 4 music passages cut short in «Музыка Древней Греции и Рима» (1995), plus a 2022 Квадривиум monograph, «Древнеримский „Ономастикон“…», which is a study whose text I have not checked. (3) The Book 4 masks, paraphrased by Поникаровская (2015) and Рыканцова (2015). (4) Single sentences from Book 8 quoted inside other works: Латышев on 8.86 (the archons' oath), Пальцева (Вестник СПбГУ, 2009), Суриков on ostracism. (5) 9.83 in ФРГФ (1989). Still to check: whether Латышев's «Известия… о Скифии и Кавказе» (reprinted in ВДИ 1947–48) includes 8.131–132 on the Scythian archers. That would be a sentence or two at most.
item_065.en_found: This refutes the "untranslated" claim for English. A complete translation is announced: S. Douglas Olson, "Julius Pollux: The Onomasticon. Text, Translation, and Notes" (CUP, 2 vols, about 1800 pp., ISBN 978-1-009-54233-3). It covers Books 1–10, so Book 8 is included. Retailers list it for 28 Feb 2027 (Hugendubel) and 31 Mar 2027 (Lehmanns), and the blurb calls it the "first translation into a modern language". This comes from the cache: in this run the CUP, Lehmanns and Blackwell's pages all returned 403, so the date is not re-confirmed. What is published so far is excerpts only: 4.99–154 on theatre in Csapo & Slater (1995, partly abridged); Barker GMW I (1984) on 4.84; London 1775 extracts on theatre and masks; L. A. Hall's 1960 Oregon honors thesis, an unpublished typescript of selections. Naomi Scott's Bristol crowdsourcing project is still at an early stage. I re-checked its blog in this run (28 Aug 2024), which says the work "has not been translated into any modern language". I found no published English translation of Book 8.
item_065.other_found: Italian, Book 8: F. Amaraschi's thesis, «Recherches sur le lexique de Pollux : les articles juridiques» (Reims/Firenze, 2013, theses.fr NNT 2013REIML011). It is written in Italian, is not openly available, and translates with commentary about half of Book 8's 157 paragraphs (the legal and constitutional lemmata) plus the letters to Commodus. Also Amaraschi in Erga-Logoi 3.1 (2015) on VIII 63, 86, 96. Bearzot, Landucci and Zecchini (eds), L'Onomasticon di Giulio Polluce (2007), has studies of Book 8 (boule and ekklesia, nomophylakes, Attic law) but no running translation. Italian, Book 4: masks volume (Castiglioni 2022); Parlato's MA thesis (2014). German: Book 5 excerpts in «Jagd und Jagdhunde» (De Gruyter). Spanish: Macua on masks 4.134–154. French: studies only. Latin: Gwalther 1541, Seber 1608. No complete translation into a modern language exists yet.
item_065.source_text: Bethe, Pollucis Onomasticon (Lexicographi Graeci IX, Teubner). Fasc. 2 (1931, Books 6–10) contains Book 8, scanned at archive.org/details/pollucisonomasti02polluoft. Bethe died in 1940, so the edition is public domain in the EU and Russia; in the US fasc. 2 becomes public domain on 1 Jan 2027. The archive.org OCR is garbled and the Greek must be re-OCRed. item_066.en_found: No English translation exists, according to Roger Pearse's blog ('No Zenobius in English?', 3 Feb 2009, and 'More Zenobius', 5 Feb 2009). On CLASSICS-L, A. Chugg said he knew of no modern English translation of the whole work, and T. Lockyer pointed only to the Leutsch–Schneidewin Greek text. Pearse wrote that there is no translation of any of it and gave the TLG count as 27,271 words. en.wikipedia 'Zenobius' lists no translation, and attalus.org's translation index has no Zenobius or other paroemiographers. Indirect English versions exist: Suda On Line translates many proverb entries that run parallel to Zenobius and Diogenianus, and the Collected Works of Erasmus (Adages) paraphrases many explanations. Neither is a translation of Zenobius. No post-2009 English translation was found, but fresh searches were impossible in this pass.

LXXIII 4942, a fragment of the fuller original Book I.
item_066.source_text: The public-domain source is Leutsch & Schneidewin, Corpus Paroemiographorum Graecorum I (Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht 1839), pp. 1–175, the vulgate in 6 centuries (552 proverbs). It is on archive.org as https://archive.org/details/corpusparoemiogr01leutuoft, flagged NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT (Robarts/Toronto copy, full text and PDF), and on Google Books; there is also an Olms reprint (Hildesheim 1965). For the vulgate this is still the standard text, and it is public domain. W. Bühler, Zenobii Athoi proverbia (Göttingen, V&R; vol. 1 1987, vol. 4 1982, vol. 5 1999; incomplete) is in copyright and should be used only for collation and commentary. P.Oxy. LXXIII 4942 (2009) is also in copyright.

It is on Google Books (id MMZiAAAAMAAJ) and the Internet Archive, and ToposText work 241 has the Greek online. item_067.research_yield: Stephanus's homonym lists (18 Alexandreiai, the Antiocheiai, Seleukeiai, Apameiai, Laodikeiai) can be compared with the Alexander Romance foundation list (Ps.-Callisthenes III.35). item_068.en_found:

item_068.other_found:
I found no chapter-level translation in French, German, Italian or Spanish. Without search access I could not run catalogue checks, so this is not exhaustive.

Partial versions of components:

Possible but unverified: a modern Greek bilingual Stobaeus from Κάκτος («Οι Έλληνες»). Check before claiming any "first in any language".
item_068.source_text:
Wachsmuth–Hense, vol. IV (ed. O. Hense, Berlin: Weidmann, 1909). IV.22 runs from about p. 494 to p. 581 in seven parts:
- 22a: that marriage is best
- 22b: that it is not good to marry
- 22c: marriage helps some and harms others
- 22d: on betrothal
- 22e: on the spouses' ages
- 22f: on choosing for character, not birth or wealth
- 22g: Ψόγος γυναικῶν

This corresponds to Meineke's Florilegium 67–73. Archive.org copies:
- https://archive.org/details/joannisstobaeian04stovuoft (flagged NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT; OCR checked)
- https://archive.org/details/adw8682.0004.001.umich.edu

Hense died in 1931, so the edition is public domain everywhere. Wachsmuth–Hense is still the standard edition of Book IV: it was only reprinted (1958) and never superseded, so no copyright issue arises for the base text. The modern fragment editions are in copyright and should be used only for readings and numbering: Kannicht's TrGF (2004), Kassel–Austin's PCG and West's IEG² (1989–92). Public-domain editions of the components: Hense's Musonius (1905), von Arnim's SVF (1903–05), von Arnim's Hierocles (1906) and Meineke's Florilegium (1855–57).

The size is underestimated. My OCR count is about 10k Greek words of text, and OCR undercounts, so the real figure is probably about 12–14k Greek words, or about 15–18k translated words. That is not 8–10k. IV.22–25 as a whole is far too big for one unit.
item_068.research_yield: Articles possible on: Stobaeus' pro/contra/conditional arrangement of the marriage debate; Stoic marriage theory (Antipater, Musonius, Hierocles, Nicostratus) as background to 1 Cor 7; the misogynist gnomic dossier (Semonides, Susarion, comedy, Euripides); late-antique gnomology and its Byzantine reception.
item_068.recommendation: Keep, merged with the duplicate item_170, and coordinate the overlaps with item_163 (Hierocles) and item_165 (Pseudo-Pythagoreans). Present it as the first translation of the chapter as a compiled whole, not of its contents. The best first unit is IV.22a–c (Wachsmuth–Hense pp. 494–531, about 5–6k Greek words), with notes citing the existing Russian versions of Antipater, Semonides, Hipponax and Susarion.

item_069.source_text:
Public-domain options:
- G. Bernhardy, Suidae Lexicon Graece et Latine (Halle 1834–53)
- T. Gaisford, Suidae Lexicon (Oxford 1834)
- J. Flach, Hesychii Milesii Onomatologi quae supersunt (Leipzig: Teubner 1881/82). Flach collects exactly the Hesychian bio-bibliographical entries, which makes it the most convenient public-domain base for this unit. Sinitsa/Bolgova used it. Archive.org copies are likely but were not checked this run.
Standard edition: A. Adler, Suidae Lexicon (Lexicographi Graeci I, Leipzig: Teubner 1928–38; reprinted Stuttgart/Munich 1967–71 and 1994–2001).
- Adler died in 1966. If the edition counts as an authorial work (see CJEU C-649/23, 2026), it is protected in the EU and Russia until the end of 2036. Under German §70 UrhG it counts as a scientific edition, whose 25-year protection has expired.
- US: vol. 1 (1928) is public domain; later volumes enter it from 2027 onward.
- Use Adler readings with citation. Base the text on Flach/Bernhardy, collated against Adler.
- Suda On Line is CC BY-NC-SA, usable for cross-checking on a non-commercial site.
item_069.research_yield: Hesychius' Onomatologos as a source for counts of plays and victories, compared with didascalic inscriptions and the Marmor Parium. Suda chronological formulas (γέγονε, Olympiads) and Apollodoran dating. Lost-work catalogues. Suda entries compared with the Vitae (after Lefkowitz). A Russian reference corpus for students.
item_069.recommendation: Keep, but lower to priority 3 (reading 5 as highest). The gap is in Russian only: English is complete and free (SOL), and many poet entries are also in Loeb testimonia. Best first unit: the tragic poets' entries (Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides and the minor tragedians, about 50–60 entries) from Flach/Bernhardy, collated with Adler and cross-checked against SOL. Before publishing, check Russian poet editions for single entries already translated.
