Use Stallbaum as the base text, check readings against van der Valk, and do not upload van der Valk into the models (De Gruyter Brill AI policy). Kolovou's French and Politi's Latin can serve as controls for checking the translation.
item_110.research_yield: First Russian translation of Eustathius' Iliad hermeneutics. Possible articles: proem imagery (Ocean, Sirens) and method; Homer as rhetorician; lost sources (Atticist lexica, Aristarchus) in Book 1 notes on μῆνις, Chryses and the plague; comparison of the Iliad and Odyssey proems.
item_110.recommendation: Keep. The claim that the Book 1 commentary is untranslated holds in Russian, English, French, German and Italian; only Politi's 1730 Latin covers it. The proem itself is not a first: it is in French (Kolovou 2018) and partly in English (Herington 1969). Start with a Russian proem (~3.5k words, checked against Kolovou), then the commentary on Il. 1.1–52 from Stallbaum.

item_111.title_short: Eustathius, Commentary on Dionysius Periegetes (non-Pontic sections)
item_111.ru_found: The sweep's "none" is wrong. V.V. Latyshev's "Известия древних писателей греческих и латинских о Скифии и Кавказе" (Scythica et Caucasica), vol. I, prints large excerpts of Eustathius' Parekbolai on Dionysius. My direct fetch of the OCR of the Greek-text volume (1890) found the heading "Εὐσταθίου Παρεκβολαί εἰς τὴν Διονυσίου" with notes on Dionysius vv. ~652–816, among them 662, 669, 700, 721, 728, 780, 801, 811 and 816. That part covers Scythia, the Maeotis, the Caucasus and the Caspian; the OCR also hints at Ister and Pontic verses. These pages fall at about pp. 186–209, just before Arrian's Periplus (https://archive.org/details/IzvestiiaDrevnikhPisateleiGrecheskikhILatinskikhOSkifiUKavkaz). The project cache (ru_series_crosscheck.json) gives the same pages: Lat. I, 187–209, plus scholia on Dionysius at 209–216. Latyshev's Russian translation appeared in vol. I, issues 1–3 (St Petersburg 1893, 1896, 1900) and was reprinted in ВДИ 1947–49 (ru.wikipedia, "Латышев, Василий Васильевич"). So the proposed pilot unit, the Pontus and Scythia sections, already exists in Russian. I found nothing on the rest of the commentary: the prooemium (the letter to John Doukas), Libya, the West, the islands, Asia Minor and India. ru.wikipedia "Евстафий Солунский" lists no translation. Ilyushechkina's Russian Dionysius (ВДИ 2005–06) may quote Eustathius in its notes, but I could not check this. One caveat: the WebSearch budget was used up when this task started, so the 4 Russian searches required did not run. These findings rest on the project cache and direct page fetches only.
item_111.en_found: No English translation found. en.wikipedia "Eustathius of Thessalonica" lists only early printings: R. Stephanus 1547, H. Stephanus 1577, Hudson's Geographi minores vol. IV and Bernhardy 1828. It gives no translation. en.wikipedia "Dionysius Periegetes" lists translations of Dionysius only: Lightfoot (OUP 2014), Jacob (FR 1990) and Amato (IT 2005), and no translation of Eustathius. The project cache (wave1 English landscape) shows English versions of Eustathius only for the Homer commentaries: Odyssey 1–8 (Brill) and the Iliad preface. The same caveat applies: the WebSearch budget was used up, so the 4 English searches did not run. A partial English version of the prooemium inside some article or thesis cannot be ruled out; its status is unknown.
item_111.other_found: I found no modern French, German, Italian or Spanish translation. Jacob (1990) and Amato (2005, Bompiani) translate Dionysius, not Eustathius. Early printed editions (Stephanus, Hudson, Bernhardy's "graece et latine") may include Latin versions, but I could not verify this. Coverage is low because web search was unavailable.
item_111.source_text: There is no modern critical edition. The standard edition is K. Müller, Geographi Graeci Minores II (Paris: Didot 1861), which is public domain. Scan: Google Books https://books.google.com/books?id=dDcOAAAAYAAJ (link from en.wikipedia "Karl Wilhelm Ludwig Müller"). There is also G. Bernhardy, Dionysius Periegetes (Leipzig 1828), with Eustathius and the scholia, also public domain. As far as I could tell no copyrighted edition supersedes Müller. TLG digitizes the Müller text under licence, but the underlying text is public domain. The Greek OCR of the old scans is noisy, so the text will need retyping or correction.
item_111.research_yield: Eustathius' lost sources: a fuller Stephanus of Byzantium and Arrian's Bithyniaca. Byzantine identification of ancient peoples with medieval ones. How Alexander and Dionysus are handled in the India section. How a 12th-c. scholar read Dionysius. A comparison with what Latyshev chose to excerpt.
item_111.recommendation: Keep at lower priority (Byzantine, not ancient), but drop the Pontus/Scythia pilot: Latyshev already has it in Russian (1893–1900; ВДИ 1947–48). Best first unit: the prooemium (the letter to John Doukas) plus the commentary on India (Dion. ~vv. 1080–1165, with the Alexander and Dionysus material). Check it verse by verse against Latyshev's list before starting.

item_112.title_short: Proclus (and Byzantine scholia), Scholia on Hesiod's Works and Days (prolegomena + WD 1–201)
item_112.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation of Proclus' commentary/scholia on Works and Days, of the Byzantine scholia, or of the pilot unit. The check was limited. The shared WebSearch budget (200 per turn) was already used up when this run started, so I could not run the required 4+ Russian searches (elibrary, cyberleninka, ΣΧΟΛΗ and the others). What I did check:
(1) ru.wikipedia, «Прокл Диадох», full list of works and translations: it records the WD commentary only as a lost work («Комментарии к „Трудам и дням“ Гесиода»). Its long list of Russian Proclus translations has nothing on Hesiod: Лосев 1972; Месяц 2000–2002; Лукомский 2001/2006; Петров 1997–2003 (Tim., Resp., Crat.); Бугай 2001; Шичалин 1994; Щетников 2013; Бородай 2008; Смыка 1988.
(2) The ancientrome.ru Hesiod page lists only the poems, with no scholia and no Proclus. Its Cyrillic came through garbled.
(3) The project cache (research/raw/ru_series_crosscheck.json) has only В.В. Латышев, «Известия древних писателей о Скифии и Кавказе», vol. I (1890–1900; ВДИ 1947–48), with short excerpts from Scholia in Hesiodum. These are probably Theogony scholia (Phasis/Istros, Caucasus). A Prometheus/Caucasus note in the WD 47–105 scholia cannot be ruled out; check Latyshev's index before release.
Not checked: whether the appendices of the Russian «Гесиод. Полное собрание текстов» (Лабиринт, 2001) translate Tzetzes' Life of Hesiod or the prolegomena.
item_112.en_found:
No complete or partial English translation of Proclus' WD commentary or of the WD scholia was found or is known. The colleague's "none", however, should become "excerpts only":
(a) F. H. Sandbach, Plutarch's Moralia XV: Fragments (Loeb Classical Library 429, 1969), translates the fragments of Plutarch's lost commentary on WD (frr. 25–112 Sandbach). Most of these are preserved only in Proclus' scholia, so a sizeable share of the Proclan layer exists in English. This comes from bibliographic knowledge: loebclassics.com returned 403 and searches were unavailable.
(b) Scholarship on Neoplatonic Hesiod reception (e.g. Lamberton) quotes individual Proclan scholia in English, but these are scattered quotations only.
Checked without result: BMCR 2014.12.27 (mentions no English translation), en.wikipedia "Proclus" and "Works and Days". As with Russian, I could not run the required English searches.
item_112.other_found:
VERIFIED. German, full for the Proclan layer: Patrizia Marzillo (ed.), Der Kommentar des Proklos zu Hesiods "Werken und Tagen", Tübingen: Narr 2010 (Classica Monacensia), ISBN 978-3-8233-6353-8. It is a critical edition with translation and commentary (per de.wikipedia "Proklos", bibliography). The colleague's "Proclus' fragments" means the whole surviving Proclan commentary, so it covers the Proclan part of the pilot unit.
VERIFIED. Italian, all Hesiod scholia: Cesare Cassanmagnago, Esiodo. Tutte le opere e i frammenti, con la prima traduzione degli scolii (Milan: Bompiani, 2009), cited in BMCR 2014.12.27 (E. E. Prodi).
Studies that are not translations: Faraggiana di Sarzana, «Le commentaire à Hésiode et la paideia encyclopédique de Proclus» (in Pépin–Saffrey, Proclus lecteur et interprète des anciens, 1987, 21–41).
No French or Spanish translation was found, but this could not be searched.
item_112.source_text:
Best public-domain text: E. Vollbehr, Hesiodi Opera et Dies … Procli et anonymorum scholia addidit (Kiel 1844), 252 pp. It is on archive.org with a Public Domain Mark (PDF and OCR): https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_-E1WAAAAcAAJ (verified).
Also public domain: T. Gaisford, Poetae Minores Graeci (Oxford 1814–20; Leipzig 1823), which carries the Proclus, Tzetzes and Moschopoulos scholia (scan URL not verified).
Standard modern editions: A. Pertusi, Scholia vetera in Hesiodi Opera et dies (Milan: Vita e Pensiero, 1955); Marzillo 2010 for the Proclan layer. Both have their prefaces, apparatus and translation in copyright (Pertusi d. 1979). The bare Greek text of the 1955 critical edition may no longer be protected under Italian law's 20-year term for critical editions, but this needs a legal check.
Safest course: base the published text on Vollbehr/Gaisford, collate Pertusi and Marzillo readings in the notes, and do not reproduce their apparatus.
item_112.research_yield: Proclus' Neoplatonic ethical allegoresis of Hesiod (Prometheus, Pandora, Ages) in school paideia. Reconstructing Plutarch's lost WD commentary (Plutarchan vs Proclan layers). Byzantine school exegesis (Tzetzes, Moschopoulos). Calendar and agrarian lore. Comparison with Marzillo's and Pertusi's attributions.
item_112.recommendation: Keep, but at priority 3 rather than 4, and present it as a first Russian translation (no Russian translation found) plus the first English rendering of the commentary as a whole. German (Marzillo 2010) and Italian (Cassanmagnago 2009) translations exist, and the Plutarchan fragments are in Sandbach's Loeb. Best first unit: prolegomena plus scholia on WD 1–201 from Vollbehr 1844 or Gaisford, using Marzillo as the reference for what is Proclan. First re-run the Russian/English searches that the exhausted budget blocked, and check Latyshev I for any WD Prometheus/Caucasus scholion.

item_113.title_short: Eustathius of Thessalonica, Prooemium to the Pindar Commentary (whole text)
item_113.ru_found:
No Russian translation of the Prooemium was found. LIMITATION: the harness's WebSearch budget for this turn (200 calls) was already used up, so I could not run the required 4+ Russian search-engine queries. I checked by fetching pages directly and from the project cache instead.
(1) Православная энциклопедия, т. 17 (2008), «Евстафий», pravenc.ru/text/187417.html. It summarizes the Prologue (two parts: Pindar's style, digressions and dialect; then biographical testimonia going back to a lost Plutarch work, the origin of the Olympic games and the strophic structure of the odes). Its «Соч.» list gives only Kambylis 1991 and Negri 2000 for this text. The only Russian item it lists for any Eustathian work is «Памятники византийской литературы IX–XIV вв.» (М., 1969), с. 234–242, described only as «переводы отрывков неск. соч.» (excerpts of several works). I could not see which works those pages cover; they are probably not this text, but this is unverified.
(2) ru.wikipedia «Евстафий Солунский»: no translations listed. The Pindar commentary is called «почти полностью утрачен».
(3) ru.wikisource «Автор:Евстафий Солунский»: only «О исправлении монастырской жизни».
(4) ancientrome.ru, Gasparov's Пиндар/Вакхилид (Литпамятники, «Наука», 1980; antlitr/pindar/vita.htm): «Жизнеописание Пиндара» there is the Vita Ambrosiana with its apophthegms, not Eustathius. The edition's notes do not mention him. Note that this Vita already gives Russian readers the Pan-singing-a-paean anecdote that Eustathius also tells (ch. 27).
(5) Project cache (ru_series_crosscheck): Латышев's Eustathian excerpts cover only the Dionysius Periegetes and Homer commentaries, not Pindar.
item_113.en_found:
No English translation was found in the sources I could reach, but I could not run any English web searches (WebSearch budget exhausted), so the status stays unverified.
What I checked: en.wikipedia «Eustathius of Thessalonica» lists only the editions of Tafel 1832 and Schneidewin 1837. The only English translation it mentions is of a different work, Melville-Jones, The Capture of Thessaloniki, 1988. en.wikipedia «Pindar» cites the Prooemium (ch. 27, p. 298.9 Drachmann) and gives no translation.
To check before a final verdict: (a) the translated Lives in the appendix of M. Lefkowitz, The Lives of the Greek Poets (2nd ed., 2012), which may include Eustathius' biographical chapters (my unverified guess); (b) English articles of 2015–2026 on Eustathius' Pindar (e.g. in Pontani–Katsaros–Sarris, Reading Eustathios of Thessalonike, De Gruyter 2017), which may translate passages; (c) DOML and other Byzantine sourcebooks. I lean towards "none" for a full translation.
item_113.other_found:
German: A. Kambylis (ed.), Eustathios von Thessalonike, Prooimion zum Pindarkommentar: Einleitung, kritischer Text, Indices (Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1991; the year comes from PE 2008, while de.wikipedia gives 1997). Its subtitle names no translation, so the colleague's "German: Kambylis 1991" is probably wrong as a translation claim. The companion study, Kambylis, Eustathios über Pindars Epinikiendichtung (also listed on de.wikipedia), may render passages in German; not verified.
Italian: M. Negri, Eustazio di Tessalonica, Introduzione al commentario a Pindaro (Brescia [Paideia], 2000), listed in PE 2008. It is believed to include an Italian translation and commentary, but this is from bibliographic knowledge and was not re-verified online.
French, Spanish and Modern Greek: nothing found (not searched). it.wikipedia and de.wikipedia list no translations.
item_113.source_text:
Best public-domain base: Drachmann, Scholia vetera in Pindari carmina, vol. III (Teubner, 1927), Epimetrum, c. pp. 285–306. That it contains the Prooemium is confirmed by en.wikipedia's citation "Proem. 27, p. 298.9 Dr". Drachmann died in 1935, so the volume is PD in the EU and in the US (pre-1929).
Also PD: Schneidewin, Eustathii prooemium commentariorum Pindaricorum (Göttingen: Dieterich, 1837), archive.org/details/eustathiiprooem00schngoog, marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT; and Tafel, Eustathii opuscula (Frankfurt, 1832), on HathiTrust.
The standard modern critical edition is Kambylis 1991 (Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht), which is in copyright, as is Negri 2000. Translate from Drachmann and consult Kambylis' readings, citing them as scholarship.
item_113.research_yield: Possible articles: the 12th-c. Byzantine poetics of Pindar (style, obscurity, digressions, Aeolic-Doric mix, triadic strophe); Plutarch's lost Life of Pindar recovered through Eustathius, compared with the Vita Ambrosiana (in Russian via Gasparov 1980); the four-book epinician corpus and the Pindar scholia tradition.
item_113.recommendation: Keep it as a fast pilot: probably the first translation in Russian and possibly the first in English. Use the whole Prooemium (~8k words) from Drachmann III (PD), translating part 1 (the poetics) first, since the biographical part overlaps the Vita Ambrosiana already in Russian. Before publication, re-run the skipped searches (Lefkowitz appendix, Памятники визант. лит. 1969 pp. 234–242, recent English articles).

item_114.title_short: Scholia vetera + Tzetzes, Aristophanes' Clouds (Σ Nub. 1–262)
item_114.ru_found: I found no Russian translation of the Clouds scholia. The session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was already used up, so none of the required Russian or English keyword searches could run. The checks below are direct fetches of named pages plus the project cache. (1) ancientrome.ru, Aristophanes page: Bergk's text and the comedies only, nothing on scholia. (2) ru.wikipedia, «Облака (комедия)»: lists four Russian translations of the play (Муравьёв-Апостол 1821, Алексеев 1893, Теплов 1897, Пиотровский 1927; reprinted 1983 with Ярхо's commentary and in 2008 by Ладомир). It does not mention scholia. Ярхо's commentary may paraphrase single scholia; I did not check. (3) ru.wikipedia, «Иоанн Цец»: Russian versions are the 1969 excerpts (Памятники византийской литературы IX–XIV вв., pp. 252–259, contents not stated) and Смыка's Carmina Iliaca. Nothing on Aristophanes. (4) Project cache (ru_series_crosscheck.json): Латышев, Scythica et Caucasica I, p. 353 has an excerpt of Scholia in Aristophanem (Russian translation in ВДИ 1947–48), play not identified. It could be Σ Nub. 109 (φασιανοί: Phasian horses or pheasants, i.e. Colchis), which would fall inside the pilot unit. The archive.org scan of Latyshev I skips pp. 307–560, so I could not check this. The editor should look at p. 353 directly.
item_114.en_found: Verified, and it covers the pilot unit. W. G. Rutherford, Scholia Aristophanica; being such comments adscript to the text of Aristophanes as have been preserved in the Codex Ravennas, arranged, emended, and translated, vol. I (London: Macmillan, 1896), public domain: https://archive.org/details/scholiaaristopha01ruthuoft. Contents: Plutus, Nubes, Ranae, Aves. The Clouds section starts at about p. 121 with Σ Nub. 1, and each Greek scholion is followed by an English rendering, checked in the full text through at least l. 249. The DNB 1912 supplement confirms "a revised text of the scholia with a translation and notes" (1896); vol. III (1905) is "A Chapter in the History of Annotation". Limits: Rutherford covers only the R (Ravennas) scholia, in a heavily emended and rearranged text. Not covered: non-R scholia vetera (V, E, Θ, N, etc. in Holwerda), the recentiora (Thomas Magister, Triclinius) and Tzetzes' commentary. I found no modern English translation of these. Single scholia may be translated in sourcebooks (e.g. Csapo–Slater, Rusten, The Birth of Comedy); I could not verify this because WebSearch was exhausted.
item_114.other_found: French: Chantry, Scholies anciennes aux Grenouilles et au Ploutos d'Aristophane (Paris, 2009), Frogs and Plutus only. Confirmed in BMCR 2014.12.27 (review of Daude et al., Scholies à Pindare I), which cites no Clouds translation. I found no French, German, Italian or Spanish translation of the Clouds scholia or of Tzetzes on Clouds, but search engines were unavailable, so this is not exhaustive.
item_114.source_text: Public domain: Fr. Dübner, Scholia graeca in Aristophanem cum prolegomenis grammaticorum (Paris: Didot, 1842; reprint 1877), https://archive.org/details/scholiagraecain00dbgoog. It mixes vetera and recentiora, and I believe it has no separate Tzetzes commentary on Clouds (to be checked). Rutherford 1896 vol. I is also public domain for the R scholia. Standard modern editions, both in copyright: D. Holwerda, Scholia in Aristophanem I.3.1, Scholia vetera et recentiora in Nubes (Groningen, 1977), and W. J. W. Koster, Scholia in Aristophanem IV.2, Jo. Tzetzae commentarii in Nubes (Groningen, 1960). I found no public-domain edition of the Tzetzes layer, so that part depends on Koster.
item_114.research_yield: Two editions of Clouds (hypotheses, parabasis scholia); reception of Socrates and Chaerephon; komodoumenoi prosopography (Leogoras, Megacles); Alexandrian sources (Didymus, Symmachus, Heliodorus); R/V/Tzetzes layering; a critique of Rutherford's 1896 version; Σ Nub. 109 on Phasis.
item_114.recommendation: Keep at priority 3, as a Russian-first project. The Russian gap holds, but the R layer of Clouds 1–262 already has a public-domain English version (Rutherford 1896), and Tzetzes is available only in copyrighted Koster 1960. Best first unit: all scholia vetera to Clouds 1–262 from Dübner, with the non-R scholia (new in English) marked and Rutherford used as a cross-check. Add Tzetzes only after Koster's rights are cleared, and check Latyshev I, p. 353 first.

item_115.title_short: Scholia vetera in Aratum (scholia on Phaen. 1–136)
item_115.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation of the scholia, in full or in part. The required searches could not be run: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was used up, and both of my queries were refused. A Russian query («схолии к Арату перевод») and an English one were attempted and returned nothing. Everything below therefore comes from opening known pages directly and from the project's own cached research.
(1) The ru.wikipedia article «Арат из Сол» lists only two Russian translations of the poem itself. One is by А. А. Россиус: «Арат. Явления», with commentary, in «Небо, наука, поэзия» (М.: Изд-во МГУ, 1992), pp. 25–61 and 119–189. The other is by К. А. Богданов (СПб.: Алетейя, 2000, 256 pp.). Under the heading «Схолии к Арату» the article cites only Maass 1898 and Maass's 1888 edition of Attalus. It names no Russian translation of the scholia.
(2) ancientrome.ru/antlitr has no entry for Aratus or his scholia.
(3) The wave-1 sweep, which used ancientrome.ru and ru-wiki, found no Russian translation of any Greek scholia corpus, Aratus included.
I could not check whether Rossius's 1992 commentary or Bogdanov's 2000 commentary translates individual scholia, so isolated excerpts there are possible but unconfirmed. I also could not check simposium.ru, cyberleninka/elibrary or the РГБ catalogue, because doing so would have needed search.
item_115.en_found:
I found no English translation. Cuypers' Hellenistic Bibliography page «Aratus and Aratea» (fetched directly) lists Martin 1974 and Maass 1898, the Achilles editions and studies, and studies of the Aratus Latinus. It lists no translation of the scholia. The en.wikipedia articles «Aratus» and «Catasterismi» name English translations of the poem only (Mair 1921 Loeb; Kidd 1997; Poochigian; Hard 2015) and of the Catasterismi (Condos 1997; Hard 2015). Neither article mentions any translation of the scholia.
Excerpts of individual scholia almost certainly appear inside commentaries such as Kidd 1997, and possibly in Hard's 2015 notes; I could not confirm Hard because the OUP page came back empty. I found no free-standing or partial English translation of the proem or Dike scholia. The English queries I planned were blocked by the search limit.
item_115.other_found:
FRENCH, an unconfirmed lead: Abbé N. Halma's 1821 volume (Paris: Merlin). Its title runs «Les Phénomènes d'Aratus de Soles et de Germanicus César, avec les Scholies de Théon, les Catastérismes d'Ératosthène et la Sphère de Léontius» and it is cited on fr.wikipedia «Aratos de Soles». From memory, the title page says these texts were "traduits pour la première fois en français", but I could not confirm that. I also could not confirm whether the vulgate scholia, then attributed to "Theon", are translated in full or only printed in Greek. The remacle.org French Aratus page linked from fr.wikipedia has the verse translation only, with no scholia. If Halma did translate them, his version is a pre-critical one, made from the old vulgate text.
LATIN: the Merovingian Aratus Latinus of the 8th century is a Latin translation of Aratus together with parts of a Greek commentary, printed in Maass 1898. The scholia to Germanicus (Breysig 1867) adapt Greek scholiastic material. Both count as medieval or ancient versions, not modern translations.
GERMAN, ITALIAN, SPANISH: de.wikipedia, it.wikipedia, fr.wikipedia and the Cuypers page list translations of the poem only: Erren's Tusculum, Schott 1958, Zannoni 1948, Gigante Lanzara 2018, Martin's Budé 1998, Tapia Zúñiga 1995 and Calderón Dorda (Gredos). None lists a translation of the scholia. Because the search limit blocked further searching, I cannot rule out a dissertation-level translation.
item_115.source_text:
The standard modern edition is J. Martin, Scholia in Aratum vetera (Stuttgart: Teubner, 1974; xxxvii + 595 pp.), and it is in copyright. The Neoscholia translation can be made from Martin, but Martin's Greek text should not be reproduced.
Public-domain options:
(a) E. Maass, Commentariorum in Aratum reliquiae (Berlin: Weidmann, 1898), full scan and OCR at https://archive.org/details/commentariorvmi00maasgoog. Its table of contents shows it contains the Isagoge material, the Anonymi, the Vitae, the Aratus Latinus, and the «Isagoga et scholia Marciana et Parisina», which are only part of the scholia. It is not the full scholia vetera, so the candidate file is wrong to treat Maass as a public-domain equivalent of Martin.
(b) For the vulgate scholia as a whole, the public-domain editions I recall are I. Bekker, Aratus cum scholiis (Berlin, 1828), and J. T. Buhle's Leipzig edition of 1793–1801. I did not confirm either online in this session.
Recommended practice: translate from Martin, print Greek lemmata from Bekker or Maass, and record Martin's numbering.
item_115.research_yield: Possible articles: Stoic allegoresis of Aratus' Zeus proem; the Dike/Parthenos myth and how its versions were transmitted (Hesiod, Eratosthenes' Erigone, the Latin Aratea); the scholia as witnesses to Eratosthenes' catasterisms, to Hipparchus and Attalus, and to doxography (Mansfeld); and the Hellenistic court context (Antigonus Gonatas) found in the prolegomena.
item_115.recommendation: Keep the candidate: no Russian or English translation was found. Two corrections are needed. First, check the possible 1821 Halma French version before claiming "first in any modern language". Second, Maass 1898 is not a public-domain substitute for Martin. Best first unit: Martin's scholia on Phaen. 1–18 (the Zeus proem) plus 96–136 (Dike), about 8–12k words, translated from Martin with lemmata from a public-domain edition. Rerun the blocked searches before announcing it.

item_116.title_short: Scholia on Euripides, Phoenissae (Ph. 1–260; Mastronarde Release 4 covers 1–689)
item_116.ru_found: No Russian translation found, but the check was weak. WebSearch was unavailable: the harness-wide budget of 200 calls was already spent when this task started, so none of the required 4 Russian searches could run. What I did check: (1) Project cache ru_series_crosscheck.json lists one possible overlap, V. V. Latyshev, Scythica et Caucasica I, p. 347, excerpt 'Scholia in Euripidem' (ВДИ 1947–48). The cache itself rates it 'low likelihood'. I scanned the full Greek text of Mastronarde's Ph. 1–689 scholia for Scythian, Pontic or Caucasian content and found none. Any Latyshev excerpt is therefore almost certainly from other plays and does not touch the unit. I could not verify p. 347 directly because the archive.org OCR of Latyshev I is unusable. (2) The ancientrome.ru antlitr author index has no Euripides or scholia entry. Not checked: elibrary/cyberleninka, vostlit, the Литпамятники Euripides of 1999 (Анненский tr., Ярхо comm., which may quote single scholia or hypotheses), ВДИ, Аристей, ΣΧΟΛΗ, RSL catalogue. Until those are searched, read 'none' as provisional.
item_116.en_found: REFUTED: the colleague's 'English: none' is wrong. D. J. Mastronarde, Euripides Scholia: An Open-Access Online Edition, Release 4 (Sept. 2026), added the Phoenissae 1–689 scholia with English translations (https://euripidesscholia.org/Edition/PhoenScholia_all.html). I downloaded the 10.6 MB page and parsed it. It has 2,521 TRANSLATION blocks across 10,440 scholia. By type: exeg 2,222 of 2,232 translated; gram 78 of 81; rhet 22 of 24; metr 87 of 307 (about 95% of metrical words); gloss 43 of 6,247; paraphr 43 of 757; artGloss 0 of 642. The hypotheses/prefatory material (Arg.), including the Peisander mythographic note, are also translated. Preface, verbatim: 'As of release 4, I have provided translations for all scholia of types ‘exeg’, ‘gram’, and ‘rhet’'. Glosses and Moschopulean/Thoman paraphrases are mostly left untranslated. For the proposed unit Ph. 1–260: 1,132 of 4,182 scholia translated, about 19.8k of 29.1k Greek words (≈68%). Every substantive note is in English; the untranslated remainder is glosses and paraphrases. Ph. 690–1766 has no English yet, but Mastronarde schedules 690–1306 for 2028 and 1307–1766 for 2030 (About page). Unverified, from memory: the Peisander note (FGrHist 16 F 10) probably has an English version in Brill's New Jacoby, and Mastronarde's 1994 Cambridge commentary translates individual scholia.
item_116.other_found: German: Mastronarde's own comments in the edition cite 'Manuwald 2012' with 'German translation and brief commentary' for several prefatory items: the Laius oracle (pp. 338–339), the Sphinx riddle (340–341), the couplets (342–343) and Aristophanes' epigram on OT (330–333). This is probably B. Manuwald, Sophokles, König Ödipus (De Gruyter 2012); I have not verified that title. Comments also cite early Latin translations, but of the play (Stiblinus 1562), not the scholia. I found no French, Italian or Spanish translation of the Phoenissae scholia. Those searches could not run because of the search-budget limit, so this is unverified, not a negative finding.
item_116.source_text: Best source: Mastronarde, EuripidesScholia.org Release 4/4.01 (2026), Greek critical text with full apparatus, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (verified on the About page). It is in copyright but openly licensed. NC fits Neoscholia. ShareAlike means pages derived from Mastronarde's text, and any use of his English, must also be BY-NC-SA, with attribution and release number. Public-domain alternatives: E. Schwartz, Scholia in Euripidem I (Berlin 1887; Or., Ph. scholia vetera) and W. Dindorf, Scholia Graeca in Euripidis tragoedias (Oxford 1863; vol. III has the Byzantine Ph. scholia, cited by Mastronarde as 'Dind. III'). Both are PD, but their scan URLs were not re-verified this session. Size correction: the unit is not ~10k words. My count gives Ph. 1–260 as about 29k Greek words (4,182 scholia, many repetitive glosses) and Ph. 1–689 as about 67k, not ~25k.
item_116.research_yield: Russian-first access to the Theban mythography (Peisander note, Dercylus, Asclepiades' riddle) and to Byzantine school exegesis (Moschopoulos, Thomas, Triclinius metrics). Best article: a methodological LLM-vs-expert study using Mastronarde's English as a gold standard.
item_116.recommendation: Downgrade. It is not a first-ever translation, since every substantive scholion on Ph. 1–689 is already in Mastronarde's open English; keep it only as a Russian-first item and AI-calibration benchmark. Best first unit: the Phoenissae hypotheses/Arg. (oracle, riddle, Peisander) plus the exegetic scholia on the prologue Ph. 1–87, translated from the Greek and checked against Mastronarde, under BY-NC-SA.

item_117.title_short: John Tzetzes, Exegesis of the Iliad (prolegomena)
item_117.ru_found:
No Russian translation found. The search budget was already spent, so no keyword searches ran; I checked by fetching pages directly and reading the project cache.
(1) ru.wikipedia «Иоанн Цец»: lists the prose «экзегеза к Илиаде» and gives no translation. The only Russian translations it names are the 1969 anthology and Smyka.
(2) Full text of «Памятники византийской литературы IX–XIV вв.» (М.: Наука, 1968/69), on facetia.ru/node/4798: the Цец section has only Carmina Iliaca excerpts, translated by Т. В. Попова (per the project cache). These are «События догомеровского времени» 1–75 and 210–245, «…гомеровского» 289–407, and «…послегомеровского» 361–467. There is nothing from the Exegesis. This settles the earlier open question about pp. 252–259.
(3) О. В. Смыка, smyka.persona.msu.ru: three volumes (2022, 2023, 2023), whose only Tzetzes items are «До Гомера», «По Гомеру» and «После Гомера».
(4) ancientrome.ru author index: no entry for Цец.
Remaining risk: the ВДИ 1952 №2 supplement to Латышев includes unspecified Tzetzes excerpts. vdi.igh.ru was blocked, but a Scythian passage in the prolegomena or Il. 1 is very unlikely. cyberleninka and elibrary were not checked.
item_117.en_found:
None found, but this is only weakly verified because no English keyword searches could run.
The en, de, it and el Wikipedia articles on Tzetzes list translations only of other works: the Allegories of the Iliad and of the Odyssey (Goldwyn & Kokkini, DOML 2015 and 2019); the Antehomerica, Homerica and Posthomerica (English, archive.org uploads sponsored by mitologia.pt, 2014); and the Chiliades (theoi.com, 2014–16). The theoi.com Library lists only the Chiliades. ToposText has a ChatGPT translation of the Lycophron scholia (work/860), but its catalogue is dynamic and I could not enumerate it to rule out a machine-translated Exegesis. Recent articles or theses on the Exegesis may contain translated excerpts and were not checked.
item_117.other_found: No full or partial modern-language translation verified. Italian: Leone's 2015 translation covers only the Carmina Iliaca. Papathomopoulos 2007 is a Greek-only edition (el.wikipedia). Secondary studies that probably quote passages in translation were not checked: H. Hunger, JÖBG 1954 (on Tzetzes' allegorical myth interpretation, cited in ru-wiki); P. Cesaretti, Allegoristi di Omero a Bisanzio (1991); V. F. Lovato's articles on the Exegesis. These would be excerpt-level at most.
item_117.source_text:
Prolegomena plus commentary on Il. 1.1–96: G. Hermann (ed.), Draconis Stratonicensis Liber de metris poeticis; Ioannis Tzetzae Exegesis in Homeri Iliadem, Leipzig 1812. It is public domain. I did not verify a scan URL because archive.org refused the connection.
The coverage up to A 96 is inferred from A. Lolos, Der unbekannte Teil der Ilias-Exegesis des Iohannes Tzetzes (A 97–609), editio princeps, Königstein/Ts.: Hain 1981 (in copyright; confirmed on de.wikipedia). So the pilot introduction is fully in the public-domain Hermann text.
The standard critical edition of the whole work is M. Papathomopoulos, Ἐξήγησις Ἰωάννου Γραμματικοῦ τοῦ Τζέτζου εἰς τὴν Ὁμήρου Ἰλιάδα, Athens 2007 (el.wikipedia), which is in copyright. Use Hermann as the base text and check readings against Papathomopoulos.
item_117.research_yield: Articles on Tzetzes' first statement of tripartite allegory (pragmatic, psychic, physical) compared with his Allegories; Byzantine accounts of Homer's life and poetic genres; Tzetzes' polemical self-fashioning compared with Eustathius' prolegomena. It would be the first Russian or English text of a Byzantine Homer-commentary preface.
item_117.recommendation: Keep at priority 3; no Russian translation was found, including in the 1969 anthology. Re-run the 4+4 keyword searches, which this run could not do, before commissioning. The best first unit is the introduction (prolegomena), from Hermann's 1812 public-domain text checked against Papathomopoulos 2007, roughly 10–15k words.

item_118.title_short: Tzetzes, Historiai/Chiliades (Book I or Alexander cluster)
item_118.ru_found:
I could not refute the claim. There is no full or substantial Russian translation, only excerpts. I am changing the label from "partial" to "excerpts_only".

SEARCH LIMIT: none of the 8 required searches ran. All 4 WebSearch calls I tried (2 RU, 2 EN) were refused because the 200-search budget was used up. I did not work around this. I used direct page fetches and the project cache instead.

What I checked:
(1) ru.wikipedia «Иоанн Цец» (fetched): the only Russian is excerpts in «Памятники византийской литературы IX–XIV вв.» (М.: Наука, 1969), pp. 252–259, with a note on pp. 251–252. The page names no translator and does not say which historiai are included. I could not see the volume.
(2) Латышев, «Известия древних писателей… о Скифии и Кавказе», vol. I (archive.org OCR, author index read this session): Tzetzes appears only as «Τζέτζης (ἐξήγ. εἰς Λυκόφρ.) 400–406», i.e. the Lycophron commentary. There is no Chiliades entry.
(3) ВДИ 1952 №2 «Дополнения» (project cache; only some pages were read): Tzetzes appears on Lycophron; the rest of the contents is unverified. The Chiliades has Scythian historiai (IV.32 Anacharsis; VIII.69 Maeotian/Caucasian Scythians; IX.21 Dexippus' Scythica; XII.54 Amazons/Sauromatae) that could be in it. None of them is in Book I or the Alexander cluster.
(4) О. В. Смыка's site (fetched): she translated only the Carmina Iliaca (До Гомера, Аристей XXIV 2021 / МГУ 2023; По Гомеру/После Гомера, 2022). Nothing from the Chiliades.
(5) The cached crawl of all vostlit A–Я indexes and its Byzantine index found no Tzetzes text apart from Латышев.
Short quotations inside Russian monographs (e.g. on Archimedes, or Hipponax fragments transmitted by Tzetzes) probably exist, but I did not verify them.
item_118.en_found:
A full English translation of all 13 books exists. It was made by volunteers for mitologia.pt from Kiessling's 1826 text.
- Translators: A. Untila (Book I), G. Berkowitz (II–IV), K. Ramiotis (V–VI), V. Dogani (VII–VIII), J. Alexander (IX–X), M. S. Fadhlurrahman (XI), N. Giallousis (XII–XIII).
- archive.org item TzetzesCHILIADES: uploaded 2015-03-21, licensed CC BY-NC-ND 3.0, the PDF says "Last Edit: 03-12-2024". It calls itself a "tentative first edition" with minimal comments (I read the downloaded text).
- Also on theoi.com, TzetzesChiliades1–13.html.
- ToposText work 617 (12,759 lines, Kiessling numbering) reuses it but was refused permission to correct it.
- It has no apparatus and is not checked against Leone. I found no print or scholarly English edition (e.g. DOML), but the search limit means this is not confirmed.
item_118.other_found:
- Latin: Paulus Lacisius' version in the 1546 Basel editio princeps (Gerbel), reprinted with Kiessling in 1826. This comes from the project cache and my memory; I did not re-check it this session.
- No complete modern French, German, Italian or Spanish translation was found. Because searches were blocked, partial translations in those languages remain "unknown".
- Leone's edition is the Greek text only.
item_118.source_text:
- Public domain: Th. Kiessling, Ioannis Tzetzae Historiarum variarum Chiliades (Leipzig 1826). ToposText and the English translation use its line numbers.
- Archive.org scan: the cache gives the ID historiarumvari00kiesgoog, but archive.org refused connections when I tried to re-check it. A Google Books scan likely also exists.
- Standard modern edition: P. A. M. Leone, Ioannis Tzetzae Historiae (Napoli 1968; 2nd ed. Galatina: Congedo 2007). It is in copyright and its line numbers differ slightly.
- Practical approach: translate from Kiessling and collate Leone's readings (facts, not copyrightable text). Cite Leone's line numbers alongside Kiessling's.
item_118.research_yield:
Possible article topics:
- Tzetzes' Alexander dossier: Bucephalus I.28, Stagira VII.41, Apelles/Lysippus VIII.42/45, X.22, Alexander's appearance XI.5–6.
- Archimedes (II.35, XII.60) and the lost sources behind it.
- How the Historiai relate to his own letters, and how he presents himself as a scholar.
- How reliable his citations of Diodorus, Dio and others are.
item_118.recommendation: Keep, but merge with item_079 (same work). Best first unit is Chiliad I (Histories 1–32, about 1,000 lines, Croesus to Xerxes, including Bucephalus); the alternative is a cross-book Alexander cluster. Before publishing, check both against the 1969 «Памятники» excerpts (pp. 252–259) and the ВДИ 1952 Дополнения, and use the English version only for cross-checking (ND license).

item_119.title_short: Hipparchus, Commentary on Aratus and Eudoxus (Book 1)
item_119.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation, full or partial. Search coverage was limited: the shared WebSearch budget (200 per turn) was already used up when this item started, so none of the planned Russian searches ran. I checked these pages directly instead.
(1) ru.wikipedia «Гиппарх». Under «Издания и переводы» it lists only Manitius 1894 for the Commentary; the other entries are the Almagest (Веселовский) and the geographical fragments. No Russian version of the Commentary.
(2) ru.wikipedia «Арат из Сол». Russian Aratus translations: А.А. Россиус, «Небо, наука, поэзия» (М.: МГУ, 1992); К.А. Богданов (СПб.: Алетейя, 2000). Hipparchus' Commentary is not mentioned. Their commentaries may quote passages of Hipparchus; not checked.
(3) Full ΣΧΟΛΗ translation index (classics.nsu.ru/scholeru/schedule.htm). It has Щетников's Geminus (5.2, 2011), Cleomedes (4.2, 2010), [Arist.] Problems XV and Euclid's Optics (13.2, 2019), and Афонасин's Heraclides fragments (2019). Nothing by Hipparchus, Eudoxus or Attalus.
(4) ancientrome.ru antlitr index: no Hipparchus, Aratus or Eudoxus.
(5) ru.wikipedia «Евдокс Книдский»: no Russian edition of the Eudoxus fragments, which are quoted in Hipparchus Book 1.
Possible scattered Russian excerpts not checked: Россиус's and Богданов's notes to Aratus; the Russian edition of van der Waerden («Пробуждающаяся наука II», 1991). The library catalogues RSL/NLR and eLibrary were not searched.
item_119.en_found:
I found no English translation, full or partial. No English search engine queries ran (budget used up), so this rests on directly fetched pages.
(1) en.wikipedia «Hipparchus», read in full. Its Translations list for the Commentary has only Manitius 1894 (Greek/German) and Cusinato & Vanin (Italian, 2022 [2013]). Its only English entry is Dicks 1960, which is the Geographical Fragments, a different work.
(2) Vanin & Cusinato, arXiv:2206.08243. The abstract and introduction (read in the PDF) call it the first modern-language translation since Manitius 1894. The introduction's history of the text mentions no English version.
(3) en.wikipedia «Aratus»: no translation of the Commentary.
(4) attalus.org translations index: no Hipparchus.
English excerpts very likely exist in scholarship (Kidd's 1997 Aratus commentary, Dicks 1970 on the Eudoxus fragments, D. Duke's star-coordinate papers). These are from memory and were not checked this run. Loeb, ToposText and BMCR were not searched.
item_119.other_found:
German: K. Manitius, Teubner 1894, facing-page translation with notes (public domain).
Italian: B. Cusinato (translation) and G. Vanin (astronomical commentary). First published in Vanin, Catasterismi (Feltre: Rheticus-DBS Zanetti, 2013), pp. 85–166. Third edition 2022, arXiv:2206.08243, licence CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, based on the Manitius text.
Latin: D. Petau (Petavius), Uranologion (Paris 1630), reprinted in Migne PG 19 (1857).
Earlier editions: editio princeps P. Vettori (Florence 1567). Per Vanin, E. Maass's Aratus commentaries (1888–98) include Book 1 and part of Book 2.
French: no translation found. fr.wikipedia lists none. There are studies by Nadal & Brunet (1984, 1989).
Spanish (Gredos): none found, not searched.
The claim that no modern-language translation exists does not hold: German 1894 and Italian 2013/2022 exist. The RU and EN gap does hold.
item_119.source_text:
Best open text: First1KGreek TEI-EpiDoc of Manitius 1894, licence CC BY-SA 4.0, with apparatus footnotes, URN urn:cts:greekLit:tlg1431.tlg003.1st1K-grc1. URL: https://github.com/OpenGreekAndLatin/First1KGreek/blob/master/data/tlg1431/tlg003/tlg1431.tlg003.1st1K-grc1.xml (I downloaded and parsed it).
Scan: archive.org McGillLibrary-hssl_hipparchou-ton-aratou_QB41H561894-18575. Metadata confirmed: Lipsiae, Teubner 1894, xxxiv + 375 pp., Greek and German.
Copyright: the standard and only critical edition is still Manitius 1894, which is public domain. I know of no newer critical edition.
Measured size, Greek words excluding the apparatus: about 28.7k in total. Book 1 ≈ 11.6k (11 chapters), Book 2 ≈ 10.3k, Book 3 ≈ 6.9k.
The open Italian translation (CC BY-NC-SA) can serve as a cross-check.
item_119.research_yield: Book 1 is the main source for the lost Eudoxus Phaenomena/Enoptron and for Attalus of Rhodes. It shows Hipparchus doing textual criticism of Aratus (e.g. I.9 ἀπλατέες/πλατέες) and science versus poetry. Its star data allow dating and comparison with the 2022 Sinai palimpsest catalogue.
item_119.recommendation: Keep at top priority; the RU and EN gap is confirmed. Pilot unit: Book 1, chapters 1–3 (≈2.5k words: the dedication to Aeschrion, the parallel quotations showing Aratus follows Eudoxus, and the programme against Attalus). Then the rest of Book 1 (≈11.6k). Plan it together with the Aratus scholia (item_115).

item_120.title_short: Alexander of Tralles, Therapeutics / On Fevers / Letter on Worms (Letter on Worms + Ther. I)
item_120.ru_found: No Russian translation found, but the check was limited. The shared WebSearch budget had run out, so none of the required Russian searches could run. What I could check: ru.wikipedia DOES have an article, «Александр Траллийский», so the colleague's claim that there is no ru.wikipedia article is wrong. It names no Russian translation. Its literature list includes S. G. Kovner, «История средневековой медицины», Kiev 1893, pp. 58–110: a 50-page chapter that may contain paraphrased or translated quotations (unverified; not a translation as such). Brockhaus-Efron and the 1861 encyclopedia have dictionary entries only. ancientrome.ru, vostlit, ΣΧΟΛΗ, elibrary and the RSL catalogue were not checked.
item_120.en_found: There is no complete English translation; the en, de, fr, it and es Wikipedia pages list none. Excerpts exist: P. Bouras-Vallianatos, 'Clinical Experience in Late Antiquity: Alexander of Tralles and the Therapy of Epilepsy', Medical History 58.3 (2014) 337–353, doi:10.1017/mdh.2014.27, CC BY. It gives his own English translations of substantial passages of Therapeutics I.15 (epilepsy, which is part of the proposed pilot unit) and of the proem to On Fevers. Possible further excerpts, unverified: F. Wallis, Medieval Medicine: A Reader (UTP 2010), which en.wikipedia cites at p. 23; I could not check its table of contents (publisher returned 403). Thorndike's History of Magic paraphrases the amulets. No English version of the Letter on Worms was found.
item_120.other_found: German, complete with facing Greek: Th. Puschmann, Alexander von Tralles, Wien 1878–79 (2 vols; repr. Amsterdam 1963). The Letter on Worms is at vol. 2, 586–99; On Fevers at vol. 1, 287–439. German excerpts (iatromagic): Grimm-Stadelmann 2020, pp. 187–536. French, complete: F. Brunet, Médecine et thérapeutique byzantines, 4 vols, Geuthner 1933–37; vol. II holds On Fevers, the Letter on Worms and Therapeutics I. Italian, selections: A. Guardasole, 'Alessandro di Tralle', in A. Garzya (ed.), Medici bizantini (UTET 2006, Greek–Italian). Bouras-Vallianatos 2014 cites its Italian rendering in the epilepsy context (p. 663), so Ther. I.15 is probably at least partly there; the exact selection is unverified. Spanish: none found. Latin and Arabic versions survive from antiquity and the Middle Ages (Latin edited in part by Langslow 2006).
item_120.source_text: Puschmann, Alexander von Tralles (Wien: Braumüller 1878–79), 2 vols, plus Nachträge (Berliner Studien 5.2, 1886), all public domain. Scans are at BSB/MDZ (linked from en.wikipedia) and on archive.org. Puschmann remains the ONLY critical edition (Bouras-Vallianatos 2014, n. 11), so the standard text is public domain. A new edition is reportedly in progress (Guardasole); its status is unverified. Brunet's French translation may still be in copyright (translator's death date unknown).
item_120.research_yield: Articles on late-antique iatromagic and amulets in a Galenic clinician; Alexander's critique of Galen and his case-based method; the anthelmintic letter as an epistolary medical genre; the medical milieu of Anthemius's family in Tralles; reception in Latin and Arabic. Strong first-ever Russian contribution to Byzantine medicine studies.
item_120.recommendation: Keep, at P4: Russian and full English translations are absent, but full German and French versions, Italian selections and English excerpts reduce the novelty. Start with the Letter on Worms (about 3k words, Puschmann II 586–99; no English found). Replace the epilepsy chapter with a less-covered unit such as the gout book or the melancholy chapter (Ther. I.17). Before committing, recheck Kovner 1893, Wallis 2010 and the Medici bizantini contents (searches blocked this run).

item_121.title_short: Stephanus of Byzantium, Ethnica (entries on the cities of Alexander and the Diadochi)
item_121.ru_found:
There is no complete Russian translation, and I found none for the proposed unit. The existing Russian versions are selective and cover only two letters:
(1) Letter Ε: Холод М. М. (with Лебедева Г. Е. and Морозов М. А.), «Страницы из византийской лексикографической литературы. Стефан Византийский», Клио № 2 (21), 2003. It is online at vostlit.info/Texts/Dokumenty/Byzanz/VI/520-540/Stefan/text.htm, translated from Meineke 1849. I counted about 140 lemmata, from Ἐαρεῖς to Ἐχῖνος. The translator's note says Ε is not complete and that only the historically most valuable entries were chosen. They include Hellenistic foundations such as Ἐπιφάνεια, Εὐμένεια and Εὐκρατιδία.
(2) Letter Δ: Лебедева Г. Е., Холод М. М., Морозов М. А., «Стефан Византийский и его „Этника“: [Δ]», Европа: Междунар. альманах 2003 № 3, pp. 166–184. The citation comes from the Russian Wikipedia bibliography. The sweep missed this one. I could not see its scope, so whether it includes Δημητριάς is unknown.
(3) Pontic and Caucasian entries appear in Латышев's SC/ВДИ excerpts (as the project cache records).
I found no Russian versions of the entries for Ἀλεξάνδρεια, Ἀντιόχεια, Σελεύκεια, Ἀπάμεια or Λαοδίκεια. One limit: the WebSearch budget was used up before the first query, so I checked by direct fetches only (vostlit, the ruwiki raw text, project files). Russian monographs on Alexander's cities (for example Пьянков, Гафуров/Цибукидис) may translate the Alexandreia list, and I could not check them.
item_121.en_found:
There is no complete published English translation.
(1) ToposText work 241: Brady Kiesling translated about 35 entries, tagged "partial". They include Arsinoe (A125.21) and Nikaia (N474.17, the former Antigoneia), which overlap with the proposed unit. Alexandreia (A70.8) is Greek only.
(2) A competitor: Macquarie University's CANOPOS project (Greta Hawes, PI; Greg Baker; G. Jower), titled "Developing a hybrid human-ML approach to support the first translation of Stephanus' Ethnica into English". It runs 1 Jan to 31 Dec 2026 (researchers.mq.edu.au/en/projects/canopos/). Nothing is published yet on manto-myth.org/canopos.
(3) Not verified, because searches were blocked: Fraser, Cities of Alexander the Great (1996), and Cohen's Hellenistic Settlements volumes may translate the Alexandreia list or single city entries. Many entries also appear in English as fragments of lost historians in BNJ (Hecataeus and others).
item_121.other_found:
- German: complete, with facing translation and notes. M. Billerbeck et al., Stephani Byzantii Ethnica, CFHB 43/1–5, De Gruyter 2006–2017.
- Latin: parallel versions in Pinedo (Amsterdam 1678; 1725) and Berkel/Gronovius (Leiden 1688).
- French, Italian and Spanish: I found no translations, but I could not search for them, so their status is unknown.
item_121.source_text:
- Meineke, Stephani Byzantii Ethnicorum quae supersunt (Berlin 1849; repr. Graz 1958): public domain. A Google Books scan is listed on en.wikipedia (id MMZiAAAAMAAJ). The Greek text is on ToposText work 241 (topostext.org/work/241).
- Billerbeck (CFHB 43/1–5, De Gruyter 2006–2017): the standard modern critical edition. Its text and German translation are in copyright and not open access. The archive.org copies of it appear to be unauthorized uploads, so use it for checking only.
- For the pilot, translate from Meineke and collate against Billerbeck's text and numbering.
item_121.research_yield:
- Stephanus's 18 Alexandrias compared with the Alexander Romance city lists and Fraser.
- Seleucid and Ptolemaic dynastic renaming of cities (Antigoneia to Nikaia, Arsinoe, Apameia, Laodikeia).
- The lost sources Stephanus cites for Hellenistic foundations (Charax, Uranius, Polyhistor).
- Ethnic-name formation as evidence of how city status was perceived.
item_121.recommendation: Keep, with Russian first: the core entries of the unit are untranslated in Russian. The best first unit is Ἀλεξάνδρεια (the list of 18 Alexandrias), followed by Ἀντιόχεια, Σελεύκεια, Ἀπάμεια, Λαοδίκεια, Στρατονίκεια, Λυσιμάχεια, Κασσάνδρεια, Πτολεμαΐς and Βερενίκη, crediting the Холод Δ/Ε versions of Epiphaneia, Eumeneia and the other entries already in Russian. Hold off on any "first English" claim until the Macquarie CANOPOS 2026 project publishes, and check Fraser 1996 first.

item_122.title_short: Galen, De simplicium medicamentorum temperamentis ac facultatibus (Book X)
item_122.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation of the work, in full or in part, and none of Book X. Caveat: the shared WebSearch budget for this turn was already used up, so my Russian and English queries did not run. I could not do the required 4+4 live searches, and I did not query elibrary, RSL or CyberLeninka. What I checked:
(1) ru.wikipedia «Гален», the «Переводы» list (fetched today). It names Кондратьев/Терновский 1971 (De usu partium); Балалыкин/Щеглов, Сочинения т. I (2014); Пролыгина (2011–2017: Quod optimus medicus, Protrepticus, Ars medica I–XXXVII, De ordine, De libris propriis); Афонасин (ΣΧΟΛΗ 2015 De sectis; 2016 De propriis placitis); Щеглов 2024 (De naturalibus facultatibus). There is no pharmacological work in the list.
(2) The contents of Балалыкин «Гален. Сочинения» vols. II–V (2015–18, trans. З. А. Барзах), from an earlier verification of item_034 in this project cache (LitRes check): vol. 2 is pathology treatises, vols. 3–4 are De placitis, vol. 5 is De nat. fac. plus the venesection works. No Simple Drugs.
(3) The project's Russian series cross-check (ΣΧΟΛΗ, Историко-философский ежегодник, ВДИ/Латышев, philology journals, vostlit, patristic and Belgorod series) records no conflict for item_122.
(4) The CMG «Galenus – Übersetzungen» list (fetched today) has no translations for no. 077. However, it records Russian only sporadically: Kondratev 1971 is there, Balalykin is not.
Residual risk: unindexed excerpts in Russian history-of-pharmacy articles or theses.
item_122.en_found:
No English translation exists of the whole work, of any book, or of Book X.
Evidence:
(1) Fichtner, Corpus Galenicum (BBAW, ed. 2023/12), no. 78. I extracted the full entry from the PDF. Its only items marked E,T are Garofalo 1985 (Italian sample) and Petit 2010 (French, I.1–3). Hasluck's «Terra Lemnia» (1929, pp. 672f.) is classed as a study (U), not a translation.
(2) The CMG «Galenus – Übersetzungen» list (online, ©2018–2026) gives no. 077 with zero translations in any language.
(3) github.com/campattison/galen_project (Zainaldin, Pattison et al., arXiv 2602.24119) does not include this work. Its AI translations cover De comp. med. per genera I.2 and De temperamentis only.
Short English quotations in secondary literature are likely but not verified: the Lemnian-earth passage in IX, and the Xenocrates/anthropophagy passage in X.1 (Kühn XII 248ff.). en.wikipedia «Xenocrates of Aphrodisias» only paraphrases it, after Smith's Dictionary of 1870. I ran no live English searches because the budget was exhausted.
item_122.other_found:
- French: C. Petit, «La tradition manuscrite du traité des Simples de Galien. Editio princeps et traduction annotée des chapitres 1 à 3 du livre I», in Boudon-Millot, Garzya, Jouanna and Roselli (eds.), Histoire de la tradition et édition des médecins grecs (Napoli 2010), 143–165. This covers I.1–3 only.
- Italian: I. Garofalo, «Un sondaggio sul De simplicium medicamentorum facultate di Galeno», in Studi arabo-islamici in onore di R. Rubinacci (Napoli 1985), 317–325. This is a short sample edition and translation; I could not verify which passage.
- German: M. Haars, Die allgemeinen Wirkungspotenziale der einfachen Arzneimittel bei Galen. Oreibasios, Collectiones medicae XV (Stuttgart 2018; QSGP 116). It translates Oribasius' abridged excerpt of the drug catalogue, not Galen's text. Fichtner classes it as a commentary (K), and I did not verify how much of Book X it covers.
- Pre-modern versions: Kühn's facing Latin (1826, public domain); medieval Latin by Gerard of Cremona and Constantinus; Arabic by Ḥubaysh; Syriac by Sergius of Rēšʿaynā and Ḥunayn.
- No Spanish translation was found. The CMG list shows none in any language.
item_122.source_text:
Best open source: First1KGreek / Digital Corpus for Graeco-Arabic Studies TEI, tlg0057.tlg075.1st1K-grc1.xml (Leipzig 2016, CC BY-SA 4.0), https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OpenGreekAndLatin/First1KGreek/master/data/tlg0057/tlg075/tlg0057.tlg075.1st1K-grc1.xml
- Content: Kühn's Greek text only. The header says "I–VI", but I parsed it and all 11 books are present, about 134k Greek words in total.
- Book X: Kühn XII 245–309, 9,942 Greek words. Ch. 1 is the preface (about 1,200 words). Ch. 2 has 30 sections (blood, milk, whey, cheese, butter, rennet, bile, sweat, urine, saliva, dung, human dirt).
- The digital text has keyboarding typos (e.g. «πόπρου», «Ξενακράτει»), so collate it against the Kühn scans on HathiTrust (hvd.hxpp8s, hvd.hxpp8r).
Public domain: Kühn, Opera omnia XI 379–892 and XII 1–377 (Leipzig 1826).
Modern edition: there is no complete critical edition. Kühn is still the standard text. Petit 2010 (I.1–3) is in copyright, and Martelli's CMG edition of Book IX is forthcoming, so Book X is free of conflict.
item_122.research_yield:
Possible articles:
- Galen's polemic against Xenocrates of Aphrodisias, the Roman ban on anthropophagy, and the ethics of human-derived drugs.
- The toxicological experiments of Attalus III as Pergamene royal science.
- Galen's empirical tests of "Dreckapotheke" remedies (dung, urine) compared with Pliny NH 28.
- Arabic and Latin reception.
- A first Russian account of Galen's drug theory.
item_122.recommendation: Keep, at priority 4. The status held up: no Russian or English translation of Book X, and the only translations of the work are French I.1–3 and an Italian sample. Best first unit: Book X, about 9.9k Greek words, roughly 14k in English, not 12–15k Greek as the item says. Start with ch. 1, the Xenocrates, Attalus and human-remedies preface of about 1,200 words, as a showcase, using the CC BY-SA TEI text checked against Kühn's scans.

item_123.title_short: Hippiatrica (CHG): Apsyrtus' prefaces and letters (Berlin recension)
item_123.ru_found: No Russian translation found, but this was NOT properly verified. WebSearch was blocked (the shared limit of 200 searches per turn was used up), so none of the required Russian searches ran: elibrary/cyberleninka, Византийский временник, the РГБ/РНБ catalogues, vostlit, Soviet histories of veterinary medicine. Checked by direct fetch only: (1) ru.wikipedia «Гиппиатрика» cites McCabe 2007, Karasszon 1988, Lazaris 2010/2015 and RE, and lists no translation; (2) the ancientrome.ru/antlitr index has no entry for Гиппиатрика, Апсирт, Иерокл, Пелагоний, Теомнест or Геопоники; (3) no ru.wikipedia article on Apsyrtus the veterinarian was found. Possible indirect overlap: the Russian «Геопоники. Византийская сельскохозяйственная энциклопедия X века» (Leningrad, AN SSSR, 1960; confirmed on ru.wikipedia). From memory, not verified: the translator is Е. Э. Липшиц, and Geoponica book XVI on horses draws partly on hippiatric sources. That is not the Hippiatrica itself, but its overlap with the Apsyrtus material should be checked.
item_123.en_found: No complete or continuous English translation of the Hippiatrica or of Apsyrtus. Anne McCabe, A Byzantine Encyclopaedia of Horse Medicine (Oxford Studies in Byzantium, OUP 2007) is a study of sources, compilation and transmission. It translates selected passages, probably including parts of Apsyrtus' preface and letter-headings; this needs checking against the book before the pilot. en.wikipedia (Hippiatrica) lists no translation. The planned English searches could not run (search limit), so the BMCR review and the OUP contents list were not checked.
item_123.other_found: Complete early-modern translations of the collection exist, made from a Paris-type text that does include Apsyrtus' excerpts. Source: de.wikipedia «Corpus Hippiatricorum Graecorum». Latin: Jean Ruel (Ruellius), Veterinariae medicinae libri II, Paris 1530. Greek editio princeps: Simon Grynaeus, Basel 1537. Italian: Michele Tramezzino, Venice 1543. French: Jean Massé, L'art vétérinaire ou grande mareschallerie, Paris 1563. German: Gregor Zechendörfer, Nuremberg 1571 (from Ruel's Latin). Modern work: A.-M. Doyen-Higuet, L'Épitomé de la Collection d'hippiatrie grecque, vol. 1 (Louvain-la-Neuve 2006, PIOL 54). From memory, this includes a French translation of the Epitome (recension E), not of the Berlin recension. Studies without translations: G. Björck 1932 (Uppsala); Doyen-Higuet 1983 (thesis); J. Schäffer, Sudhoffs Archiv 71 (1987); Lazaris 2010. No complete modern translation into any language was found. The pilot unit as proposed (B-recension Apsyrtus) has no modern translation beyond McCabe's excerpts.
item_123.source_text: Standard edition: E. Oder and K. Hoppe, Corpus Hippiatricorum Graecorum I (Hippiatrica Berolinensia, 1924) and II (Hippiatrica Parisina, Cantabrigiensia, Londinensia, 1927), Leipzig: Teubner; reprinted Stuttgart 1971. The Apsyrtus prefaces and letters in the B recension are in vol. I. Both volumes are public domain in the US (published before 1930). In Germany the 25-year protection for scholarly editions (§70 UrhG) expired long ago, so the Greek text is free to use. Oder died in 1926; Hoppe's death date was not verified, which matters only for the editors' Latin prefaces and apparatus. Free fallback: the Grynaeus editio princeps (Basel 1537), which is public domain but a different, inferior text. Scans of Oder–Hoppe are probably on HathiTrust or archive.org, but no URL was confirmed this session. Doyen-Higuet's 2006 Epitome is in copyright.
item_123.research_yield: Apsyrtus' letters to named officers and landowners: prosopography of Constantine's Sarmatian campaign (332–334) and the Danube army. Also late-antique horse breeding and regional breeds, Latin loanwords in Greek technical prose, hippiatric charms, comparison with Pelagonius, and how the 10th-century compilers worked.
item_123.recommendation: Keep the candidate. No refutation was found: Russian is apparently none and English is excerpts only (McCabe 2007). The 16th-century Latin, Italian, French and German translations do not weaken the case. Best first unit: Apsyrtus' preface and his letter-chapters in CHG I (Berlin recension), about 8–10k words, checked against McCabe's excerpts. Re-run the blocked RU/EN searches before committing.

item_124.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation of the whole work or of any chapter. Note: the WebSearch quota for this run was already used up, so no general web searches ran. I checked direct sources and catalogue APIs instead.
(1) ru.wikipedia «Прокл Диадох», fetched today. It names the work twice, as «Обзор астрономических предположений» and «Очерк астрономических гипотез», but lists no translation. Its translation list covers only the Hymns, Elements of Theology, Elements of Physics, Platonic Theology, and the commentaries on the Timaeus, Republic, Cratylus, Alcibiades and Euclid, plus «О самостоятельном существовании зла».
(2) Project cache (research/raw/ru_series_crosscheck.json): an index of ΣΧΟΛΗ translations for 2007–2026, read issue by issue. Its Proclus entries are Shchetnikov's Euclid extracts (2008), Garadzha's Chrestomathy (2023), and Mesyats' Timaeus II (2025–2026). None is the Hypotyposis.
(3) CyberLeninka API, queries «Прокл астрономия», «Прокл гипотезы астрономов», «Прокл Птолемей эпициклы», «Прокл спасение явлений», «Прокл Гипотипоза» and «Прокл Диадох астрономия». No translation turned up. I read the full text of the closest hits: «Измерение астрономических расстояний в Древней Греции» (ΣΧΟΛΗ 2010), Afonasin's «Гераклид Понтийский. Астрономические фрагменты» (ΣΧΟΛΗ 2019) and the article on Pappus, Theon and Hypatia (2021). They quote Proclus' In Euclidem and In Timaeum, never the Hypotyposis.
(4) ru.wikisource has no page for Proclus (404).
Not checked: the RSL and NLR catalogues, elibrary, or a Russian excerpt possibly embedded in a history of astronomy.
item_124.en_found:
This REFUTES the claim of no English. A complete English translation exists: Argyro Lithari, "Proclus, ›Hypotyposis Astronomicarum Positionum‹: Introduction, Text, Translation, and Commentary with a Study of the Diagrams and Illustrations" (Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter, 2025). It is vol. 16 of the series Science, Technology, and Medicine in Ancient Cultures and grew out of a Humboldt-Universität Berlin dissertation (2023). Details:
- Pages: XXVI + 723. Hardback ISBN 978-3-11-151284-6 (EUR 149.95); e-book ISBN 978-3-11-151601-1; DOI 10.1515/9783111516011.
- The DNB blurb states that it "includes the Greek text with an English translation" of "the entire Hypotyposis".
- Contents (DNB table of contents and Crossref): "B. Text and translation" pp. 77–288, covering Ch. I Proemium (p. 86), II On the astronomical hypotheses (100), III Sun (118), IV Moon (156), V Five planets (202), and the rest. Then "C. Commentary" pp. 289–634 and "D. Diagrams" pp. 635–690.
- Sources: d-nb.info/132659334X; services.dnb.de/plus/idn/132659334X/blurb/; the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (SEP) "Proclus" entry (revised 2 Oct 2026) also lists it.
- Related: Lithari's chapter on the Proemium, "Platonic Teachings and Astronomers' Hypotheses in the Proemium of Proclus' Hypotyposis", in Polemics and Networking in Graeco-Roman Antiquity (Brepols, Lectio, 2021), DOI 10.1484/M.LECTIO-EB.5.126928.
The colleague's evidence (en.wikipedia) is out of date.
item_124.other_found:
This also REFUTES the claim that Manitius' German is the only translation.
- French, complete, Greek with facing French: N. Halma, «Hypothèses et époques des planètes, de C. Ptolémée, et Hypotyposes de Proclus Diadochus, traduites pour la première fois du grec en français» (Paris, 1820). Public domain. I checked the OCR: there is a long section titled HYPOTYPOSES with French running alongside the Greek. archive.org/details/halma-ptolemaiou-hypotheseis-kai-planomenon-archai-gr-fr-1820
- German, complete: C. Manitius (Teubner, 1909; reprinted 1974, DOI 10.1515/9783110936926).
- Latin: Giorgio Valla's Renaissance translation, which Halma's preface criticises as obscure. Not verified separately.
- Greek editio princeps: Basel, 1540 (Grynaeus). archive.org ARes62514; also on wilbourhall.
I could not check for Italian or Spanish versions (unknown).
item_124.source_text:
Best public-domain text: C. Manitius, Procli Diadochi Hypotyposis astronomicarum positionum (Leipzig: Teubner, 1909), Greek with German. Copies:
- https://www.wilbourhall.org/pdfs/proclus/ProclusHypotosis.pdf (the link resolves: HTTP 200, 60 MB)
- archive.org/details/manitius-hypotyposis-astronomicarum-positionum-gr-lat-1909
- the 1974 Teubner photographic reprint is archive.org prokloudiadochou0000proc
The 1909 edition is public domain in the US. EU status depends on when Manitius died, which I did not verify; it is very likely public domain. A second public-domain text for checking is Halma (1820, Greek and French), which archive.org marks with the Public Domain Mark.
The standard modern edition is now Lithari (De Gruyter, 2025). It has a revised Greek text with a "Note on the Greek text", a study of the manuscripts and diagrams, an English translation and a commentary. It is in copyright and sold at EUR 149.95; I found no sign that it is open access. It should be used only as a reference and for checking readings.
item_124.research_yield:
Possible articles on:
- Proclus' instrumentalism: epicycles and eccentrics as fictions, set against In Timaeum and In Rempublicam.
- His sources: Ptolemy's Almagest and Planetary Hypotheses.
- Instruments: the armillary sphere, the dioptra, and measuring the Sun's apparent diameter with a water clock.
- The work's Byzantine school use.
- Russian terminology for Greek astronomy.
item_124.recommendation: Keep, but only as a Russian-first candidate: the claim that there is no English is false (Lithari 2025 is complete and has a commentary; Halma 1820 French and Manitius 1909 German are also complete). Best first unit: the Proemium plus ch. 1 on the hypotheses (Lithari's chs. I–II, about 4–5k words), translated from Manitius and checked against Halma, with Lithari consulted for readings and terms.

item_130.title_short: Galen, De compositione medicamentorum per genera (Book I)
item_130.ru_found:
