item_130.en_found:
There is no published English translation, but there are expert excerpts, which corrects the sweep's "none".
Zainaldin, Pattison, Marai, Wu and Schiefsky, "Evaluating LLM-Based Translation of a Low-Resource Technical Language" (arXiv 2602.24119, v2 April 2026), §2.3: no reference translation existed, so M. Marai prepared expert English translations of 10 passages, each about 214 Greek words:
- I.2 = XIII 367,10–369,1 K.
- I.15–16 = 431,4–432,13
- II.4–5, III.2, III.7–8, IV.5, V.2, V.13, VI.10 and VII.7
The Greek and English are public at github.com/campattison/galen_project, file mt_eval/input/on_comp.txt, under the repo's MIT licence. The English runs to c.2,000–3,000 words. The same repo has 30 LLM translations of these passages (GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro). The paper itself states that Comp. "has never been translated into English".
Fichtner, Corpus Galenicum 2023/12, no. 82, lists no translation (T) entries. The CMG «Galenus – Übersetzungen» list (entry 080) lists no translations.
Scattered quotations of the I.1 proem (the fire of 192) in secondary literature are likely, but I did not verify them this run.
item_130.other_found:
I found none in French, German, Italian or Spanish.
- Fichtner 2023/12 no. 82 lists only one edition: Hultsch, Metrologicorum scriptorum reliquiae I (1864) 209–218, which covers a metrological excerpt. It also lists three studies: Helmreich 1918, Jacques 1996 and Marganne 1980. It lists no modern translation.
- The CMG Übersetzungen list also gives none. For comparison, the companion work De comp. med. sec. loc. has Santana Henríquez 2005, Book II, in Spanish.
- Pre-modern versions only:
  - Latin: Guinterius (16th c.), and the Latin facing the Greek in Kühn
  - Syriac: Sergius of Rēšʿainā; Ḥunayn
  - Arabic: Ullmann 48, no. 50b
  - Hebrew: Zerahiah b. Isaac b. Shealtiel
- The Latin "Liber cathagenarum" (Fichtner no. 406) may be an excerpt from this work.
item_130.source_text:
Kühn, Claudii Galeni Opera omnia XIII (Leipzig 1827), 362–1058, Greek with Latin. It is public domain and still the standard and only edition.
- No modern critical edition exists, and none is in preparation: the CMG "in Vorbereitung" page lists only Martelli's Simpl. med. IX. So no copyrighted standard edition stands in the way.
- Kühn's text is acknowledged to be poor, and corruption is suspected in places (Zainaldin et al.; Nutton 2002, "In Defence of Kühn").
- Scans: BIU Santé Medica, cote 45674x13 (redirects to numerabilis.u-paris.fr; returned 503 when checked). Archive.org and Google Books copies of Kühn vol. 13 were not verified this run.
- Digital Greek: TLG 0057.077 (licensed). The 10 benchmark passages are in the MIT-licensed repo.
- Manuscript: Laur. Plut. 74.25 is online.
- Hultsch 1864 (metrological excerpt) is also public domain.
item_130.research_yield: Articles on: Galen's rewriting of Books I–II after the fire of 192; how he classifies plasters and wound drugs; fragments of Andromachus, Heras, Asclepiades Pharmakion and other lost pharmacologists; drug trade and metrology; a methods paper benchmarking Neoscholia against Zainaldin et al. 2026.
item_130.recommendation: Keep at priority 3, with English corrected to excerpts only (10 expert passages, 2026); the claim of the first full translation into any modern language still holds. Pilot Book I (XIII 362–c.460 K., c.15k words), starting with I.1–2 (the fire proem and the theory chapters), and use Marai's I.2 and I.15–16 references as a calibration set. Build a pharmacological term lexicon first.

item_131.title_short: Theon of Alexandria, Commentary on Ptolemy's Almagest (Book I or III)
item_131.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation of the commentary as a whole or of any book of it. Caveat: the shared web-search budget was already used up when this check started, so none of the required 4 Russian and 4 English searches could be run. All checks below were direct page fetches.
(1) The ΣΧΟΛΗ translation index (classics.nsu.ru/scholeru/schedule.htm), read in full: no Theon of Alexandria, Almagest commentary or Pappus. The only Theon is Theon of Smyrna (tr. Shchetnikov, ΣΧΟΛΗ 3.2, 2009). The closest Shchetnikov items are Geminus, Cleomedes, Nicomachus and Euclid's Optics.
(2) ru.wikipedia «Теон Александрийский»: its literature section lists only Rome and Tihon editions, with no Russian translation.
(3) ru.wikipedia «Альмагест»: the only Russian Almagest is Veselovsky's (Наука, 1998, ed. G. E. Kurtik). Theon is only named among the commentators, and no translation of him is mentioned.
(4) The project cache (research/raw/*.json) has no prior verification of this item.
Not checked, because search was unavailable: cyberleninka, elibrary, ВДИ, and Russian history-of-mathematics readers (Yushkevich's «Хрестоматия по истории математики»; the Russian van der Waerden «Пробуждающаяся наука», 1959). These may contain paraphrases or short excerpts of Theon's square-root method. So "none" means no full, partial or excerpt translation was found; it does not rule excerpts out.
item_131.en_found:
I found no complete or book-length English translation. en.wikipedia «Theon of Alexandria» lists only Rome's edition (Studi e Testi, 1931–43), and MacTutor's Theon biography lists no translation. Excerpts exist:
(a) en.wikipedia «Hypatia» translates the Book III title ("edition revised by my daughter Hypatia, the philosopher"). It cites Cameron, Long and Sherry 1993, pp. 45–47, and Cameron 2016, pp. 193–194, who discuss and partly translate the Book III material, including the tabular method of division.
(b) Heath, A History of Greek Mathematics I (1921), paraphrases Theon's sexagesimal operations and square-root extraction (confirmed via MacTutor's citation).
(c) From memory, not checked this session: Ivor Thomas, Greek Mathematical Works I (Loeb 335, 1939), prints Greek and English extracts from Theon's commentary on Almagest I.10 (sexagesimal multiplication, division and square root). The Loeb page returned 403.
So the arithmetic chapter of Book I is partly available in English, but the rest of Books I–XIII is not.
item_131.other_found:
The colleague's claim needs correcting: Halma's French translation (with Greek text) covers Books I, II and III, not just I–II. fr.wikipedia «Théon d'Alexandrie» lists:
- Book I: Paris, Merlin, 1821, gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k6211371c
- Book II: 1821, gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k6211372s
- Book III: Paris, A. Blanchard, 1822, gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k3974x
Gallica returned 403, so I could not open these myself.
Rome's Studi e Testi volumes are a critical edition with French notes, not a translation: Theon I–II in ST 72 (1936), III–IV in ST 106 (1943); Pappus V–VI in ST 54 (1931). Tihon, "Le livre V retrouvé du Commentaire à l'Almageste", L'Antiquité Classique 56 (1987), pp. 201–218, reports a rediscovered Book V; I found no translation of it. Tihon's French translations cover the Handy Tables commentaries, not the Almagest commentary.
de.wikipedia lists no German translation. I could not check Italian or Spanish because search was unavailable.
Net result: Books IV–XIII appear to have no translation in any modern language, and Books I–III exist only in Halma's 1820s French.
item_131.source_text:
Public domain:
- Halma, Paris 1821–22, Greek text with French translation of Books I–III (Gallica scans as listed above).
- Basel 1538 editio princeps (Grynaeus/Camerarius, with the Almagest), the only printed Greek text for Books V–XIII. Not located online this session.
Standard modern edition: A. Rome, Commentaires de Pappus et de Théon d'Alexandrie sur l'Almageste, BAV Studi e Testi 72 (1936) and 106 (1943), covering Books I–IV. Treat it as in copyright: it is a Vatican publication of 1936/43, and I believe Rome died in 1971 (not verified).
Practical plan: translate from Halma's public-domain Greek, collate privately against Rome's readings, and do not reproduce Rome's text.
item_131.research_yield:
First Russian and first English versions could support articles on:
- Hypatia's role and the Book III division table (Cameron's thesis)
- late-antique sexagesimal computation and teaching
- Theon's school and the rediscovered Book V versus Pappus
- Byzantine and Arabic Almagest reception, with Veselovsky's Russian Almagest as companion
item_131.recommendation: Keep at priority 2: no Russian version exists, and English has only excerpts. The best first unit is Book III, translated from Halma's 1822 public-domain Greek: it has the Hypatia title and division method, and Halma's French serves as a cross-check. The proposed Book I is a weaker first unit because its arithmetic chapter (on Almagest I.10) already has English excerpts (Heath; probably Thomas's Loeb), and Halma's French covers all of I–III. Books IV–XIII are the only parts untranslated in any modern language, but they lack a public-domain critical text.

item_132.title_short: Symmachus, Epistulae (Book 2, letters to Nicomachus Flavianus)
item_132.ru_found:
This check was limited. The shared WebSearch budget for the run was already used up, so neither of my two searches (RU 'Симмах письма перевод…', EN 'Symmachus letters Book 2…') ran. I did not query cyberleninka or elibrary through their search functions, as that would get around the limit. Below is what direct page fetches confirmed.
(1) The ru.wikipedia article on Квинт Аврелий Симмах, 'Тексты и переводы' section, lists only two Russian translations. One is И. П. Стрельникова, 'Симмах. Письма', in Памятники позднего античного ораторского и эпистолярного искусства (М., 1964), pp. 205–212: an unspecified handful of letters. I could not check whether any Book 2 letter is among them. The other is А. Б. Ранович, 'Письмо об алтаре Победы' (= Relatio 3), in Античные критики христианства (М., 1990), pp. 450–457.
(2) ancientrome.ru/antlitr has no Symmachus entry.
(3) The ru.wikipedia articles on Вирий Никомах Флавиан and Веттий Агорий Претекстат cite no Russian translation of the letters. They do cite М. А. Ведешкин (НВ БелГУ 2011; Аристей 13, 2016). He is the leading Russian specialist on the late pagan senatorial milieu, and his publications must be checked for journal translations of individual letters before work starts.
Verdict: the whole collection exists only in Russian excerpts. No Russian translation of Book 2 as a unit was found. That is not the same as 'partial', which the sweep claimed.
item_132.en_found:
Whole collection: only Book 1 exists in English, as M. R. Salzman & M. Roberts, The Letters of Symmachus: Book 1 (SBL, Writings from the Greco-Roman World 30, 2011). Open Library lists Salzman's 'The letters of Symmachus' (2011, 2012). The Relationes ('Book 10') exist as R. H. Barrow, Prefect and Emperor (Oxford 1973). Relatio 3 also circulates in the Medieval Sourcebook. en.wikipedia says 'little of his work has been translated into English'.
Book 2: I found no English translation in en.wikipedia (Symmachus; Virius Nicomachus Flavianus) or in the Open Library listing. A full SBL/TTH/publisher catalogue search was not possible, because SBL returned 403 and the search budget was used up. Individual Book 2 letters are probably quoted in translation in scholarly works (e.g. Croke & Harries 1982; A. Cameron, Last Pagans of Rome 2011), but I did not verify this. Book 2 verdict: none known.
item_132.other_found:
FRENCH, complete: J.-P. Callu, Symmaque: Lettres, Budé, 4 vols. (1972–2002), confirmed on en.wikipedia. Vol. 1 (1972) covers Books I–II.
ITALIAN:
- G. A. Tedeschi, Lettere di Q. Aurelio Simmaco (Roma: G. Mainardi, 1724). This is an early vernacular version, listed on it.wikipedia and Open Library; I could not confirm whether it is complete.
- Pisa/Giardini 'Commento storico' series by book: Roda IX (1981, confirmed on it.wikipedia); Cecconi II (2002), Pellizzari III, Marcone IV and VI, Rivolta Tiberga V (from the sweep, not re-verified). These volumes reportedly include text and Italian translation. Cecconi's volume, which would be an Italian translation with historical commentary of exactly the proposed unit, is unverified this session.
- Relatio 3 only: R. Del Ponte (1987).
GERMAN: no translation of the letters found. de.wikipedia lists Forst, Relationes, Latin–German (De Gruyter 2020); Pabst, Orationes (WBG 1989); Klein, Relatio 3 with Ambrose (1972).
item_132.source_text:
Best public-domain text: O. Seeck, Q. Aurelii Symmachi quae supersunt, MGH Auctores Antiquissimi 6.1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1883). It covers the Epistulae from p. 1, the Relationes p. 279, the Orationes p. 318 and the indices, and is free on dMGH (https://www.dmgh.de/mgh_auct_ant_6_1/index.htm). There is also an archive.org scan with full text (https://archive.org/details/qaureliisymmach00seecgoog; a 1961 reprint record). Latin e-texts also exist on digilibLT, Musisque Deoque and PHI (licences unverified).
The standard modern edition, Callu's Budé (Les Belles Lettres, 1972–2002; Books I–II in 1972), is in copyright, as is Cecconi 2002. Translate from Seeck, and use Callu and Cecconi only for checking.
item_132.research_yield: Book 2 (383–394) supports articles on Symmachus–Flavianus political friendship, letter dating, the 'pagan revival'/Eugenius debate (vs. Cameron), and the son-editor's possible suppression after 394. It also supports Russian prosopographical notes, PLRE corrections, and analysis of late Latin epistolary formulae.
item_132.recommendation: Keep, at priority 4 rather than 5: in Russian the letters exist only as excerpts, and Book 2 has no Russian or English translation, but French (Callu 1972) and probably Italian (Cecconi 2002) versions already exist. Start with Book 2, letters 1–30 from Seeck MGH AA 6.1, after first checking М. А. Ведешкин's bibliography and the Стрельникова 1964 selection for Book 2 letters.

item_133.title_short: Ennodius, Epistulae & Dictiones (Letters Book V; not the Panegyric)
item_133.ru_found: The sweep's "none" is wrong. It relied on ru.wikipedia, which lists no translations. REFUTED for the Panegyric: V. M. Tyulenev (tr., intro., comm., indices), «Эннодий Павийский. Житие блаженнейшего мужа Епифания, епископа Тицинской церкви; Панегирик королю Теодориху; Житие блаженного монаха Антония; Благодарение за свою жизнь», СПб.: Изд-во Олега Абышко, 2013 (intro. «Магн Феликс Эннодий – человек уходящей эпохи», pp. 5–52). item_133.other_found: French: Gioanni, Budé/CUF, Lettres I (Books I–II, 2006) and II (Books III–IV, 2010), with facing French translation. Whether a third volume (Books V+) has appeared since 2010 is unverified. German: Panegyric, Ch. Rohr, MGH Studien und Texte 12, 1995 (edition, translation, commentary; Vienna diss. 1994). item_133.source_text: Letters Books V–IX have no modern critical edition beyond the 19th-century ones, which remain standard and are public domain. Vogel, MGH AA 7 (Berlin 1885), PD scan: archive.org monumentagermani07geseuoft and magnifelicisenn00vogegoog. Hartel, CSEL 6 (Vienna 1882), PD. A machine-readable Latin text is in OpenGreekAndLatin csel-dev (stoa0114a.stoa008, from Hartel, open licence). In copyright: Gioanni Budé 2006/2010 (Books I–IV only), Rohr 1995, Rota 2002.
item_133.research_yield: First Russian and first human-reviewed English versions of the letters beyond Budé I–IV would enable articles on: Ennodius' letter network (Faustus, Avienus, Boethius' circle), the Laurentian schism, rhetorical schooling, Ostrogothic patronage, and a comparison of AI and human translations of a notoriously mannered Latin style.
item_133.recommendation: Keep the letters but drop the Panegyric pilot: it has a full Russian translation (Tyulenev 2013) as well as English (Haase 1991), German and Italian ones. Best first unit: Letters Book V from Vogel's MGH AA 7. Before starting, check whether Budé vol. 3 has appeared and whether Tyulenev is translating the letters, and note the existing romanletters.org AI English translations as a comparison point.

item_134.title_short: Marcellus Empiricus, De medicamentis liber (preface, prefatory letters, ch. 8)
item_134.ru_found: No Russian translation of any part found. I ran 9 Russian searches covering: Марцелл Эмпирик «О лекарствах» перевод; заговоры/галльский; Марцелл Бурдигальский / из Бордо; Т. А. Михайлова (галльские заговоры); «Марцелла Эмпирика» заговор/рецепт; КиберЛенинка; диссертация/статья. I also fetched the cyberleninka search page directly. ru.wikipedia «Марцелл Эмпирик» lists only the German translation and no Russian literature. The ESBE entry is purely encyclopedic. ru.wikipedia «Галльский язык» quotes 10 Gaulish formulas in the original only, with no Russian translation. The 1980 anthology «Медицина в памятниках латинской литературы» named in the candidate file turned up nowhere and probably does not exist. One MSU file on istina.msu.ru came up in the results but could not be downloaded (SSL error), so it is unchecked. Not checked because the search budget ran out: eLibrary, the RSL catalogue, and Russian Celtological publications, where single charms might appear in Russian.
item_134.en_found: This refutes the claim of no English translation. Source Library (sourcelibrary.org, Embassy of the Free Mind, Amsterdam; collection launched 2026) hosts a nearly complete AI English translation of Helmreich's 1889 Teubner edition (420 of 424 pages: preface, De ponderibus, ch. 1–36), licensed CC BY-SA 4.0: https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af462cb8e08960c7fbb7a2. The pages are labelled 'AI translation, not yet reviewed by a scholar', and the site says its Latin is translated by Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite. A second AI translation covers the 1536 Cornarius edition (265 of 266 pages): https://sourcelibrary.org/book/de-medicamentis-empiricus. The pilot unit, ch. 8 included, is covered by this AI translation. Human or scholarly English exists only as excerpts, e.g. the Gaulish throat charm (Must, Language 36, 1960) and maryjones.us/ctexts/classical_marcellus.html. Cilliers, Acta Academica 38.1 (2006), studies the prefatory letters; whether it translates them is unchecked. No published human English translation of the whole work or of any chapter was found.
item_134.other_found: German, complete: Niedermann, 2nd ed. revised by E. Liechtenhan, translated by J. Kollesch and D. Nickel, CML V, 2 vols, Akademie-Verlag 1968 (bilingual; Wellcome record confirms; De Gruyter reprint 2024). Italian, partial: A. Maiuri, Medicina per verba: formule magiche nel De medicamentis liber di Marcello Empirico (Alpes Italia 2025). Its contents include text, translation and commentary of the closing poem, and it studies the charms, so some formulas are probably translated. French: a Renaissance adaptation by Antoine du Moulin, Souverainetés contre toutes maladies, tirées et traduites de Marcellus (Lyon 1550), seen only in a Wellcome catalogue snippet. No modern French translation found. Spanish: none found. The Gaulish formulas are probably translated piecemeal in French and German Celtological works (e.g. Meid and Anreiter 2005); not verified.
item_134.source_text: Helmreich, Teubner 1889, public domain: archive.org/details/demedicamentisli00marcuoft; HathiTrust mdp.39015029761254; Google Books MC0IAAAAIAAJ. The item's archive.org link was not checked. Niedermann, CML V (1916, Latin only) is the better text. It is public domain in the US (published before 1930) and, since Niedermann died in 1954, in the EU from 2025; I did not find a scan. The standard edition is Niedermann–Liechtenhan 1968 (CML V, 2 vols, with the German translation). It is in copyright: De Gruyter reprinted it in 2024 and the translators are modern.
item_134.research_yield: Gaulish charms and plant names (Russian Celtology); Christian versus pagan healing ritual in Theodosian Gaul; the elite around Ausonius; the forged or fictive prefatory physician letters; how Marcellus reworked Scribonius and Pliny; late Latin vocabulary. The online Gemini translation could also be used to compare model-made and editor-reviewed translations.
item_134.recommendation: Keep, but only as the first Russian translation; drop the 'first English' claim, since an unreviewed AI English translation of almost the whole text is already online. Best first unit: the dedicatory letter to his sons plus the seven prefatory physician letters (short, literary and rich in names), then ch. 8 with its charms.

item_135.title_short: Avienus, Aratea and Descriptio orbis terrae (Aratea proem or full Descriptio)
item_135.ru_found: Aratea: no Russian translation of any part found. Searches covered «Авиен "Явления Арата"», «Аратея Авиена», «Руфий Фест Авиен перевод», a dissertation search and the 1992 anthology «Небо, наука, поэзия», which has Aratus in Russian but showed no sign of Avienus. Descriptio: excerpts only. The Russian Wikipedia bibliography for Авиен lists «Сведения о Скифии и Кавказе» (ВДИ 1949, № 4, pp. 237–243; Latyshev series, translator not named) and S. P. Kondratiev, «Античная география» (М., 1953, pp. 324–337). Both are excerpt-level. The 1953 pages are probably mostly Ora maritima, but I could not check. Ora maritima, which is not part of this candidate, is complete in Kondratiev's translation (ВДИ 1939). Limits: simposium.ru/node/10568 and ancientrome.ru failed to connect on every attempt, and the shared web-search budget ran out before I could check the РГБ catalogue or the contents of «Античная география» 1953.
item_135.en_found: This refutes the sweep's EN "none". (1) Source Library (sourcelibrary.org; Embassy of the Free Mind with TU Delft and others; translations CC BY-SA 4.0, added March 2026) has an English machine translation of the 1488 Venice editio princeps (Antonius de Strata). It reports 238 of 240 pages translated, covering all of Avienus's Aratea ("Phaenomena"), Descriptio ("Geography of the World", from p. 62) and Ora maritima. Pages are labelled "AI translation, not yet reviewed by a scholar", and the model named is Gemini 3 Flash: https://sourcelibrary.org/book/arati-phaenomena-geographia-ora-maritima-avienus. The same site also hosts Breysig's 1882 Aratea, OCR only so far, flagged as a "possible first translation". (2) Human scholarly English, excerpts only: the Aratea proem in Emma Gee, Aratus and the Astronomical Tradition (OUP 2013), pp. 233–239, quoted by Dimoglidis, Ariadne 28 (2021–22). No human English version of the Descriptio was found. Twyne's 1572 'Surveye of the World' translates Dionysius, not Avienus. Murphy and Graham–Shipley (CUP 2024) cover Ora maritima only.
item_135.other_found: Spanish, complete (all three poems): José Calderón Felices, Avieno, Fenómenos; Descripción del orbe terrestre; Costas marinas (Gredos BCG 296, 2001; ISBN 9788424923143). French: Aratea by J. Soubiran (CUF/Budé 1981); Descriptio by E. Despois and E. Saviot (Panckoucke 1843, public domain). German, partial: Lothar Willms (WVT Trier, 2014) translates and comments the zodiac section, Aratea vv. 1014–1325. Commentaries by D. Weber (Wien 1986; vv. 1–366, 618–635, 1170–1193) and M. Fiedler (2004; vv. 367–746) exist, but I could not confirm whether either includes a full German translation. Italian: no translation of the Aratea or Descriptio found. A. A. Raschieri's 2010 study of the Descriptio is a monograph, and whether it includes a translation is unconfirmed. There is also a Polish monograph, «Aratea Rufiusa Festusa Awienusa. Zarys monograficzny» (AMU repository); I could not reach it to see whether it includes a translation.
item_135.source_text: Public domain: Aratea, ed. A. Breysig (Teubner, Leipzig 1882), https://archive.org/details/rufifestiavieni00aviegoog (second scan: archive.org/details/rufifestiavienia00avieuoft). All poems: A. Holder, Rufi Festi Avieni Carmina (Innsbruck 1887). Descriptio also in C. Müller, Geographi Graeci Minores II (1861). Standard modern editions, both still in copyright: Soubiran, Budé 1981 (Aratea), and P. van de Woestijne, Bruges 1961 (Descriptio). Breysig, Holder and Müller are usable bases, but the translation should be checked against Soubiran's text and notes.
item_135.research_yield: Articles possible: Avienus's Stoic-Jovian proem as fourth-century senatorial paganism, compared with Aratus and Germanicus; his use of Aratus scholia and the Catasterisms; Descriptio against Dionysius and Priscian on Pontus and Scythia; and a critique comparing a reviewed translation with the existing unreviewed AI one.
item_135.recommendation: Keep, but only as a Russian-first candidate at priority 3 (5 = highest). An unreviewed AI English translation of the whole text exists, and the Spanish is complete. Best first unit: the Aratea proem and the opening of the constellation catalogue (about vv. 1–300), which has no Russian at all. Check the line count against the Russian Aratus (1992), Gee 2013 and Soubiran. The full Descriptio is a second choice, after confirming exactly which passages ВДИ 1949 and «Античная география» 1953 cover.

item_136.title_short: Anonymous, Expositio totius mundi et gentium (entire text, both Latin versions)

item_136.en_found: REFUTES "partial". R.J.A. Talbert translated it as "Expositio totius mundi et gentium (Account of the Whole World and its Peoples) and Iunior Philosophus", ch. 33 (Part V, Late Antique) in D.G.J. The Cambridge chapter abstract calls it a "new, annotated translation melding the two Latin versions". It is very probably complete; I inferred this from the abstract because the full text is paywalled. Earlier: Jesse Woodman, MA thesis, Ohio State University, 1964, translation online via OhioLINK ETD (osu1166462501). en.wikipedia's line that no widely available printed English translation exists is out of date.

item_136.source_text: Public domain: A. Riese, Geographi Latini Minores (Heilbronn 1878), which contains 'Expositio totius mundi et gentium (Iunior philosophus)', https://archive.org/details/geographilatinim00ries. Also C. Müller, GGM II (Paris 1861) pp. 513ff (vetus versio and Descriptio), Godefroy 1628 and Mai 1831. Copyrighted: the standard edition, Rougé, SC 124 (1966). The new standard edition is C. Cioffi, Expositio totius mundi et gentium cum redactione altera quae Totius mundi descriptio inscribitur, Bibliotheca Teubneriana, De Gruyter Brill 2026 (ISBN 9783111636252; e-ISBN 9783111637112), listed as 'ahead of publication'. item_136.research_yield: First complete Russian translation with commentary. Possible articles: the two Latin redactions compared; the commodity and trade map of the empire under Constantius II; the image of Persians and Saracens; Antioch and Alexandria spectacles; testing Cioffi's new witness; reuse in the Georgian Kartlis Tskhovreba; vulgar-Latin lexicon.
item_136.recommendation: Keep it as a Russian-only project at lower priority: Russian has only Pigulevskaya's five paragraphs (1951), but English (Talbert 2024), French and German now exist. Best first unit is the whole text in Russian with both versions in parallel (about 6–7k words), starting with §§ 1–34 (the eastern peoples, Syria and Palestine), which have never been rendered into Russian.

item_138.research_yield: Theoderic's 507 diplomacy before Vouillé (III.1–4); Ostrogothic administration and the office-formulae (VI–VII); Gothic–Roman 'civilitas' ideology; natural-history digressions; Russian reception of Cassiodorus. item_138.recommendation: Deprioritize or drop. English and Italian translations are complete, and Izosin is translating the Variae into Russian book by book on ancientrome.ru (2025–26), so Neoscholia would overlap with him. Before going further, have someone with access check ancientrome.ru for Book III and later, or contact Izosin. If his series has stopped, take Books VI–VII (formulae) rather than Book III, which already has two published Russian excerpts (III.7 and III.48).

item_139.title_short: Servius (+ Servius Danielis), In Aeneidem (pilot: Aen. 6 or 2)
item_139.ru_found: One translation found, of Book 1 only: N. A. Fedorov, in «Вергилий. Энеида. С комментариями Сервия», Москва: Лабиринт, 2001 (Osherov's Aeneid edited by Petrovsky, with Servius translated and annotated by Fedorov). Russian Wikipedia (ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Сервий) links its text at ancientrome.ru/antlitr/servius/serv1.htm. The publisher's blurb on readli.net (https://readli.net/eneida-s-kommentariyami-serviya/) says Servius had never been translated into Russian before. Its "доп. информация" field says the book has only an excerpt of the Book 1 commentary, so the translation may not even cover all of Book 1. I could not open ancientrome.ru to check this (the connection kept resetting). Russian searches turned up nothing for Aen. 2–12, the Danielis layer or Aen. 6 in particular. Covered: Сервий комментарий к Энеиде перевод; Сервий + Энеида + Федоров + Лабиринт 2001; Сервий комментарий к VI книге; «Мавр Сервий Гонорат» перевод; комментариями Сервия Лабиринт 2001. Russian scholarship (Kazanskaya in Вестник СПбГУ 2016, cyberleninka articles on Homeric quotations in Servius ad Aen. 1, 7, 12) quotes single scholia only. So for Aen. 2–12, Russian has excerpts at most, and the pilot unit (Aen. 6 or 2) has no Russian translation.
item_139.en_found: Human scholarly translation covers Book 4 only: C. M. McDonough, R. E. Prior, M. Stansbury, "Servius' Commentary on Book Four of Virgil's Aeneid: An Annotated Translation" (Bolchazy-Carducci, 2002; BMCR 2005.03.16; reprinted 2004). It translates Servius only, not the Danielis additions. That makes the candidate's '2004' a reprint date. The REFUTATION is that machine-made full English versions exist. (1) Source Library (sourcelibrary.org, an Embassy of the Free Mind project) has all three Thilo–Hagen volumes marked "first translation, done": Vol. I Aen. 1–5 (768 pp.), Vol. II Aen. 6–12 (662/668 pp.), Vol. III Ecl./Georg. (475 pp.). The site says its translations are AI-generated, not peer-reviewed, and CC BY-SA 4.0. I could not view the translated pages (the site sits behind a Cloudflare bot check), so their completeness is unverified. (2) "Servius' Commentary on Virgil's Aeneid: A Rough First English Translation", EPUB, 2024, credited to "Authors of Mitologia.pt" (unilibro.it, EUR 9.99), described by its seller as 'unedited and may contain numerous flaws'. Bottom line: no reviewed English exists beyond Aen. 4, but Neoscholia cannot claim a first English translation.

item_140.ru_found: No Russian translation of the whole work, of excerpts or of the pilot unit turned up. I ran 9 Russian-language searches: Пелагоний ветеринария перевод; «Ars veterinaria» латинский трактат; гиппиатрика IV век; Пелагония/Пелагонием together with Вегеций and Mulomedicina; история ветеринарии with Апсирт; латинская ветеринарная терминология; cyberleninka; site:ancientrome.ru (no hits); Сергеенко/Колумелла. Russian Wikipedia has an article «Пелагоний», but its only Russian source is A. I. Malein's entry in the Brockhaus-Efron encyclopedia, which is a reference article, not a translation. Russian Wikipedia's list of surviving Latin works names the treatise but links no translation. The ancientrome, vostlit and simposium checks in the candidate file also found nothing. One Belarusian vet-academy PDF (repo.vsavm.by, 2025) could not be opened.
item_140.en_found: This contradicts the sweep's "none". (1) Jennifer Nilson, "Pelagonius' Ars Veterinaria: A Translation with Notes", Kalamazoo College, Classics Senior Integrated Project, 2002: https://cache.kzoo.edu/handle/10920/21938. It is an unpublished undergraduate translation made from Fischer's edition. The abstract says she picked the text for its short length, and that Fischer told her no English translation existed. The repository returns 403, so I could not check whether it is complete; it may cover the whole text. (2) J. N. Adams, An Anthology of Informal Latin 200 BC–AD 900 (CUP 2016), ch. 29: "Pelagonius, Ars veterinaria 34", with text, English translation and commentary. (3) A. McCabe, A Byzantine Encyclopaedia of Horse Medicine (OUP 2007), which translates some Pelagonius passages from the Greek Hippiatrica (pp. 161–162 are cited). (4) An English version of preface §1 (letter to Arzygius) and ch. 283 by "Ɔ. Martiana" on a blog (hellenicfaith.com/pelagonius-on-sun-and-horses/), partly based on McCabe. So the preface in the pilot unit already exists in English in part. (5) The HIPPO project at Lund (2021–25) plans English translations of Apsyrtus and Pelagonius material in the Hippiatrica manuscripts; I found nothing published yet. Adams 1995 (Brill) is a linguistic study, not a translation.
item_140.other_found: Italian: G. Sarchiani, ed. and Italian translation, Veterinaria (published after his death by G. Cioni, Florence: Pezzati, 1826), the first edition. Antonio Sestili, Pelagonio, Arte veterinaria (Rome: Società Editrice Dante Alighieri, 2014; 671 pp.; ISBN 9788853437600; Latin and Italian; Open Library lists Sestili as editor and translator). The sweep did not name this translator. Sestili also published Morbidus equus (Dante Alighieri, 2012; Italian, Greek, Latin), covering Pelagonius and Apsyrtus. German: Karl Wilberg, Berlin dissertation 1943 (title reported as "Die Pferdeheilkunde des Pelagonius"), a German translation made from Ihm's text. Its extent is not verified. French: V. Gitton, Lyon II thesis 1999 (edition, translation, commentary); V. Gitton-Ripoll, Pélagonius, Recueil de médecine vétérinaire, CUF/Budé, Les Belles Lettres 2019 (CXLIV + 624 pp.), the first complete critical edition with a full French translation. Spanish: none found.
item_140.source_text: Public domain: M. Ihm, Pelagonii Artis veterinariae quae extant (Teubner, Leipzig 1892), on archive.org (https://archive.org/details/pelagoniiartiav00pelagoog) and HathiTrust (records 100387951, 012445047, 008910816, 100462335). Sarchiani 1826 is also public domain, and BIU Santé (Medica) hosts digitised old editions. digilibLT has an online text (DLT000404); its base edition and licence are unverified because the site did not respond. In copyright: K.-D. Fischer, Pelagonii Ars veterinaria (Teubner 1980; reprinted by K. G. Saur 1998, now De Gruyter) and Gitton-Ripoll (CUF 2019). Caveat: Ihm's spelling is normalised towards classical Latin. Ihm also lacks the fragments found later (the Einsiedeln codex, ed. Corsetti 1989) and the passages that survive only in Greek. Gitton-Ripoll's numbering and text differ from his, so readings from Fischer and Gitton-Ripoll would have to be cited in the notes.
item_140.research_yield: Russian articles on Latin veterinary terminology (building on Adams); prosopography of the named addressees and 4th-c. circus-horse culture; how the Latin relates to the Greek Hippiatrica and Apsyrtus; ritual and solar formulae (ch. 283); dating under Julian; Pelagonius as Vegetius' source.
item_140.recommendation: Keep as a Russian-first candidate: no Russian translation exists, and full Italian, French and German versions give good controls. Drop any "first English" claim: an unpublished 2002 student translation plus excerpts exist, so the English should be called the first published, annotated one. Start with the preface (letter to Arzygius) and the fever and head chapters, using Ihm 1892 and noting Fischer and Gitton-Ripoll readings.

item_141.research_yield: Low as a first translation, because RU, EN and FR are all complete. A philological Russian version of Book 1 could still support articles on: the narrative of Plotinus' death; the defence of astrology under Constantine; an author who wrote both Mathesis and De errore; and a critique of the 2020 esoteric-press translation.
item_141.recommendation: Drop the candidate: it fails criterion 1. A full Russian translation exists (Zennikov, 2 vols, 2020; reissued in Kharkiv 2023), and an online samizdat translation covers the proposed pilot unit, Books I–II. If it is kept at all, it should only be an annotated retranslation of Book 1 from Latin, after checking the 2020 translation's source language and quality.

item_142.ru_found: The only confirmed Russian item is E. V. Silvestrova's "Новеллы Феодосия II" in История Древнего Рима. Тексты и документы, ч. 2 (М., 2005), pp. 231–232. ru.wikipedia's "Кодекс Феодосия" bibliography lists it. At two pages it is a sample from a corpus of about 35–40k words, so the colleague's "partial" rating should come down to "excerpts only". The same anthology and related journal work cover only the Code itself: CTh I and XVI.1–2 by Silvestrova (Вестник ПСТГУ 2009, 2010), CTh XVI.10 by M. A. Ведешкин (НВ БелГУ 2013), and Codex texts on coloni by A. V. Коптев. ru.wikipedia also notes that O. V. Ауров's grant-funded full annotated translation (2008–10) was still unpublished in 2017. For the Novels of Valentinian III, Marcian, Majorian, Severus and Anthemius I found nothing in Russian. For the pilot unit, ru.wikipedia's "Майориан" only paraphrases the laws' titles and content, citing Mommsen–Meyer and Pharr. Searches run: новеллы Майориана перевод; новеллы Валентиниана III перевод; постфеодосиевы новеллы; новелла Маркиана/Антемия; Nov. Val. 17 (Лев–Иларий) на русском; Nov. Maj. 4 «Об общественных зданиях»; Ведешкин/Коптев/Сильвестрова; cyberleninka/vostlit/ancientrome. None turned up a translation. RSL and NLR catalogues were not checked directly, and the search budget ran out.
item_142.en_found: C. Pharr with T. S. Davidson and M. B. Pharr, The Theodosian Code and Novels and the Sirmondian Constitutions (Princeton UP, 1952; Corpus of Roman Law 1; reprinted by Lawbook Exchange, 2001). HeinOnline's catalog entry says its Novels run from 438 to 468, which covers every emperor through Anthemius, Majorian included; ru.wikipedia cites Pharr for Nov. Maj. 4. The archive.org copy (theodosiancodeno0000unse) is lending-only. There may be a partial English translation in C. McBurnie, "A Commentary of Majorian's Sixth Novel" (MA thesis, Dalhousie, 1997), but I could not confirm that it contains one. No newer complete English translation was found.
item_142.other_found: French: Sources Chrétiennes 497 (2005) and 531 (2009), Les lois religieuses des empereurs romains (Latin text by Mommsen, translation by J. Rougé, notes by R. Delmaire). Catalog records list CTh XVI, CTh I–XV, CJ and the Sirmondian Constitutions, with no Novels. Italian: M. Bianchi Fossati Vanzetti, Le Novelle di Valentiniano III. I. Fonti (Padova, 1988), a source study; whether it includes a translation is unconfirmed. F. De Iuliis (2025) studies Nov. Maj. 5, 6, 7 and 9 on women (an article, not a translation). Other studies: Wieling, "Iniusta lex Maioriani" (RIDA 1991); Livorsi on Nov. Val. 23 (CQ 2024); Schmidt-Hofner (2025) on the narratology of the post-Theodosian novels; an Academia.edu TEI-XML digital edition of the Novellae Valentiniani (author not seen, page access denied). The Cologne Leges database lists no translations. Searches in German, Spanish and Polish found no translation.
item_142.source_text: The standard edition is still P. M. Meyer, Leges novellae ad Theodosianum pertinentes (Mommsen–Meyer, Theodosiani libri XVI, vol. II, Berlin: Weidmann, 1905; Majorian at pp. 156–178). It is public domain and archive.org marks it NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT, with a downloadable PDF: https://archive.org/details/theodosianilibri00codeuoft. There is no newer critical edition. Older printed editions are also public domain: Amaduzzi 1767 (BSB digital) and Pithou 1571 / Rittershausen 1615 (Salamanca). Pharr's English translation (1952) is probably still in copyright, but I did not verify renewal; use it only as a check, not as a base text.
item_142.research_yield: This would be the first Russian annotated corpus. It supports articles on Majorian's reform programme (curiales, defensores, tax remission, monuments, women and nuns), on Ricimer, on Nov. Val. 17 and papal primacy, on barbarian settlement and the fiscal collapse after Africa was lost, and on the rhetoric of the preambles.
item_142.recommendation: Keep it as a Russian-gap item, since English has the full Pharr translation, and start with the Novellae Maioriani (about 9 surviving laws, roughly 8k words) from Meyer 1905, checked against Pharr. Valentinian III's Novels are the natural second unit.

item_143.ru_found: The claim of "none" is refuted. A. I. Malein translated excerpts with notes under the title «Перечисление почетных должностей» in Latyshev, Известия древних писателей о Скифии и Кавказе, vol. II (Latin writers), part 1, SPb 1904, pp. 449–450; I checked this in the OCR of the volume. They were reprinted in ВДИ 1949 №4 (30) and have been online on vostlit since 2022: https://www.vostlit.info/Texts/Dokumenty/Italy/V/400-420/Notitia_dignitatum/text1.phtml (I fetched and read the page). The excerpts are Or. XIII (the comites commerciorum lines only), Or. XXVI (the provinces of the vicar of Thrace) and Or. XXXIX (the full dux Scythiae unit list, with 16 notes). So the sweep's statement "absent from vostlit" is wrong. The proposed unit, Or. I–IX, is not covered. Possible further fragments that I could not verify: Lomouri, ВВ 46 (1986), pp. 59–74, on the Pontic limes, likely quotes Or. XXXVIII in Russian, and Mekhamadiev's 2019 monograph on the military may do the same. Russian monographs I sampled, such as Sinitsa and Bolgov 2022, only paraphrase Or. I/II or quote the Latin. The ru.wikipedia article lists no translation, and the vostlit letter indexes Н, П and С have no other entry. Caveat: my WebSearch calls failed because the shared search budget was used up, so I could not run the required 4+4 searches. I checked by fetching pages directly instead, plus the project's own crosscheck file.
item_143.en_found: 1) William Fairley, 'Notitia Dignitatum or Register of Dignitaries', Translations and Reprints from the Original Sources of European History VI.4, Philadelphia (Univ. of Pennsylvania) 1899. This is partial, about 48 pp. of extracts, and troop lists are often summarized or omitted. Online at Fordham: https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/source/notitiadignitatum.asp. It covers the eastern prefects, the magistri militum in praesenti and per Orientem, and others. 2) Source Library, 'Register of Dignitaries', added March 2026 and marked 'First translation' and 'Complete'. It is a transcription and translation of the Froben edition (Basel 1552), with a parallel facsimile, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. The project's bibliography calls the site 'AI-translated': https://sourcelibrary.org/book/notitia-dignitatum-cum-orientis-tum-occidentis-various. 3) Partial English versions in R. Rees, Diocletian and the Tetrarchy (Edinburgh 2004) and in Rathbone & Rathbone, Literary Sources for Roman Britain, 5th ed. (2023), pp. 86–88, which covers the British sections. Net result: there is no scholarly full English translation, but a complete AI English version made from the 1552 print now exists.
item_143.other_found: Spanish, full: A. D. Duarte Sánchez (intro. and transl.), 'Notitia dignitatum. Relación de dignatarios', Murcia 2007. Neira Faleiro 2005 (CSIC) is a critical edition with historical commentary; no translation is noted for it. French, partial: P. Richardot, 'La fin de l'armée romaine 284–476', 3rd ed., Paris, Economica 2005, which includes 'une traduction de la Notitia Dignitatum'. German, partial: K. Wachtel in 'Griechische und lateinische Quellen zur Frühgeschichte Mitteleuropas' (1992), pp. 296–305, with the unit lists for Valeria, Pannonia I, Noricum ripense, Raetia and Mogontiacum. Italian and Portuguese: J. Svejk, Kindle 2016 ('Traduzione libera' and 'Tradução livre'), both made from Fairley's partial English. All of these come from the bibliography at notitiadignitatum.org (pages D04, D05, D06 and D07); I could not search to verify each one independently.
item_143.source_text: Seeck, Notitia dignitatum; accedunt Notitia urbis Constantinopolitanae et laterculi provinciarum, Berlin, Weidmann 1876. It is public domain; archive.org lists it as NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT: https://archive.org/details/notitiadignitat00seecgoog. Böcking's 19th-century edition (1839–53) is also public domain. A Seeck-based Latin text is on la.wikisource, The Latin Library and Bibliotheca Augustana. Bodleian MS Canon. Misc. 378 is digitized for the insignia. The standard modern editions are in copyright: Neira Faleiro (CSIC, Madrid 2005) and the Ireland Teubner (1999).
item_143.research_yield: The pilot unit would support articles on the eastern field armies (Or. V–IX) and the court ranks. The wider text would support work on the Pontic limes (Or. XXXVIII, extending Lomouri), the Lower Danube against Malein's 1904 notes, fabricae and scholae, insignia as iconography, and dating debates (Mekhamadiev).
item_143.recommendation: Keep it at priority 3 and drop the "untranslated" framing. Russian has only Malein's excerpts (Or. XIII, XXVI, XXXIX). English now has a complete AI translation from the 1552 print, and Spanish has a full translation (2007). The best first unit is still Pars Orientis chs. I–IX, translated from Seeck with commentary on the units. Credit and avoid duplicating Malein's chapters.

item_144.ru_found: Only one Russian translation was found: N. A. Fedorov (Фёдоров), Servius commentary in «Вергилий. Энеида. С комментариями Сервия» (Moscow: Лабиринт, 2001; Aeneid text tr. S. Osherov). It covers only an excerpt of the Book 1 commentary. This is confirmed by ru.wikipedia «Сервий» and the readli.net book page, and the ancientrome.ru page serv1.htm is Book 1 only (that site refused connections on every attempt). No Russian translation of the Aen. 6 commentary was found. Limitation: the shared WebSearch budget was used up before my first query ran, so none of the required Russian searches happened (elibrary, cyberleninka, ВДИ, Philologia Classica, RSL catalogue). Journal excerpts or dissertation translations of Aen. 6 notes therefore cannot be ruled out.
item_144.en_found: The only scholarly English translation is of Book 4: McDonough, Prior & Stansbury, Bolchazy-Carducci 2002. Its BMCR review mentions no other English translation of Servius. For Aen. 6 itself, an English translation already exists but is not scholarly. Source Library (sourcelibrary.org, Embassy of the Free Mind, Amsterdam) hosts an AI English translation of the full Thilo–Hagen vol. II (Aen. 6–12), labelled "AI translation, not yet reviewed by a scholar" and licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. Its page for Aen. 6.1 is at /book/servius-in-vergilii-carmina-commentarii-vol-ii-thilo-hagen-servius/page/69af2334f98f6eff774cdd82, and the site also has vol. I (Aen. 1–5) and vol. III. The colleague also cites a rough complete e-book from Mitologia.pt (2024), which I did not re-check. So no scholarly English translation of Aen. 6 was found, but the unit has already been translated by machine.
item_144.other_found: FRENCH, THE UNIT ITSELF (this refutes the colleague's "no modern translation"): Emmanuelle Jeunet-Mancy, Servius, Commentaire sur l'Énéide de Virgile, Livre VI. Critical text, French translation and commentary, Collection des Universités de France (Budé), Paris: Les Belles Lettres, 2012. This is listed on de.wikipedia «Maurus Servius Honoratus», and I also know it independently. OTHER CUF VOLUMES: Livre IV, J.-Y. Guillaumin, 2019; Livre VIII, G. Ramires & M. Lafond, 2022; Livre I, D. Vallat & M. Béjuis-Vallat, 2023. Also A. Baudou & S. Clément-Tarantino, «À l'école de Virgile» (Septentrion, 2015), a French translation of the Aen. 1 commentary. ITALIAN: G. Ramires published editions of Aen. 9 (Pàtron 1996) and Aen. 7 (2003), both with the DServ additions; I did not verify whether they include a translation. Nothing on Aen. 6 was found. GERMAN and SPANISH: none found, but not properly searched. LATIN EDITIONS: Harvard Servius covers Aen. 1–2 (1946) and 3–5 (1965), and Murgia–Kaster (OUP 2018) covers Aen. 9–12, so Aen. 6 has no Harvard volume.
item_144.source_text: Thilo–Hagen, Servii grammatici qui feruntur in Vergilii carmina commentarii, vol. II (Aen. 6–12), Leipzig: Teubner, 1884, public domain. Aen. 6 starts on p. 15. Scans: archive.org; also sourcelibrary.org, whose OCR is complete. The Latin text is online at Perseus (Thilo, Perseus:text:1999.02.0053), which includes the Book 6 commentary. Perseus texts are usually CC BY-SA, but I did not see a licence on the page. The current critical edition of Aen. 6 is Jeunet-Mancy's CUF volume (2012), which is in copyright. Use it only to check readings and to separate Servius from the DServ layer; it must not be reproduced.
item_144.research_yield: First Russian Servius on Aen. 6 enables: late-antique eschatology and Neoplatonism in a grammarian (vs Macrobius); Donatus/DServ layer on Roman ritual and religion; Sibyl/golden bough lore; fragments of Varro and lost authors; a comparison of the AI and CUF translations as a methods piece.
item_144.recommendation: Keep for Russian, which is still unverified but probably untranslated, but drop the claim that it is untranslated in English or modern languages. Aen. 6 has a scholarly French Budé translation (2012) and an online AI English translation. Best first unit: Servius + DServ on Aen. 6.1–263 from Thilo (PD), checked against Jeunet-Mancy.

The only Russian translation it lists is the Ars minor (Донат. Краткая наука о частях речи, пер. М. С. Петровой, Диалог со временем 1/99, ИВИ РАН 1999, с. 306–334), plus the 16th-c. item_145.en_found: en.wikipedia 'Aelius Donatus' (fetched) says of the Terence commentary: 'It has never been translated to English as parts are missing from the original manuscript' and 'It has partially been translated to German.' No English searches ran (budget exhausted). Unverified possibility to check: an English translation of the prefatory theory texts (Evanthius 'De fabula' / Donatus 'De comoedia') in classical/medieval literary-criticism anthologies such as Preminger–Hardison–Kerrane, Classical and Medieval Literary Criticism (1974). Even if it exists, it covers only the general preface, not the Adelphoe commentary. I found no evidence of an English translation of the Adelphoe commentary.

Confirmed by fr.wikipedia 'Aelius Donatus' (fetched). en.wikipedia also links it (http://hyperdonat.ens-lyon.fr/; now hyperdonat.huma-num.fr). item_145.source_text: P. Wessner, Aeli Donati quod fertur Commentum Terenti, Teubner, Leipzig 1902–1908. Vol. 1: praefationes, Andria, Eunuchus. Vol. 2 (1905): Adelphoe, Hecyra, Phormio. Vol. 3: Eugraphius/scholia Bembina. It is public domain (Wessner d. 1933), and scans should be on archive.org / Google Books; I could not confirm an exact URL because guessed archive.org IDs returned 404. The HyperDonat online Latin text is probably based on Wessner but its license is unchecked. For Adelphoe the standard modern text is still Wessner. The recent Andria edition (Cioffi 2017, De Gruyter) is in copyright.
item_145.research_yield: Donatus on Adelphoe is a basis for articles on: Roman staging and actor delivery (pronuntiatio, gesture); Menander comparisons and Greek models; colloquial Latin; ethos and characterisation (Micio/Demea, education debate); late-antique school exegesis; Renaissance reception of comic theory.
item_145.recommendation: Keep as a strong Russian and English first-translation candidate. Before committing, check on HyperDonat whether Adelphoe already has a French translation, and run the Russian searches that could not be done here (e.g. 'Донат комментарий Теренций', 'Эванфий О комедии'). Best first unit: the preface to Adelphoe (praefatio) plus the Act 1 notes (~8k words), from Wessner vol. 2 (1905).

item_146.ru_found:
This partly refutes the claim that Russian has nothing. There is no full or partial Russian translation, but Russian excerpts exist. None of them touch the Ars poetica.

(1) VERIFIED excerpts. В. В. Латышев, «Известия древних писателей греческих и латинских о Скифии и Кавказе», т. II (Latin authors, 1904), pp. 32–34, section «Схолиасты Горация: Помпоний Порфирион». Text is from Holder 1894, with Latin and Russian on facing pages. It has 14 lemmata, all on Odes and Epodes: Od. 1.35.9 and 1.35.40; 2.13.8; 2.20.16; 3.4.34; 3.10.1; 3.24.9; 3.29.28; 4.14.42; 4.15.24; Epod. 3.9, 5.21 and 16.58 (Scythians, Colchis, Hyperboreans, Tanais, Medea). I checked these in the archive.org OCR (archive.org/details/Latyshev2). The project crosscheck says this volume was reprinted in ВДИ 1949. The same section also translates Scholia Vindobonensia on Ars poetica 118 and 124. Those are not Porphyrio.
(2) Russian scholarship quotes Porphyrio in Latin and paraphrases him. М. М. Позднев, «"Почтенный Ахилл" — герой двух "поэтик"», Philologia Classica 2015 (cyberleninka), quotes the scholium on Ars poetica 120 in Latin and glosses only «reponis». It is not a translation and cites none.
(3) Negative checks:
- ru.wikipedia «Помпоний Порфирион» lists only the Brockhaus–Efron entry and the Latin text on horatius.net.
- Earlier project checks found horatius.net/ru gives Porphyrio in Latin only. CyberLeninka API queries (Порфирион Гораций, схолии Гораций) and a CrossRef query in Russian turned up nothing more.
- ancientrome.ru refused connection this session.
CAVEAT: the WebSearch budget for the session was already used up. Both searches attempted here (RU: «Порфирион комментарий к Горацию перевод»; EN: «Porphyrio commentary Horace English translation») were refused, so the required 4+4 searches could not be run. Evidence comes from direct page fetches, archive.org primary texts and earlier project verification. Not checked: Гаспаров's notes to the Ars poetica (likely a one-line paraphrase of the Neoptolemus note), elibrary and the RSL catalogue.
item_146.en_found:
I found no English translation, whole or partial, of Porphyrio or of his Ars poetica section.
- en.wikipedia 'Pomponius Porphyrion' lists only the editions (Hauthal 1864, Meyer 1874, Holder 1894).
- The Perseus catalogue (phi1512) lists only Meyer's Latin.
- attalus.org and tertullian.org list no Porphyrio.
- Roger Pearse's blog (2013, 2019) says no translation exists.
- Zetzel's review of Kalinina (BMCR 2009.02.06) mentions none.
- Earlier project checks of CrossRef, Open Library, archive.org and the BMCR search found only editions and studies: Diederich 1999, Kalinina 2007, Breuer 2019, Oakley 2023, Jacobson CQ 2012.
Single notes, especially the Neoptolemus note on Ars poetica 1, are very probably quoted and translated in studies of the Ars poetica (Brink-type commentaries, work on Neoptolemus). That would be excerpt level only, and I verified no such item this session because no web search was available.
item_146.other_found:
None found in French, German, Italian or Spanish, as either a full translation or a translation of the Ars poetica section. Only studies with embedded passage translations turned up:
- Italian: C. Formenti, 'Riassunti delle odi nei commenti oraziani di Porfirione e Pseudo-Acrone', in Epitome (MOM Éditions 2020). It gives Italian renderings of the introductory notes to the Odes, not the Ars poetica. Also Mastellone Iovane 1998, and Longobardi 2017 (ETS, on scholia to the Odes).
- it.wikipedia lists no translation.
- German: Diederich 1999 and Kalinina 2007 are monographs, not translations. de.wikipedia lists only the Meyer and Holder editions.
- Spanish: C. Amado Román, Fortunatae 36.2 (2022), covers scholia on Odes 1.4, 4.7 and 4.12 and gives excerpts. Dialnet items on the humanist reception of the Ars poetica scholia are studies.
- French: nothing found.
Unpublished theses could not be checked.
item_146.source_text:
Public-domain sources:
- Holder, Pomponi Porfyrionis Commentum in Horatium Flaccum (Scholia antiqua in Q. Horatium Flaccum I, Innsbruck: Wagner 1894). This is still the standard critical edition; the Olms 1967 and Arno reprints are facsimiles. archive.org/details/scholiaantiqvai00kellgoog is flagged NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT.
- Meyer, Teubner 1874: archive.org/details/pomponiiporphyri00pomp (NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT). The Ars poetica commentary is at pp. 344–359.
- Hauthal 1864–66 is also public domain.
No newer complete critical edition exists; Kalinina 2007 is a study. So the standard edition is out of copyright, but the edition team should confirm that no new critical edition has appeared.
Digital Latin texts are also on horatius.net and digilibLT. Their licences are unclear, so use them for checking only.
SIZE CORRECTION: the Ars poetica section is about 4,750 OCR tokens including apparatus, so about 3,500–4,000 Latin words, not the sweep's 8–10k. The whole commentary is about 111k OCR tokens, about 80–90k words. Rough per-book figures: Epistles II about 11k tokens, Odes I about 13.5k, Satires I about 19k.
item_146.recommendation: Keep, but correct the record. Russian has only Latyshev's Odes and Epodes excerpts, and nothing exists in Russian or English for the Ars poetica. Since the Ars poetica section is only about 4k words, publish it as the pilot and extend the unit to Porphyrio on Epistles II, about 12k words in total for the literary epistles.

item_147.other_found: Italian, Book 1 only: Tiberio Claudio Donato, Interpretationes Vergilianae. Libro I. Edizione critica, traduzione e commento, ed. Luigi Pirovano (Bologna: Pàtron 2025, 481 pp.), confirmed on Pirovano's unibo publications page. The it.wikipedia and de.wikipedia articles (both fetched) list no modern translations. Their bibliographies give only studies: Squillante Saccone 1985, Starr 1992, Pirovano 2006, Jakobi and Gärtner in ZPE 118 (1997), and Landis 2009. item_147.source_text: Public-domain text: H. Georgii, Tiberi Claudi Donati ... Interpretationes Vergilianae, Teubner, Leipzig 1905 (vol. I, Aen. 1–6, which includes Book 4) and 1906 (vol. II). Scans are on archive.org (linked from en.wikipedia), and there is a Teubner reprint of 1969. Caveat: de.wikipedia says Georgii is outdated by numerous new manuscript finds but has still not been replaced ("veraltet ... aber immer noch nicht ersetzt"). The 1997 ZPE articles on the "neuer TCD" show that textual problems remain, so Book 4 would need a light check against the later manuscript literature. Copyright: the only modern critical edition, Pirovano 2025, is in copyright and covers Book 1 only, so Book 4 can be translated from Georgii without any copyright conflict.
item_147.research_yield: Possible articles: Donatus's defence of Aeneas in the Dido episode, reading the poem as praise (laudatio); Donatus versus Servius on Aeneid 4; late-antique rhetorical reading practices; the Renaissance reception of Donatus; the first Russian introduction to the author.
item_147.recommendation: Keep it: no Russian or English translation of any book has turned up, and only Book 1 exists in Italian. Start with Book 4 (Dido) from Georgii 1905 vol. I, or a sub-unit such as Aen. 4.1–392 (about 15–20k words) for the pilot. Before release, check Latyshev's Aen. 4.366–367 excerpt and the English excerpts in Starr 1992.

item_148.ru_found: I found no Russian translation, but I could not run the required Russian searches: the shared web-search limit for this turn ran out before my first query, so neither of my two searches executed. Direct fetches: ru.wikisource 'Децим Юний Ювенал' lists only Minaev's partial versions of the Satires and Pushkin's Sat. X sketches, with no scholia or vitae. ancientrome.ru returned connection errors three times and could not be checked. From memory, not verified: the Russian Juvenal translations (Nedovich and Petrovsky, 1937; later reprints) use the scholia in their notes but do not translate them. Still unchecked: elibrary/ВДИ/Philologia Classica articles that may translate single scholia, such as Sat. 4 and the Statius fragment.
item_148.en_found: No full or partial translation found. Only isolated excerpts exist. (1) Roger Pearse, blog post of 2 May 2020 ('More thoughts on the scholia vetustiora of Juvenal'): an informal English version of the first scholion, on Sat. 1.1 (vita and exile material). (2) Anna McCullough's English rendering of the gloss on Sat. 6.251 ('gladiatrix'), quoted by Pearse, 2 May 2020. (3) Pearse's English versions of the Vitae Iuvenalis, for example Jahn III (Jan 2021); the Vita is also in Ramsay's Loeb (1918) and Courtney (2013). The Vita is a separate text, not the scholia. (4) From memory, not verified: the De bello Germanico fragment of Statius, quoted in schol. 4.94, has an English translation in Shackleton Bailey's Loeb Statius (2003). Negative evidence: Pearse wrote in 2011 that 'the scholia could usefully be translated', and in 2013 he wished they existed in English. Zetzel's review (BMCR 2012.03.42) of Grazzini's recentiora edition mentions no translation of either corpus. None of Pearse's later posts on Juvenal (to 2021) report one.
item_148.other_found: None found, but French, German, Italian and Spanish could not be searched because the search limit ran out. As far as I know there is no Budé, Tusculum or Valla translation of the scholia. Grazzini (Pisa: Edizioni della Normale, 2011; vol. 2 later) is a Latin-only critical edition of the later Carolingian scholia (the recentiora), not a translation.
item_148.source_text: Standard edition: P. Wessner, Scholia in Iuvenalem vetustiora (Leipzig: Teubner, 1931; Stuttgart reprint 1967). Wessner died 11 May 1933 (confirmed on de.wikipedia). The text is therefore public domain in Russia and the EU (70 years after the author's death). It is a 1931 publication, so it should enter the US public domain on 1 Jan 2027. Fully public-domain alternatives: O. Jahn, D. Iunii Iuvenalis Saturarum libri V cum scholiis veteribus (Berlin, 1851). Also an 1839 edition of the 'scholia vetera' on Google Books (id=5y4IAQAAMAAJ), cited by Pearse. These are pre-critical, so use them only as a backup. Manuscript images: St Gall, Sangallensis 870 on e-codices; the Montpellier manuscript (Pithoeanus) via Bibliotheca Laureshamensis. Whether a scan of Wessner is online (archive.org) was not verified. Grazzini's recentiora (2011) is in copyright but is a different corpus.
item_148.research_yield: Possible articles: Domitian's council and the turbot (Sat. 4) with Statius' De bello Germanico fragment; the ancient tradition of Juvenal's exile in the Vita and scholion 1.1; the 'gladiatrix' gloss and women in the arena; late antique school commentary compared with Servius and Donatus; Flavian prosopography and realia.
item_148.recommendation: Keep. The 'untranslated' claim held up in every source I could check; the English side is solid, and the Russian side and other languages need re-checking once searches are available. Best first unit: the scholia on Satires 1 and 4 (vita/exile material and Domitian's council), then Sat. 6. Work from Wessner 1931, checking against Jahn 1851.

item_149.ru_found: Confirmed: only Paul the Deacon's epitome has a Russian translation, by A. A. Pavlov. Selected glosses appeared in ВДИ 2012 №2, pp. 230–268, and a book followed: Павел Диакон, «Эпитома сочинения Секста Помпея Феста „О значении слов“», translated with introduction and commentary by Pavlov (Сыктывкар: Изд-во СыктГУ, 2012, 300 pp.). Both are cited on ru.wikipedia under «Секст Помпей Фест». Paulus covers every letter, so Russian readers already have the abridged M entries. I found no Russian translation of Festus' own Farnesianus text. ru.wikipedia «Веррий Флакк» cites no translations either. Caveat: the shared WebSearch budget ran out before my first query, so I ran none of the required 4 Russian searches. ancientrome.ru refused connections, and I did not query search pages on cyberleninka, elibrary or the RSL catalogue. Two things remain unchecked: whether Pavlov later translated Festus proper, and whether isolated Festus glosses appear in Russian in sourcebooks or monographs.
item_149.en_found: No human scholarly English translation has been published. ACLS Fellowship 2026, B. W. Fortson (Univ. of Michigan), 'Festus Project', is described as the "first-ever full English translation and commentary" (acls.org/fellow-grantees/benjamin-w-fortson/), so a scholarly English version is coming. The colleague missed a refutation: Source Library (sourcelibrary.org, Embassy of the Free Mind, Amsterdam; Gemini-based OCR and translation; CC BY-SA 4.0) has an AI English translation of Thewrewk's 1889 edition, 621 of 640 pages done. It includes Book XII (M), with headwords such as Mamercus, Mamuri Veturi and Mamilia turris. Each page is labelled "AI translation, not yet reviewed by a scholar". URL: https://sourcelibrary.org/book/festus-de-verborum-significatu-thewrewk-ed-festus. The same site also has an AI translation of Egger's 1838 Paris edition, 660 of 676 pages: /book/m-verrii-flacci-fragmenta-et-sexti-pompei-festi-de-verborum-festus. Beyond these, there are probably scattered excerpts in sourcebooks (religion, law, Roman historians), but I could not check them because WebSearch was unavailable.
item_149.other_found: French, complete: Aug. Savagner, 'Sextus Pompeius Festus, De la signification des mots', Paris: Panckoucke 1846. The site calls it the first French translation, and it follows K. O. Müller's 1839 text, which includes Paulus. It is online at remacle.org/bloodwolf/erudits/Festus/ (verified: the M page gives French renderings of Farnesianus entries such as Matronae, Mundus, Manalis fons, Municipalia sacra, Mater Matuta and Maximus praetor). German: P. Pieroni 2004 (Peter Lang), an introduction and partial commentary on Lindsay 154,19–186,29 (cited on de.wikipedia; I did not check whether it includes a German translation). Italian: A. Di Marco 2021 (Olms), a study with a sample critical text of letter O (translation not verified). No Italian or Spanish full translation is cited on it/de/en Wikipedia. The colleague's Portuguese USP thesis is still unverified.
item_149.source_text: Lindsay, W. M., Sexti Pompei Festi De verborum significatu quae supersunt cum Pauli epitome (Teubner, Leipzig 1913; Olms reprint 1965). This is still the standard edition and is public domain (Lindsay died 1937; HathiTrust record 008900043). Also public domain: Thewrewk de Ponor, Budapest 1889, Pars I, scanned at archive.org/details/deverborumsignif00festuoft and transcribed on sourcelibrary.org; and Müller 1839/1880, which Savagner used. No copyrighted modern critical edition replaces Lindsay. Restorations of the damaged codex must still be marked.
item_149.research_yield: Letter M is unusually rich for Roman religion (mundus, Manalis lapis, Mater Matuta, municipalia sacra, minora templa, muta exta, auspicia, Mamuri Veturi) and for early-Republic magistracies (maximus praetor, maior consul). It also preserves Verrius' sources (Messala, Ateius Capito, Veranius), which supports source-criticism and Festus-versus-Paulus abridgment studies.
item_149.recommendation: Keep it only as a Russian-first project. The English "first translation" claim no longer holds: an unreviewed AI English version is online (Source Library) and Fortson's scholarly translation is coming. Best first unit: Festus' own Farnesianus entries of letter M, set beside Pavlov's Paulus, with supplements marked.

item_150.title_short: Varro, De lingua Latina (Books V–VII; pilot Book VI or V)
item_150.ru_found:
I could not refute the claim, but I could only check it in a limited way. The session's WebSearch budget was used up (limit reached before my first query), so none of the required RU/EN searches could run. Direct fetches of ancientrome.ru, philology.ru, simposium.ru, search.rsl.ru and philol.msu.ru failed (connection reset or DNS). I therefore checked the ru.wikipedia article «Марк Теренций Варрон» through the API (wikitext) and scanned related ru.wiki and uk.wiki articles and ru.wikiquote.
Confirmed Russian translations:
(1) Я. М. Боровский, excerpts from VIII, IX and X only: VIII 1–7, 9–23; IX 1–5, 37–41 etc.; X 3, 7, 9–10 etc. Published in «Античные теории языка и стиля», М.–Л.: Соцэкгиз 1936, pp. 80–83, 94–104, 120; reprinted СПб.: Алетейя 1996, pp. 85–88, 99–110, 118, 127.
(2) В. В. Каракулакова (ru.wiki spells it Каракулаков), «О латинском языке [отрывок]», Вопросы теории языкознания, Калинин 1975, pp. 72–87. It is 16 pages and its books are unidentified. She also wrote the 1969 study «Марк Теренций Варрон и его место в истории языкознания» (cited on uk.wiki). Because her topic is linguistic theory, the 1975 excerpt may contain the theoretical passages of V.1–10 or VI.35–40. This is the main unresolved risk for the unit.
No full or partial Russian translation of Books V–VII was found. Still to check: the 1975 Kalinin volume; Хрестоматия по истории Древнего Рима (1962/1987), which may contain topographical excerpts from Book V; recent journals (ΣΧΟΛΗ, Philologia Classica, Аристей, ИЯиКФ).

Online text: thelatinlibrary.com/varro.ll5.html, ll6.html and ll7.html, all reachable. My counts: Book V about 11.1k Latin words, VI about 6.3k, VII about 5.4k, so V–VII total about 23k, a little below the colleague's 25–30k estimate.
